question: What does استشهدوا ask the parties to do?

positions.position: Istashhidū means obtain or call witnesses.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): Al-Ṭabarī prefers that the verse obligates an already appointed witness to perform testimony before an authority or judge who can secure the right owed. TAB-FULL (author): Al-Ṭabarī reasons that “the witnesses” names identifiable people already entrusted with testimony, as established by the earlier command to appoint them; it cannot mean everyone merely capable of witnessing. TAB-FULL (author): Al-Ṭabarī says an initial request to witness is obligatory only when no other suitable witness is available, by broader duties to preserve a fellow Muslim's right, not by this verse itself. TAB-FULL (author): Written documentation makes testimony more accurate because it preserves the parties' exact acknowledged words, keeps witnesses' accounts aligned, and makes judgment clearer; obeying God's command is itself more just than abandoning it. TAB-FULL (author): Writing every debt, large or small, makes the transaction more just, gives witnesses a sounder basis, and helps prevent doubt about the amount and due date. TAB-FULL (مجاهد): Mujāhid says a requester harms a busy scribe or witness by insisting “fear God, you were commanded” when other people can be found; they need not interrupt their work or feel pressured. TAB-FULL (author): The command is to appoint two witnesses over one's rights; “your men” means free Muslim men, excluding slaves and free non-Muslims. TAB-FULL (سفيان بن عيينة): Some readers of the light-kāf form interpret the two women's testimony together as equivalent to one man's, so each woman makes the other a “male” witness; this is reported from Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah. TAB-FULL (قتادة): Qatāda urges reliance on God's assurance in documenting rights: writing protects property, benefits the pious, and makes even a wicked debtor more likely to pay because witnesses exist. TAB-FULL (قتادة): Qatāda says the clause forbids refusing an initial request to witness rights; he recounts a man calling through a large encampment with no one answering, and reads the verse as testifying for one person against another. TAB-FULL (الشعبي): Al-Shaʿbī says answering an initial request is optional when others are available, but obligatory if no other witness can be found. IBNABIHATIM (الربيع): The verse was revealed after people declined to help someone who went around seeking witnesses; Qatada reports similarly. FARISI-HUJJA (author): أن تضل cannot attach directly to استشهدوا شهيدين; the following alternative of one man and two women signals an omitted command to call those witnesses. THALABI (author): The sīn in استشهدوا marks a request: call for two witnesses. MAWARDI-FULL (author): The writing makes doubt less likely either about the debtor denying what is owed or about a witness erring. WAHIDI-BASIT (author): Istashhidū means ashhidū, to call someone as witness; the saying that people testify but are not istushhidūn is explained as saying that they do not testify. WAHIDI-BASIT (author): Written records make testimony more reliable because they remind witnesses, instead of leaving them to impressions; aqwam means more fully upright, and adnā means closer to removing doubt about amount and term. WAHIDI-WAJIZ (author): Writing is fairest before God, makes testimony more reliable because the record reminds witnesses, and best prevents doubt about amount or due date. JISHUMI (author): The instruction is to seek witnesses and have them testify to the written record; two men suffice generally, except that adultery requires four. JISHUMI (author): Some reject interpreting the call as bearing testimony because the people have not yet become witnesses; Jishumi answers that the command to seek two witnesses makes them witnesses. KASHSHAF-FULL (author): Seek two male witnesses from believing men; most scholars require witnesses to be Muslim, free, and adult. IBNATIYYA-FULL (عكرمة): ʿIkrima reads the first rāʾ with kasra and makes “scribe” and “witness” accusative, so that the rights-holder is forbidden to begin harming them. TABRISI (الزجاج): Al-Zajjāj says the first reading is clearer because deliberate falsification makes someone a wrongdoer more plausibly than summoning a busy witness does. RAZI-FULL (author): Accepting testimony is already included in the command to appoint two witnesses, so reading the later command as performance gives it a distinct legal function; concealing testimony is separately forbidden. | mentions 2:283 RAZI-FULL (author): Al-Razi rejects that interpretation as contrary to the general exegetical view: without a man, women’s testimony is not accepted, so the second woman does not simply make the first a witness. RAZI-FULL (ابن عباس ومقاتل والربيع): Ibn ʿAbbas, Muqatil, and al-Rabiʿ say the wali is the creditor, but al-Razi rejects this because a claimant’s assertion alone would make documentation and witnesses pointless. RAZI-FULL (author): The purpose of witnesses is to let the creditor establish the claim if the debtor later denies it; istashhidu means make someone testify, and shahidayn means two witnesses. QURTUBI-FULL (author): Seeking witnesses is recommended, not obligatory, as al-Qurṭubī explains later. QURTUBI-FULL (author): Because testimony is a grave authority that makes another person liable, God requires approved and upright witnesses with distinguishing qualities. QURTUBI-FULL (قتادة والربيع وابن عباس): Qatāda, al-Rabīʿ, and Ibn ʿAbbās interpret the summons as a request to bear witness and enter it in writing. QURTUBI-FULL (مجاهد): Mujāhid interprets the summons as a request to give testimony already held; he and others say an initial invitation to witness may be declined. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): “Seek two witnesses” is a request for testimony or equivalent to “make two witnesses”; shahīd is intensive, suggesting experienced witnesses whose repeated use indicates acceptance and integrity. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): “Among witnesses whom you approve” most likely modifies “seek witnesses,” applying approval to all combinations; adjective and substitution analyses are weak. SAMIN-DURR (author): استشهدوا may retain the request sense of استفعل, or استفعل may mean أفعل, as in استعجل/أعجل and استيقن/أيقن. SAMIN-DURR (author): من رجالكم may attach to استشهدوا with من marking source, or be an adjective of شهيدين with partitive من. SAMIN-DURR (أبو البقاء): Abu al-Baqa notes that an accusative reading would imply فاستشهدوا. SAMIN-DURR (الشيخ): The Sheikh attaches ممن ترضون directly to استشهدوا so the qualification applies to every witness; its late position signals this scope. IBNKATHIR-FULL (author): Other reports condemn witnesses who testify before being asked, whose oaths and testimony precede each other, or who testify without a request; these are false witnesses. BIQAI-FULL (author): Writing and testimony are not automatically linked, so the verse separately directs people to seek two witnesses, with the word shahid emphasizing established insight and experience. DURR-FULL (ابن عباس): Debt should be witnessed to prevent denial or forgetting; someone who refuses a needed request to testify despite holding evidence disobeys, while a requester must not burden a scribe or witness when another is available. ITQAN (author): One explanation takes the dual phrase as covering two or more by naming the minimum; the better analysis makes the pronoun refer back to the two witnesses already mentioned without qualification. ALUSI-FULL (أبو حيان): The phrase 'from those you approve' can modify the male-and-female pair, the two male witnesses, or all solicited witnesses; Abū Ḥayyān attaches it to 'seek witnesses,' which al-Alusi says awkwardly separates the women's provision from its rationale. ALUSI-FULL (author): Istashhidū means request two people to bear witness to the transaction; alternatively its extra sīn and tāʾ may be redundant and mean simply 'witness.' The intensive noun suggests experienced, capable witnesses and may hint at recognized reliability. ALUSI-FULL (author): The command to seek witnesses is considered recommended or obligatory according to the broader disagreement over these commands. ALUSI-FULL (author): If two men are not sought, the alternatives can be parsed elliptically as one man and two women testifying, serving as witnesses, or being requested as witnesses. ALUSI-FULL (author): Other analyses make the exception detached from both writing and witnessing, or attach it to both; al-Alusi favors the first analysis. ELMALILI (author): Justice is also required by the instruction in 65:2 to appoint two just witnesses from among you. | mentions 65:2 ELMALILI (author): For any sale, including a cash sale, make it openly in the presence of witnesses rather than secretly; this precaution protects property and legal security. ELMALILI (author): Qatada relates that the verse was revealed after a man went from camp to camp seeking a witness and no one paid attention. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The documentation rule extends to all transactions for which parties seek written records and witnesses. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Istashhidū can mean simply have witnesses, with the s and t adding emphasis, or request two witnesses, making the creditor responsible for seeking testimony. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The creditor’s request is within a person’s capacity; the following ban on refusing then addresses the person asked to witness. IBNASHUR-FULL (أبو حنيفة): The author applies the earlier disagreement about scribes: accepting the request to bear witness becomes individual when designated, and giving testimony is individually obligatory if it causes no bodily or financial harm; Abū Ḥanīfa makes performance communal unless uniquely required, subject to court integrity, proximity, admissibility, and a claimant’s request.

question: Must a debt have witnesses as well as writing?

positions.position: Witnesses are an additional safeguard for deferred debt.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (الحسن والشعبي): Al-Ḥasan and al-Shaʿbī treat witnessing at sale as recommended or optional, citing the permission to rely on trust. | mentions 2:283 TAB-FULL (author): Al-Ṭabarī rules that witnessing every purchase and sale is an obligatory duty, because divine commands bind unless evidence shows a recommendation; he rejects abrogation by the trust clause. | mentions 2:283 IBNABIHATIM (ابن عباس): Writing and witnessing debts prevents denial and forgetfulness; one who fails to witness has disobeyed. NAHHAS (الفراء): Some say recording deferred debts and witnessing sales are recommendations, by analogy with commands that grant permission after a prohibition. | mentions 2:282 NAHHAS (عبد الله بن عمر): Ibn Umar says witnessing is obligatory for every sale, large or small, citing the command to witness sales. | mentions 2:282 THALABI (الضحاك ومحمد بن جرير): Al-Dahhak treats witnessing as a firm divine command for every transaction, small or large and cash or deferred; Muhammad ibn Jarir prefers this view. THALABI (آخرون): Other scholars treat witnessing sales as recommended, leaving the parties free to call witnesses or not. MAWARDI-FULL (الضحاك وداود بن علي): Witnessing sales is obligatory. MAWARDI-FULL (الحسن والشعبي ومالك والشافعي): Witnessing sales is recommended. WAHIDI-BASIT (عطاء وابن جريج وإبراهيم وابن جرير): A group, chosen by Ibn Jarīr, treat writing and witnessing deferred debts as obligatory to protect wealth and deter denial; Ibrāhīm says even a tiny handful of greens should be documented. WAHIDI-WAJIZ (author): After prohibiting usury, God permits forward-credit sales and commands writing and witnessing deferred debts to protect property; the trust exception in 2:283 abrogates this command. | mentions 2:283 WAHIDI-WAJIZ (author): An immediate exchange of goods is exempt from writing because the risks of delayed payment are absent; witnessing spot sales is also no longer obligatory under the abrogated ruling. JISHUMI (الشعبي): Al-Shaʿbī reports that writing, witnessing, and pledging were once obligatory and were abrogated by the following verse’s allowance when parties trust each other; Jishumi prefers the view that writing is recommended as a means of securing rights. | mentions 2:283 JISHUMI (الحسن والشافعي): Al-Ḥasan and al-Shāfiʿī regard witnessing sales as recommended, which Jishumi says is the jurists’ position. JISHUMI (الضحاك): Al-Ḍaḥḥāk considers witnessing a sale obligatory. JISHUMI (author): The term must be known: that is the force of specified, and an unknown term defeats the purpose of writing and witnessing. JISHUMI (author): Writing and witnessing are guidance and recommendation, not obligation, since a creditor may waive the right itself and need not document it as a precaution. BAGHAWI-FULL (author): Some consider writing obligatory, but most deem the command recommendatory; al-Shaʿbi says writing, witnessing, and pledging were obligatory then abrogated by the trust provision. | mentions 2:283 BAGHAWI-FULL (الشعبي): Al-Shaʿbi holds that writing, witnessing, and pledging were initially obligatory and that the instruction to fulfill a trusted deposit abrogated all three. | mentions 2:283 BAGHAWI-FULL (الضحاك): He considers witnessing a binding command for both small and large transactions, cash or credit; Abu Saʿid al-Khudri leaves it to mutual trust, while others call it recommended. | mentions 2:283 KASHSHAF-FULL (الضحاك): Al-Ḍaḥḥāk considers witnessing obligatory even for a bunch of greens. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): The sound view is that witnessing makes a transaction prudent while mutual trust leaves room; no abrogation follows, because documentation is recommended as a precaution for rights people may waive, and 2:283 instructs debtors to repay when trusted. | mentions 2:283 IBNATIYYA-FULL (الحسن والشعبي): Al-Ḥasan, al-Shaʿbī, and others say witnessing a transaction is recommended; Ibn ʿAmr and al-Ḍaḥḥāk say it is obligatory, followed by Ibn ʿUmar's practice and ʿAṭāʾ, with al-Ṭabarī preferring obligation. IBNATIYYA-FULL (القاضي أبو محمد): Ibn ʿAṭiyya finds obligation untenable: witnessing tiny sales is burdensome, while larger dealings may rely on social trust or customary practice. He prefers recommendation unless an excuse prevents it. TABRISI (الحسن وجميع الفقهاء): Al-Ḥasan and the jurists regard witnessing sales as recommended; the Ẓāhirīs make it obligatory. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (author): Witnessing is recommended for transactions where it is customary. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (الجمهور): The majority treat writing debts and witnessing sales or debts as recommended, so the command remains operative without abrogation. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (ابن عمر): A group including Ibn ʿUmar, Abu Musa, Mujahid, Ibn Sirin, and others regard writing and witnessing as obligatory. RAZI-FULL (author): Al-Qaffal takes ذالكم as referring to the commanded writing and witnessing; writing is more just because it is closer to certainty and truth and further from ignorance and falsehood. | mentions 60:8, 49:9, 33:5 RAZI-FULL (عطاء وابن جريج والنخعي والطبري): ʿAtaʾ, Ibn Jurayj, al-Nakhaʿi, and al-Tabari hold that writing and witnessing deferred debts are obligatory; al-Nakhaʿi even requires witnessing a tiny vegetable purchase. QURTUBI-FULL (الطبري): Al-Ṭabarī reads the witnessing command as covering small and large sales; Abū Mūsā, Ibn ʿUmar, and others hold it obligatory, and ʿAṭāʾ demands witnesses for tiny purchases. QURTUBI-FULL (الشعبي والحسن): Al-Shaʿbī and al-Ḥasan treat witnessing as recommendation and guidance rather than a binding duty; Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and other jurists are also said to hold this. QURTUBI-FULL (ابن عطية): Ibn ʿAṭiyya finds mandatory witnessing impractical for small sales and sometimes socially awkward; he treats it as recommended for its usual benefit unless an excuse intervenes. QURTUBI-FULL (الطبري): Al-Ṭabarī rejects abrogation: the pledge clause addresses inability to find a scribe and an unrequired pledge, a different case from writing and witnessing. | mentions 2:283, 4:43, 5:6 QURTUBI-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās says the debt verse is established, not abrogated, and writing, pledges, and witnesses are alternative means of securing debt; witnessing is recommended like pledging. | mentions 2:283 NASAFI-FULL (author): Witnessing sales is recommended for immediate and deferred exchanges as a precaution, or the command concerns immediate trade alone, where testimony suffices without writing. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): The sequence moves from obedience to God's just judgment, to reliable testimony, to eliminating doubt; writing and witnessing reassure the parties. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Witnessing all sales, immediate or deferred, is safer against disagreement; another interpretation limits the command to present trade. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (أبو موسى الأشعري، ابن عمر، الضحاك، ابن المسيب، جابر بن زيد، مجاهد، عطاء، إبراهيم، الشعبي، النخعي، داود بن علي): They hold witnessing obligatory; al-Ḍaḥḥāk requires it even for greens and ʿAṭāʾ for any price. Al-Ṭabarī says an unwitnessed sale defies God's Book. IBNKATHIR-FULL (الجمهور): The majority treats witnessing sales as guidance and recommendation, not obligation; the report of the Prophet's disputed horse purchase and Khuzaima's extraordinary testimony supports this. ALUSI-FULL (author): Writing and witnessing make doubts about a debt’s kind, amount, and maturity less likely; the omitted preposition before an taرتابوا is variously understood as ila, lam, min, or fi. ALUSI-FULL (author): Other analyses make the exception detached from both writing and witnessing, or attach it to both; al-Alusi favors the first analysis. ELMALILI (author): The majority of exegetes regard witnessing a sale here as a recommendation for precaution. IBNASHUR-FULL (جمهور السلف): The majority of early authorities interpret the command to obtain two witnesses as obligatory. IBNASHUR-FULL (مالك): The later majority of jurists, including Mālik, Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Shāfiʿī, and Aḥmad, regard witnessing as recommended; the discussion continues at the command to witness sales. IBNASHUR-FULL (أبو موسى الأشعري): Abū Mūsā, Ibn ʿUmar, Abū Saʿīd, Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, Mujāhid, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿAṭāʾ, Ibn Jurayj, al-Nakhaʿī, Jābir ibn Zayd, Dāwūd, and al-Ṭabarī take witnessing at sales as obligatory. IBNASHUR-FULL (مالك): Al-Ḥasan and al-Shaʿbī, followed by Mālik, Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Shāfiʿī, and Aḥmad, regard witnessing as recommended; they cite the Prophet’s sales without witnesses. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): Writing and witnessing are both required because they complement one another in securing the transaction rather than substitute for one another.

question: Which men qualify as witnesses?

positions.position: The men are qualified members of the believing community.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): The command is to appoint two witnesses over one's rights; “your men” means free Muslim men, excluding slaves and free non-Muslims. TAB-FULL (مجاهد): Mujāhid glosses “your men” as free men. IBNABIHATIM (مجاهد): The two male witnesses must be free men, not slaves. IBNABIHATIM (سعيد بن جبير): The male witnesses must be free Muslims. IBNABIHATIM (ابن عباس): A needed Muslim may not refuse a summons either to give testimony about another witness or to provide testimony already in his possession; al-Hasan says the verse covers both situations. THALABI (مالك والشافعي وأبو حنيفة وسفيان وأكثر الفقهاء): The required male witnesses are free adult Muslims, excluding slaves, minors, and free non-Muslims. THALABI (author): An acceptable witness must meet ten conditions: freedom, adulthood, Islam, uprightness, knowledge of the matter, no personal gain or avoidance of harm, few errors, proper social conduct, no excessive leniency, and no adverse testimony from his slave. THALABI (آخرون): Other scholars treat witnessing sales as recommended, leaving the parties free to call witnesses or not. MAWARDI-FULL (الجمهور): Acceptable witnesses are free, Muslim, upright people. MAWARDI-FULL (شريح وعثمان البتي وأبو ثور): Acceptable Muslim witnesses may be upright even if enslaved. WAHIDI-BASIT (author): The two men are free, adult members of the believers’ community, excluding children and enslaved people. WAHIDI-BASIT (author): The source lists ten qualities for an admissible witness: freedom, adulthood, Islam, uprightness, knowledge, no self-serving interest or self-protective motive, no frequent error, no breach of propriety, and no enmity with the party testified against. WAHIDI-WAJIZ (author): Witnesses are two free adult men of the believers, acceptable for their merit and religion; if one woman forgets, the other reminds her of the testimony. JISHUMI (مجاهد وجماعة من الفقهاء): Mujāhid and many jurists restrict the male witnesses to free, adult Muslims, excluding non-Muslims, slaves, and children. JISHUMI (author): A witness should meet ten qualities: freedom, adulthood, Islam, integrity, knowledge of the testimony, no self-interest or self-protection, few errors, manly virtue, alertness, and not being heedless. BAGHAWI-FULL (author): Most scholars require two free Muslim male witnesses, excluding slaves, children, and unbelievers; Shurayh and Ibn Sirin allow slave testimony. BAGHAWI-FULL (author): A witness must be approved in religion and trustworthiness; seven qualifications are Islam, freedom, sound mind, adulthood, uprightness, social propriety, and absence of suspicion. KASHSHAF-FULL (author): Seek two male witnesses from believing men; most scholars require witnesses to be Muslim, free, and adult. KASHSHAF-FULL (أبو حنيفة): Abū Ḥanīfa permits non-Muslims to testify within their own religious communities. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): The phrase ‘from your men’ excludes unbelievers, children, and women, while its wording includes enslaved men. TABRISI (مجاهد): Mujāhid limits the two male witnesses to free, adult, Muslim men; al-Ṭabrisī rejects freedom as a condition, requiring Islam and probity instead. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (مجاهد): Mujahid says “your men” means free men. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (الزجاج): Al-Zajjaj and Qadi Abu Yaʿla take “your men” to mean Muslims, supported by the verse’s opening address to believers. RAZI-FULL (جمهور الفقهاء المجتهدين): Most jurists treat the commands as recommendations, citing Muslims’ customary deferred sales without records and the hardship obligatory documentation would cause. RAZI-FULL (author): One reading treats the ban on a writer’s refusal as guidance: writing for another Muslim is gratitude for God’s gift of literacy and legal knowledge. | mentions 28:77 RAZI-FULL (author): Min rijalikum is variously read as men of the Muslim community, free men, or men considered fit to testify because of justice. RAZI-FULL (author): The qualification ممن ترضون and the parallel divorce instruction show that not everyone may testify; jurists enumerate ten conditions, including freedom, adulthood, Islam, justice, knowledge, and lack of personal conflict or benefit. | mentions 65:2 QURTUBI-FULL (مجاهد): He says رجالكم means free men; Shurayh, Uthman al-Batti, Ahmad, Ishaq, and Abu Thawr accept an upright slave's testimony, unlike Malik, Abu Hanifa, al-Shafiʿi, and the majority; al-Qurṭubī prefers the majority, while al-Shaʿbi and al-Nakhaʿi permit slaves' testimony in minor matters. QURTUBI-FULL (جمهور): The majority infer that probity is an additional qualification beyond being Muslim, since the verse requires witnesses whom people approve. QURTUBI-FULL (شريح وعثمان البتى وأبو ثور): Shurayḥ, ʿUthmān al-Battī, and Abū Thawr count Muslims as upright witnesses even if enslaved. NASAFI-FULL (author): Two witnesses are sought from believing men; Islam, freedom, and adulthood are conditions, while the author's school accepts non-Muslims testifying among themselves. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Addressing believers as “your men” indicates non-Muslims are not witnesses here; the verse does not address testimony among non-Muslims, which Abū Ḥanīfa allows even across religions. It also indicates adult male witnesses. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Another view requires ten traits: freedom, adulthood, Islam, integrity, knowledge, no personal gain or self-protection, no habitual error, preserved social decency, and no enmity toward the accused. SAMIN-DURR (author): The comparison’s second term is omitted because context supplies it: writing is more equitable, stable, and doubt-free than leaving the debt undocumented. NASHR (حذيفة بن اليمان): Around 30 AH, Ḥudhayfa saw Muslims in Armenia and Azerbaijan disputing whose recitation was more correct and urged ʿUthmān to intervene before they divided like Jews and Christians. BIQAI-FULL (author): The phrase your men implies Muslim witnesses and, by the verse's wording and conditions, free witnesses; the witness must be reliable and accepted. DURR-FULL (سعيد بن جبير): The witnesses should be two free Muslim men or one man and two women; one woman may forget and the other remind her, and witnesses who hold testimony must respond when called. DURR-FULL (مجاهد): Acceptable witnesses are two just, free Muslims. BURSEVI (author): ‘From your men’ means free adult Muslims of your community; in transactions between unbelievers or where the debtor is an unbeliever, unbelievers may be witnesses according to the author’s school. ALUSI-FULL (author): The expression 'from your men' is linked to the command or describes the witnesses partitivally; its address to believers is taken to imply Muslim, adult, male, and free witnesses, based on the customary sense of complete men. ALUSI-FULL (الإمامية): The Imāmīs, along with Shurayḥ, Ibn Sīrīn, Abū Thawr, and ʿUthmān al-Battī, do not require a witness to be free, provided he is Muslim and upright; this differs from the report that ʿAlī rejected slave testimony entirely. ELMALILI (author): The wording “your men” excludes children and non-Muslim men’s testimony against Muslims as sufficient testimony. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Men among you means adult Muslim men: the address is to believers, minors lack judgment to assess the circumstances and suspicions, and the wording of rijāl itself excludes women and boys. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The author argues non-Muslims are excluded because religious difference prevents familiarity with one another’s integrity and duties; earlier religious communities did not clearly guarantee equal rights to outsiders. | mentions 3:75 IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The Qur’an alludes to non-Muslims’ asserted exemption from obligations toward the unlettered, as a reason not to rely on their testimony for Muslims. | mentions 3:75 KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): The requirement for witnesses from among your men means they must be adults and Muslim men; jurists generally exclude non-Muslims from witnessing Muslim legal relations except a dying Muslim's will while travelling, arguing Muslims cannot reliably identify which non-Muslims will protect their rights. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli explained changing theological positions on divine essence and attributes, God's speech, predestination, and free will through changes in time, place, and social environment.

question: May an enslaved man testify?

positions.position: An upright enslaved Muslim may testify
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI-FULL (author): Most scholars require two free Muslim male witnesses, excluding slaves, children, and unbelievers; Shurayh and Ibn Sirin allow slave testimony. BAGHAWI-FULL (شريح وابن سيرين وأنس بن مالك): Most reject slave witnesses, but Shurayh, Ibn Sirin, and Anas allow them; Ibn ʿAbbas rejects children's testimony, and an insane person has no testimony. KASHSHAF-FULL (علي): ʿAlī rules that an enslaved person’s testimony is invalid in any matter. IBNATIYYA-FULL (شريح وإسحاق بن راهويه وأحمد بن حنبل): These jurists allow an enslaved person’s testimony when he is upright, giving priority to the verse’s wording. IBNATIYYA-FULL (مالك والشافعي وأبو حنيفة وجمهور العلماء): They disallow an enslaved person’s testimony, giving priority to the impairment of legal status. RAZI-FULL (شريح وابن سيرين وأحمد): Shurayh, Ibn Sirin, and Ahmad accept an enslaved man’s testimony, arguing that the verse is general and that intellect, religion, and justice—not legal status—prevent lying. RAZI-FULL (author): Al-Razi calls the argument against slave testimony strong, while noting that the general wording can be restricted to people already recognized as qualified witnesses. QURTUBI-FULL (مجاهد): He says رجالكم means free men; Shurayh, Uthman al-Batti, Ahmad, Ishaq, and Abu Thawr accept an upright slave's testimony, unlike Malik, Abu Hanifa, al-Shafiʿi, and the majority; al-Qurṭubī prefers the majority, while al-Shaʿbi and al-Nakhaʿi permit slaves' testimony in minor matters. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (شريح، ابن سيرين، ابن شبرمة، عثمان البتي): They accept a slave's testimony; reports also attribute acceptance to ʿAlī, with Ibrāhīm permitting testimony in trivial matters and Anas saying he knows no one who rejected it.

RAZI-FULL (الشافعي وأبو حنيفة): Al-Shafiʿi and Abu Hanifa reject an enslaved person as a witness, reasoning that the command to attend testimony cannot be obligatory for slaves. QURTUBI-FULL (author): He rejects slave testimony because the address concerns transacting believers, while slaves do not own such assets independently; he also invokes the later restriction on witnesses refusing a summons. QURTUBI-FULL (author): An enslaved person is excluded from the witness class because he cannot independently answer a summons, just as he lacks independent authority in other duties. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الجمهور): The majority, including leading Ḥanafīs, Mālik, and al-Shāfiʿī, reject slave testimony in all matters; this is also narrated from ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, and al-Ḥasan. ALUSI-FULL (الإمامية): The Imāmīs, along with Shurayḥ, Ibn Sīrīn, Abū Thawr, and ʿUthmān al-Battī, do not require a witness to be free, provided he is Muslim and upright; this differs from the report that ʿAlī rejected slave testimony entirely.

question: May children testify?

positions.reasons: IBNABIHATIM (ابن عباس): Children are not acceptable witnesses because they are not among those whose testimony is approved. QURTUBI-FULL (الشافعي وأبو حنيفة وأصحابه): They reject children's testimony because children lack the qualifications of men, approved witnesses, and just adults named elsewhere in scripture. | mentions 5:95 DURR-FULL (ابن عباس): Children's testimony is not admissible because they are not among the witnesses believers approve.

question: Can a blind or mute person testify?

positions.position: The admissibility of blind or mute witnesses depends on the kind of knowledge available.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL (الشافعي وابن أبي ليلى وأبو يوسف): They accept testimony after blindness when the witness already knew the person before losing sight, analogizing the impairment to absence or death; al-Qurṭubī sees no reason to reject testimony previously borne while sighted and accepts public knowledge for lineage. QURTUBI-FULL (author): Some accept a blind person's voice-based testimony as certain, but al-Qurṭubī rejects this because it would imply that a sighted person could likewise rely on sound alone. QURTUBI-FULL (مالك): Malik permits an established voice-based testimony by a blind person, including on divorce; Ibn Qasim reports him accepting testimony from a man who heard his neighbor divorce through a wall, with several early jurists sharing the view. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): The apparent requirement is simply that the two principal witnesses be men; jurists disagree over testimony by a blind witness. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (أبو حنيفة، محمد): They categorically reject testimony by a blind witness; the same view is narrated from ʿAlī, al-Ḥasan, Ibn Jubayr, and Iyās b. Muʿāwiya. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (ابن أبي ليلى، أبو يوسف، الشافعي، زفر، شريح، الشعبي، مالك، الليث): They differ: Ibn Abī Laylā, Abū Yūsuf, and al-Shāfiʿī accept testimony learned before blindness; Zufar permits only lineage; Shurayḥ and al-Shaʿbī accept it generally; Mālik and al-Layth rely on voice recognition in some matters but reject testimony in adultery or false accusation. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Some accept a mute witness through gestures and some reject the testimony; deaf witnesses are rejected for spoken claims but accepted for other sensory matters.

question: When may one man and two women replace two men?
words: فَإِن لَّمْ يَكُونَا رَجُلَيْنِ فَرَجُلٌۭ وَٱمْرَأَتَانِ

positions.position: The alternative applies only when two men cannot be found
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): If two men cannot be found, the clause permits a man and two women; several nominative and accusative parses are grammatically possible. Approved witnesses are upright in religion and character. ZAJJAJ (author): If two men are unavailable, one man and two women may witness; ‘whom you approve’ means people whose standing or judgment you approve, implying some witnesses are not acceptable. THALABI (author): If two men are unavailable, the transaction may be witnessed by one man and two women. KASHSHAF-FULL (author): If two men are unavailable, one man and two women may witness; Abū Ḥanīfa accepts women’s testimony with men except in ḥudūd and retaliation. IBNATIYYA-FULL (قوم): Some read the clause as meaning that two men cannot be found, so two women may be summoned only when no men are available; the author calls this weak and says the wording favors the majority. TABRISI (author): If two men are unavailable, the witness set is one man and two women whose outward probity and trustworthiness the parties accept; this makes justice a condition of testimony. BAYDAWI-FULL (author): If two men are unavailable, one man and two women may testify; the source's school limits this to financial matters, while Abu Hanifa extends it outside fixed penalties and retaliation. NASAFI-FULL (author): If two men are unavailable, one man and two women may witness; male testimony with women is accepted outside fixed punishments and retaliation. BIQAI-FULL (أبو الحسن الحرالي): Al-Harali sees the wording as broad accommodation for two women when two men cannot be found, while suggesting disagreement over cases where a man might be sought. BURSEVI (author): If two men are unavailable, one man and two women may witness financial matters by consensus; women do not testify in fixed punishments or retaliation, where men are required.

positions.position: One man and two women may be chosen even if two men exist
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD (author): “If the two are not men” means if the two witnesses are not both men, not if two men cannot be found. QURTUBI-FULL (قول): Another parsing says the female witnesses may be used only when no men can be found; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls this weak because the verse's apparent sense allows one man and two women even when two men are available.

positions.position: One man and two women are the stated alternative to two men.
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-BASIT (الزجاج والفراء وصاحب النظم): The phrase one man and two women can mean the witnesses sought should be one man and two women, let there be that combination, or let that number suffice; each syntactic paraphrase is sound.

question: How is فرجل وامرأتان supplied syntactically?

positions.position: An omitted verb or predicate supplies the nominal witness phrase.
positions.reasons: SIBAWAYH (author): Adding wa-l-ṣaghīru wa-l-kabīru permits nominative because the phrase means “all of them.” SIBAWAYH (author): Some Arabs use nominatives such as متعرض or صادق والله; Sibawayh also explains غضب الخيل على اللجم through an implied verb, with some speakers raising it instead. SIBAWAYH (author): إن of condition does not directly govern a noun: any accusative or nominative after it depends on an omitted verb, while a genitive name belongs to a suppressed prepositional phrase such as مررت بزيد. FARISI-HUJJA (أبو الحسن): Abu al-Hasan supplies فليكن رجل وامرأتان; Abu Ali calls this a good analysis because it gives أن تضل an implied verb that raises the indefinite and governs the clause. FARISI-HUJJA (author): A third attachment is possible: أن تضل may depend on the predicate of an implied nominal clause, in addition to the implied command to witness or the verb فليشهد. FARISI-HUJJA (author): In 20:52, لا يضل ربي means the book does not go astray from my Lord. Here أن is accusative and attaches to one of the previously proposed implied verbs. | mentions 20:52 FARISI-HUJJA (author): ممن ترضون describes the nominative رجل وامرأتان, not the earlier accusative شهيدين; the case mismatch rules out the earlier noun phrase as its antecedent. THALABI (author): Small or large describes whether the debt or amount is slight or substantial; the forms can be parsed as circumstantial modifiers or as predicates of an implied kāna. WAHIDI-BASIT (author): The purpose clause an taḍilla attaches to an implied command to seek one man and two women; it may attach to an implicit verb or to a supplied predicate. JISHUMI (علي بن عيسى): Ali ibn ʿIsa gives four sound expansions for the nominative phrase: let there be witnesses, let a man and two women testify, the witnesses are these, or they testify. BAGHAWI-FULL (حمزة): Hamza reads in tadhilla with kasra and fa-tadhakkara in the nominative, construing the phrase as a conditional continuation; the following verb is resumed after the conditional fa. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): He gives three possible syntactic expansions for the nominative ‘a man and two women’: summon them, let them be, or have them testify; each supplies the governing verb for the purpose clause. TABRISI (author): With the nominative reading, كان means “occur” or “happen,” so the phrase means that a present trade occurs. RAZI-FULL (علي بن عيسى): Ali ibn ʿIsa gives four permissible implied predicates for the nominative phrase رجل وامرأتان, including let there be, let testify, or the witnesses are. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): “One man and two women” admits several ellipses and parses: an omitted witness, a subject with omitted predicate, or a man as subject or passive object of an implied verb. SAMIN-DURR (السجاوندي): Al-Sajawandi treats ‘small or large’ as the predicate of an implied kāna; the author says this is unnecessary and unsupported here. SAMIN-DURR (author): The cited poetic phrase has an accusative after a comparative; one analysis supplies an implied verb indicated by the comparative. SAMIN-DURR (الزمخشري): Al-Zamakhshari supplies فليشهد رجل, meaning let a man and two women testify; this avoids deleting a construct noun and is the best analysis. SAMIN-DURR (ابن عطية): Ibn Atiyya makes the conditional and answer a nominative adjective of the two women; the Sheikh objects to the awkward order and possible intervening phrase. BURHAN (author): Zarkashi rejects that necessity because the implied verbal noun in contracting a debt could itself supply the antecedent for the pronoun. ALUSI-FULL (author): Other grammarians make the implied subject refer to the transaction and treat trade as a verbal noun; most readers use the nominative, with trade as subject and the clause as predicate, or take kāna as complete. ALUSI-FULL (author): The object of writing may be the debt, right, or written record implied by the verb; the verb can take it directly, or an understood preposition may be omitted. IBNASHUR-FULL (سيبويه): Al-Sībawayh cites ʿAmr ibn Shās’s verse with an implied repeated subject and predicate as a parallel for the incomplete-kāna reading.

question: In which cases may women testify?

positions.position: The formula expressly admits one man and two women in property matters.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (سفيان بن عيينة): Some readers of the light-kāf form interpret the two women's testimony together as equivalent to one man's, so each woman makes the other a “male” witness; this is reported from Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah. FARISI-HUJJA (سفيان بن عيينة): Sufyan ibn Uyayna interprets the phrase as one woman making the other a reminder, but Abu Ali judges this weak because women still need a man for a valid testimony. MAWARDI-FULL (سفيان بن عيينة): One woman reminding the other may mean making her count like a male witness. WAHIDI-BASIT (سفيان بن عيينة): Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna instead interprets it as making the other woman a male witness, so their joint testimony counts as a man’s; this is also attributed to Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ and reported through a narration. WAHIDI-BASIT (المفسرون): Exegetes reject the male-equivalence interpretation: women without a man still cannot testify, forgetting should be paired with its opposite, remembering, and equal male status would apply across all legal rulings. JISHUMI (علي بن عيسى): Ali ibn ʿIsa gives four sound expansions for the nominative phrase: let there be witnesses, let a man and two women testify, the witnesses are these, or they testify. JISHUMI (سفيان بن عيينة): Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna instead understands the reminder as making one woman like a male witness. BAGHAWI-FULL (سفيان بن عيينة): He interprets the wording as making one woman the equivalent of a male witness, but the author prefers the reminder interpretation because it is coordinated with forgetting. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): He gives three possible syntactic expansions for the nominative ‘a man and two women’: summon them, let them be, or have them testify; each supplies the governing verb for the purpose clause. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (سفيان بن عيينة): Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna and al-Asmaʿi’s report from Abu ʿAmr take the light reading to make two women’s testimony equivalent to one man’s; Qadi Abu Yaʿla prefers this. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (أبو علي): Abu ʿAli rejects Ibn ʿUyayna’s view: no number of women’s testimony suffices without a man, and forgetfulness should be answered by a reminder. RAZI-FULL (سفيان بن عيينة): Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna interprets the second woman as making the first a male-equivalent witness, rather than reminding her of forgotten testimony. RAZI-FULL (author): Al-Razi rejects that interpretation as contrary to the general exegetical view: without a man, women’s testimony is not accepted, so the second woman does not simply make the first a witness. QURTUBI-FULL (author): Because two women replace one man, he reasons by analogy that their testimony can be accompanied by an oath just as one man's testimony can; al-Shafiʿi agrees, while Abu Hanifa and his companions reject the oath as an extra division beyond the text. QURTUBI-FULL (المهدوي): Al-Mahdawī says most jurists reject women's testimony in criminal penalties, marriage, and divorce, and do not let them transmit testimony where they cannot testify directly. QURTUBI-FULL (سفيان بن عيينة وأبو عمرو بن العلاء): Ibn ʿUyayna and Abū ʿAmr understand the lighter reading of the reminder verb as returning a woman's testimony to memory, so two women's testimony totals a man's. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (أبو حنيفة، أبو يوسف، محمد، زفر، عثمان البتي): They reject women's testimony with men in penalties and retaliation but accept it for other rights. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (أبو عمرو بن العلاء، سفيان بن عيينة): They explain the light reading as making the two women's combined testimony equivalent to a man's; al-Zamakhsharī calls this aberrant and Ibn ʿAṭiyya distant and wrong. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): He agrees with al-Zamakhsharī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya: the reading fails linguistically because the verb is not recorded with that causative sense, and logically because both women's testimony, not one woman's reminder, would make the equivalent. SAMIN-DURR (بعضهم): An eccentric interpretation takes فتذكر to mean making the other woman a male witness, so their joint testimony equals a man's. SAMIN-DURR (الزمخشري): Zamakhshari calls making one woman a male witness a far-fetched interpretation, without limiting the criticism to one reading. SAMIN-DURR (الزمخشري): Al-Zamakhshari supplies فليشهد رجل, meaning let a man and two women testify; this avoids deleting a construct noun and is the best analysis. BIQAI-FULL (author): The two women must be among those whose uprightness is approved; testimony is penetrating perception of hidden meaning through an apparent form. ALUSI-FULL (حسين بن علي المغربي): Al-Maghribi takes the first one of them as one of the two testimonies and the second as one of the two women, so one woman recalls the forgotten testimony. ELMALILI (author): He calls a woman’s becoming manlike a degradation and says both feminized men’s and masculinized women’s testimony is inadmissible because they depart from their sex-specific perfection and may distort truth. ELMALILI (author): He treats women’s comparatively lower retention of external events as a consequence of their sex-specific nature, while saying a woman who later recalls an event fully can testify. ELMALILI (author): Two women can confer before testifying and remind one another without outside prompting, strengthening their recall and preserving both their dignity and the right entrusted to them. IBNASHUR-FULL (الخفاجي): Al-Khafājī says the repetition conveys generality: either woman may forget or remind, so neither is merely a secondary reminder rather than a witness in her own right. STUDYQURAN (author): Other verses give equal consideration to male and female testimony in accusations of adultery by either spouse. | mentions 24:6, 24:9

positions.position: One man and two women may testify in financial matters
positions.reasons: MUQATIL (author): For a debt, use two acceptable male witnesses or one man and two women; if one woman forgets, the other reminds her, and a summoned witness should serve when free. THALABI (author): Jurists agree that women may testify alongside men in property matters, but dispute other matters: Malik and several others limit them to property, while Abu Hanifa and Sufyan allow them generally except in fixed penalties and retaliation. WAHIDI-BASIT (author): There is consensus that women’s testimony is admissible in matters of property. JISHUMI (author): For matters that are neither property, a prescribed punishment, nor a defined right, Abu Hanifa accepts women's testimony while al-Shafiʿi rejects it. BAGHAWI-FULL (author): Jurists agree women may testify alongside men in financial cases, with one man and two women sufficient. BAGHAWI-FULL (author): Another group requires two upright men outside financial cases; al-Shafiʿi accepts one man and two women or four women in matters women ordinarily observe, such as birth, nursing, and sexual status. All reject women's testimony in criminal penalties. IBNATIYYA-FULL (ابن القاسم عن مالك): Another transmission from Malik permits women’s testimony in property, property agencies, and anything leading to property; Ashhab and others disagree, and the school has two positions when the testimony concerns a nonfinancial consequence. IBNATIYYA-FULL (ابن وهب عن مالك): One transmission from Malik allows women’s testimony only in the debt matters specified by the verse or in matters only women can observe, by necessity. QURTUBI-FULL (القاضي أبو محمد عبد الوهاب): Among jurists accepting oath-plus-witness, its use is limited by consensus to property and related rights, not bodily rights; property rights are lower because women's testimony is accepted there. BAYDAWI-FULL (author): If two men are unavailable, one man and two women may testify; the source's school limits this to financial matters, while Abu Hanifa extends it outside fixed penalties and retaliation. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): The apparent wording permits one man's and two women's testimony in all debt contracts, including consideration, marriage, benefits, and intentional blood claims; excluding a contract requires evidence. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الشافعي): Al-Shāfiʿī rejects women's testimony with men outside property matters; for wills he accepts men for nonfinancial dispositions and women for financial dispositions. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الحسن، الضحاك؛ عمر، عطاء، الشعبي؛ شريح؛ عمر وابنه عبد الله؛ علي): Other reported views limit women to debt, allow divorce, allow emancipation, allow one man with two women in marriage, or allow testimony in a contract, respectively. IBNKATHIR-FULL (author): Witnesses accompany writing for additional assurance. In financial matters, one man and two women may testify; Ibn Kathir connects this arrangement to a hadith describing women's testimony as half a man's and explaining their lesser reason and religious practice. BURSEVI (author): If two men are unavailable, one man and two women may witness financial matters by consensus; women do not testify in fixed punishments or retaliation, where men are required. ALUSI-FULL (author): A man and two women suffice in testimony outside ḥudūd and qiṣāṣ according to al-Alusi's school, while al-Shāfiʿī confines it to property cases and excludes matters such as marriage. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): Financial testimony requires either two men or one man and two women, as a precaution to protect rights rather than because women are intellectually or morally deficient; the second woman helps the first remember, and a woman counts as one witness. STUDYQURAN (IK, Q, R, Ṭ): The one-man-and-two-women witness provision is specific to these commercial transactions and differs from other testimony.

positions.position: The two women require a man alongside them
positions.reasons: IBNABIHATIM (يزيد بن عبد الرحمن بن أبي مالك): In legal claims, four women cannot replace two men; women’s testimony requires a man alongside them, and one man and one woman do not suffice. FARISI-HUJJA (author): On either analysis, the phrase means that testimony by one man and two women should occur, not that the man and women themselves should occur; the noun testimony is omitted and its complement stands for it. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): The verse permits two women’s testimony only when paired with a man. TABRISI (author): If two men are unavailable, the witness set is one man and two women whose outward probity and trustworthiness the parties accept; this makes justice a condition of testimony. NASAFI-FULL (author): If two men are unavailable, one man and two women may witness; male testimony with women is accepted outside fixed punishments and retaliation. DURR-FULL (سعيد بن جبير): The witnesses should be two free Muslim men or one man and two women; one woman may forget and the other remind her, and witnesses who hold testimony must respond when called. ALUSI-FULL (author): If two men are not sought, the alternatives can be parsed elliptically as one man and two women testifying, serving as witnesses, or being requested as witnesses. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The condition means that if two men are not present at the transaction, one man and two women may testify; the answer clause is elliptical, understood from the command to obtain witnesses.

positions.position: Women alone may testify in matters men cannot observe
positions.reasons: THALABI (author): Women may testify without men in four matters: women's bodily defects, nursing, childbirth, and the first cry after birth; bodily evidence is limited to the specified private areas. JISHUMI (author): Women alone may testify in matters men cannot observe, such as female defects, childbirth, and the newborn's first cry; jurists disagree about nursing. JISHUMI (أبو حنيفة): In fields where women's testimony alone is accepted, Abu Hanifa accepts one woman, while Muhammad requires four. QURTUBI-FULL (author): Women may testify alone in matters that no one else can observe, out of necessity. QURTUBI-FULL (author): Mālik's school accepts two women's testimony in matters unavailable to other witnesses, such as childbirth and a newborn's first cry, though details are disputed. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): There is no disagreement that women may testify alone about childbirth, virginity, a newborn's first cry, women's defects, and comparable matters specific to women. ALUSI-FULL (مالك): Mālik excludes such testimony from ḥudūd, qiṣāṣ, clientage, and proof of chastity, but accepts it for agency and wills where emancipation is not involved; women alone may testify in matters such as birth or virginity.

positions.position: Their testimony with men extends beyond finance except penalties and retaliation
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL (author): If two men are unavailable, one man and two women may witness; Abū Ḥanīfa accepts women’s testimony with men except in ḥudūd and retaliation. STUDYQURAN (Q): Classical law generally excluded women’s testimony in corporal punishment and qiṣāṣ cases, though this appears to be preference because women could testify without a male witness. | mentions 2:178 STUDYQURAN (author): Because women of the time generally lacked experience with complex finance, two women could make testimony more practical and protect them from bullying or manipulation, rather than indicting their reliability.

question: Can a claim be proved by one witness and an oath?

positions.position: A claim can be established by one witness and an oath
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (أبو علي وأكثر الفقهاء): Abu ʿAli and most jurists infer that judgment cannot rest on one witness plus an oath because that exceeds the divinely set limit; Abu Hashim and al-Shafiʿi permit it. RAZI-FULL (الشافعي): Al-Shafiʿi permits judgment on one witness plus the claimant’s oath, citing the Prophet’s practice; Abu Hanifa rejects it because the verse specifies two men or one man and two women. QURTUBI-FULL (مالك): He accepts the pledgee's sworn account only up to the collateral's value, treating the pledge and oath as supporting him; al-Qurṭubī says the verse instead favors the debtor, and collateral value need not match the debt. QURTUBI-FULL (الثوري والأوزاعي وعطاء والحكم بن عتيبة وطائفة): They oppose judgment by an oath with a witness; some call that practice abrogated by the Quran, and ʿAṭāʾ alleges ʿAbd al-Malik first ruled that way while al-Ḥakam attributes it to Muʿāwiya. QURTUBI-FULL (مالك): He argues that when a defendant denies a claim and refuses the oath, the claimant may swear and establish it; because this accepted procedure is absent from the Quran's witness list, its existence proves the list is not exhaustive and supports the oath with one witness. QURTUBI-FULL (author): Al-Qurṭubī rebukes those who reject judgment by an oath and one witness despite sound reports and early authorities' practice. QURTUBI-FULL (ابن عباس): The Prophet ruled by an oath together with one witness; ʿAmr ibn Dīnār restricts the report to property cases. QURTUBI-FULL (author): Al-Qurṭubī endorses the majority position allowing an oath with one witness, based on transmitted reports and generations of Medinan practice; Mālik allowed it in every region. QURTUBI-FULL (أبو داود): A report of Ibn ʿAbbās transmitted by Abū Dāwūd expressly says the Prophet judged by one witness and an oath in rights cases. QURTUBI-FULL (القاضي أبو محمد عبد الوهاب): Among jurists accepting oath-plus-witness, its use is limited by consensus to property and related rights, not bodily rights; property rights are lower because women's testimony is accepted there. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): The verse's apparent rules require two men or one man and two women, and thus do not allow judgment on one witness plus an oath; the Ḥanafīs and others agree. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (مالك، الشافعي، أحمد، إسحاق، أبو عبيد): They permit one witness plus an oath in financial claims, citing the four caliphs and Medinan practice; reports from al-Zuhrī differ on whether this was innovation and when it began.

positions.position: One witness and an oath are disputed as proof in property cases.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL (author): Al-Qurṭubī calls those accusations mistaken: the verse does not negate the Prophet's ruling by an oath and one witness, and an exclusive reading would also invalidate claims proved when a defendant refuses to swear, contrary to consensus. QURTUBI-FULL (author): Although one might call the oath-and-witness ruling case-specific, al-Qurṭubī reads it as establishing a general legal rule. QURTUBI-FULL (author): Since the debtor is trusted to dictate, a pledgor's sworn account of the debt prevails while the collateral remains; most jurists and Ibn al-Mundhir agree because the creditor claims the excess, in keeping with the rule that the claimant bears proof and the defendant swears. IBNKATHIR-FULL (author): Other reports condemn witnesses who testify before being asked, whose oaths and testimony precede each other, or who testify without a request; these are false witnesses.

positions.position: One witness and an oath do not suffice
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL (الزهري): One report from al-Zuhrī calls judgment by oath and witness an innovation and insists on two witnesses; another says he first ruled by it. QURTUBI-FULL (المازري): Al-Māzarī reports agreement on oath-plus-witness for pure money claims and rejection for marriage or divorce as such; claims leading only to money are disputed.

question: What makes witnesses acceptable?

positions.position: Known probity beyond apparent Islam is required
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): If two men cannot be found, the clause permits a man and two women; several nominative and accusative parses are grammatically possible. Approved witnesses are upright in religion and character. IBNABIHATIM (الضحاك): The witnesses must be men of probity. IBNABIHATIM (إبراهيم): Acceptable witnesses are those not known to have a defect. THALABI (إبراهيم النخعي): Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi defines uprightness as having no apparent cause for suspicion. THALABI (الشعبي): Al-Shaʿbi defines an upright witness as one not accused of sexual or financial misconduct. THALABI (الحسن): Al-Hasan defines uprightness as having no known disgrace. THALABI (author): An acceptable witness must meet ten conditions: freedom, adulthood, Islam, uprightness, knowledge of the matter, no personal gain or avoidance of harm, few errors, proper social conduct, no excessive leniency, and no adverse testimony from his slave. MAWARDI-FULL (الجمهور): Acceptable witnesses are free, Muslim, upright people. WAHIDI-BASIT (author): The source lists ten qualities for an admissible witness: freedom, adulthood, Islam, uprightness, knowledge, no self-serving interest or self-protective motive, no frequent error, no breach of propriety, and no enmity with the party testified against. JISHUMI (author): Acceptable witnesses are upright in religion, trustworthy, and competent; another gloss requires that no suspicion or accusation attach to them. BAGHAWI-FULL (author): A witness must be approved in religion and trustworthiness; seven qualifications are Islam, freedom, sound mind, adulthood, uprightness, social propriety, and absence of suspicion. BAGHAWI-FULL (author): Uprightness means avoiding major sins and not persisting in minor ones. KASHSHAF-FULL (author): Acceptable witnesses are those whose uprightness is known. KASHSHAF-FULL (author): Following Sībawayh, aqsaṭ and aqwam may derive regularly from verbs or by analogy from qāsiṭ and qayyim, meaning possessed of justice and uprightness. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): The emphatic form shahidayn suggests witnesses who have testified repeatedly, implying probity. TABRISI (مجاهد): Mujāhid limits the two male witnesses to free, adult, Muslim men; al-Ṭabrisī rejects freedom as a condition, requiring Islam and probity instead. TABRISI (author): If two men are unavailable, the witness set is one man and two women whose outward probity and trustworthiness the parties accept; this makes justice a condition of testimony. QURTUBI-FULL (author): Because testimony is a grave authority that makes another person liable, God requires approved and upright witnesses with distinguishing qualities. QURTUBI-FULL (جمهور): The majority infer that probity is an additional qualification beyond being Muslim, since the verse requires witnesses whom people approve. QURTUBI-FULL (شريح وعثمان البتى وأبو ثور): Shurayḥ, ʿUthmān al-Battī, and Abū Thawr count Muslims as upright witnesses even if enslaved. QURTUBI-FULL (علماؤنا): Probity means religious steadiness: avoiding major sins, preserving respectable conduct and avoiding minor sins, while appearing trustworthy and alert; another definition stresses apparent integrity. QURTUBI-FULL (author): Upright witnesses are even more important for marriage than debt, given its effects on lawful status, punishment, and lineage; al-Qurṭubī rejects Abū Ḥanīfa's view. | mentions 2:204, 63:4 QURTUBI-FULL (author): Apparent profession of Islam does not establish probity, since impressive speech or appearance may conceal disqualifying conduct. | mentions 2:204, 63:4 BAYDAWI-FULL (author): Witnesses must be people whose uprightness is known; one woman may remind the other if she forgets, with reminder the real rationale and forgetting its trigger. NASAFI-FULL (author): The witnesses should be people whose uprightness is known; this implies some witnesses are not approved. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (ابن عباس، الشعبي، الحسن، النخعي، الخصاف): They define approved witnesses as people of merit, religion, and competence; untainted in sex or lineage; not known for misconduct or suspicion; or with good deeds outweighing bad deeds while avoiding major sins. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (ابن أبي ليلى، أبو حنيفة، أبو يوسف، محمد): They accept upright witnesses from sectarian groups except the Khaṭṭābiyya among the Rāfiḍa; Muḥammad rejects Kharijites but accepts Ḥarūriyya because he distinguishes their treatment of Muslims' property. IBNKATHIR-FULL (author): The condition that witnesses be approved implies their probity; al-Shafi'i uses it to specify other unqualified Qur'anic witness commands, and some use it to reject unknown-status witnesses. BIQAI-FULL (author): The two women must be among those whose uprightness is approved; testimony is penetrating perception of hidden meaning through an apparent form. BURSEVI (author): The requirement that witnesses be approved applies to both the man and the women; women are included by grammatical predominance, and the phrase points to trust and known integrity. ELMALILI (author): Witness competence requires sound retention; witnesses lacking moral probity or reliable acquisition or retention of evidence are not admissible. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Here al-ʿadl means the right or truth, not the moral probity required of a witness, because the preposition bi rules out that sense. BINTSHATI-IJAZ (author): Sadd means a barrier or protection; sadad shifts to uprightness and sound guidance in speech, action, and affairs, while adl usually concerns judgments and opposes injustice.

positions.position: Approved witnesses must have reliable, upright character.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (الربيع): Al-Rabīʿ says the witness formula concerns debts and that approved witnesses are just. IBNABIHATIM (ابن عباس): Children are not acceptable witnesses because they are not among those whose testimony is approved. JISHUMI (إبراهيم): Ibrāhīm defines an acceptable witness as someone who has not shown cause for suspicion. JISHUMI (author): The command identifies witnesses, their number, method, and qualifications, and indicates a duty to establish testimony. JISHUMI (author): A witness should meet ten qualities: freedom, adulthood, Islam, integrity, knowledge of the testimony, no self-interest or self-protection, few errors, manly virtue, alertness, and not being heedless. TABRISI (author): The wording requires witnesses acceptable to the parties, since people cannot know whom God approves except from outward reliability and integrity. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbas says witnesses “whom you approve” are people of merit and religious integrity. QURTUBI-FULL (الشافعي وأبو حنيفة وأصحابه): They reject children's testimony because children lack the qualifications of men, approved witnesses, and just adults named elsewhere in scripture. | mentions 5:95 QURTUBI-FULL (ابن بكير): Ibn Bukayr and others take the address requiring approved witnesses to be directed to judges. QURTUBI-FULL (author): The requirement of witness approval supports inference from signs and entrusts judges with discretion to detect carelessness or suspicion and reject testimony. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): “Seek two witnesses” is a request for testimony or equivalent to “make two witnesses”; shahīd is intensive, suggesting experienced witnesses whose repeated use indicates acceptance and integrity. BURHAN (author): The author’s preferred reading takes شهيدين as two witnesses of either sex, then qualifies them as men; the pronoun returns to the unqualified pair, so the condition negates their being men and fits the fallback. DURR-FULL (مجاهد): Acceptable witnesses are two just, free Muslims. ITQAN (author): One explanation takes the dual phrase as covering two or more by naming the minimum; the better analysis makes the pronoun refer back to the two witnesses already mentioned without qualification. ELMALILI (author): Requiring at least two witnesses removes suspicion and the possibility of error or forgetfulness, displaying the strength of their retention and justice. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The verse names one scribe and two witnesses because people who are both literate and qualified to witness are uncommon. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The author objects to making testimony depend on each witness’s own varying judgments about these conditions, calling that a door to excessive legal qualification. IBNASHUR-FULL (أبو حنيفة): The author applies the earlier disagreement about scribes: accepting the request to bear witness becomes individual when designated, and giving testimony is individually obligatory if it causes no bodily or financial harm; Abū Ḥanīfa makes performance communal unless uniquely required, subject to court integrity, proximity, admissibility, and a claimant’s request. IBNASHUR-FULL (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): The Prophet had a sale witnessed and wrote a document for al-ʿAdāʾ ibn Khālid describing the purchased slave as free of defects and prohibited liabilities. BINTSHATI-IJAZ (author): Qur'anic contexts use adl for equality, compensation, and justice in judgment, arbitration, and testimony, supporting its broad semantic range and frequent legal use. | mentions 6:1, 6:150, 4:3, 4:129, 4:135, 2:48, 2:123, 6:70, 5:95, 5:106, 65:2, 4:58, 49:9, 5:8, 6:115, 6:152

question: Whom does ممن ترضون describe or address?

positions.position: The approval qualification governs the witnesses.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (الضحاك): Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says God commands two just men, or, if unavailable, one man and two approved women. QURTUBI-FULL (الشافعي وأبو حنيفة وأصحابه): They reject children's testimony because children lack the qualifications of men, approved witnesses, and just adults named elsewhere in scripture. | mentions 5:95 SAMIN-DURR (الشيخ): The Sheikh attaches ممن ترضون directly to استشهدوا so the qualification applies to every witness; its late position signals this scope. SAMIN-DURR (author): من الشهداء may be a circumstantial of the omitted relative pronoun in ممن ترضون, or apposition to its من with a repeated preposition. BURSEVI (author): The requirement that witnesses be approved applies to both the man and the women; women are included by grammatical predominance, and the phrase points to trust and known integrity.

positions.position: The address is to all contracting believers
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): Grammatically, ‘among those whom you approve’ modifies ‘a man and two women’; Abu Ali excludes ‘two witnesses’ from the adjective because its case differs, but the author says approval applies in meaning to both witness arrangements. IBNATIYYA-FULL (ابن بكير وغيره): They take ‘among those whom you approve’ as an address to judges; the author says the address is to everyone, although judges handle the actual case. RAZI-FULL (author): The qualification ممن ترضون and the parallel divorce instruction show that not everyone may testify; jurists enumerate ten conditions, including freedom, adulthood, Islam, justice, knowledge, and lack of personal conflict or benefit. | mentions 65:2 QURTUBI-FULL (ابن عطية): Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects limiting the address to judges: it addresses everyone, although judges carry out the case in practice. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): “Among witnesses whom you approve” most likely modifies “seek witnesses,” applying approval to all combinations; adjective and substitution analyses are weak.

positions.position: The phrase modifies the man and two women
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA (author): ممن ترضون describes the nominative رجل وامرأتان, not the earlier accusative شهيدين; the case mismatch rules out the earlier noun phrase as its antecedent. TABRISI (author): For Ḥamza's conditional reading, رجل وامرأتان forms a nominative description of the two women, while ممن ترضون refers back to that nominative pair rather than accusative شهيدين. SAMIN-DURR (author): ممن ترضون may be a nominative adjective of رجل وامرأتان; the Sheikh rejects this because it would exclude the two male witnesses.

QURTUBI-FULL (ابن بكير): Ibn Bukayr and others take the address requiring approved witnesses to be directed to judges. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): The address in “you approve” is apparently to believers, implying that witnesses are not presumed upright by status alone; other views address judges or creditors.

question: Why are two women specified?

positions.position: Two women allow one to remind the other if memory fails.
positions.reasons: MUQATIL (author): For a debt, use two acceptable male witnesses or one man and two women; if one woman forgets, the other reminds her, and a summoned witness should serve when free. TAB-FULL (author): Most Hijaz, Medina, and some Iraqi reciters read “an taḍilla” with open أن and subjunctive verbs, meaning the second woman reminds the first if she errs; the wording places the reminder after the error for its intended sense. TAB-FULL (الربيع): Al-Rabīʿ explains that one woman may forget and the other reminds her. TAB-FULL (السدي): Al-Suddī says one woman may forget the testimony and the other reminds her. ZAJJAJ (بعض أهل اللغة): For the majority’s open أن reading, some grammarians posit a condition moved forward: appoint two women so the remembering one can remind the forgetful one. ZAJJAJ (سيبويه والخليل وجميع النحويين الموثوق بعلمهم): The reliable grammarians take أن as purpose: appoint two women so one can remind the other; forgetting is mentioned because it causes the reminder. IBNABIHATIM (الحسن): If one of the two women forgets, the other reminds her; Saʿid ibn Jubayr, al-Rabiʿ, al-Suddi, Muqatil, and al-Dahhak report similarly. IBNABIHATIM (سعيد بن جبير): One of the women reminding the other means she makes her remember. FARISI-HUJJA (author): The testimony is called so one woman may forget and the other remind her; as Sibawayh explains, forgetting is the cause that makes reminding necessary, not the intended outcome. WAHIDI-BASIT (author): An is accusative with a purpose sense: call two women as witnesses so that one can remind the other. WAHIDI-BASIT (المفسرون): Exegetes reject the male-equivalence interpretation: women without a man still cannot testify, forgetting should be paired with its opposite, remembering, and equal male status would apply across all legal rulings. DAMGHANI (author): Ḍalāl can mean forgetting; one of the two women may forget. BAGHAWI-FULL (author): The majority read an tadhilla in the subjunctive, coordinated with fa-tadhakkara, meaning one woman may forget her testimony and the other remind her of the hearing. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): The purpose clause does not mean that testimony is taken in order for a woman to err; two women are appointed so one can remind the other if she forgets. Sibawayh compares this construction to preparing a prop for a wall if it leans. TABRISI (author): The particle أن is accusative here, with the sense “because one woman may forget, then the other remind her.” IBNJAWZI-ZAD (الزجاج): Al-Zajjaj says the construction means appoint two women so that one may remind the other, or for that purpose. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (الضحاك): The majority take the light and doubled readings alike: the second woman recalls the matter after the first forgets. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (أبو علي): Abu ʿAli rejects Ibn ʿUyayna’s view: no number of women’s testimony suffices without a man, and forgetfulness should be answered by a reminder. RAZI-FULL (سفيان بن عيينة): Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna interprets the second woman as making the first a male-equivalent witness, rather than reminding her of forgotten testimony. RAZI-FULL (author): Al-Razi explains the two-women provision by saying a second woman can prompt the first if she forgets, which he attributes to women’s bodily temperament. BAYDAWI-FULL (author): The verse's explanation implies women's lesser reason and memory; it expresses reminder through its cause, like preparing a weapon to repel an enemy if one comes. NASAFI-FULL (author): The two-witness clause explains that one woman may forget the testimony and the other remind her; Ḥamza reads the verb with nominative and gemination under the conditional, while Makki and Baṣri read it accusatively from dhikr. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): He agrees with al-Zamakhsharī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya: the reading fails linguistically because the verb is not recorded with that causative sense, and logically because both women's testimony, not one woman's reminder, would make the equivalent. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (قيل): An interpretation links women's forgetfulness to cold and moisture, says one woman's forgetting is more likely than both forgetting, and infers men's superiority. SAMIN-DURR (الأصمعي): Al-Asma'i transmits from Abu Amr two readings of meaning: doubled فتذكر recalls after forgetting, while light فتذكر makes the second woman a reminder by joining her testimony. IBNKATHIR-FULL (author): If one woman forgets, the other reminds her; another reading intensifies the verb. Ibn Kathir rejects the claim that having two women together makes them equivalent to a man and prefers the reminder interpretation. BURHAN (author): The two women serve to ensure reminder, not to cause error; since forgetting triggers the other’s reminder, the cause is put in place of the intended outcome. BIQAI-FULL (أبو الحسن الحرالي): Al-Harali says the readings with light and doubled consonants distinguish women who forget once from those who repeatedly forget; either may forget different details, allowing mutual correction. DURR-FULL (سعيد بن جبير): The witnesses should be two free Muslim men or one man and two women; one woman may forget and the other remind her, and witnesses who hold testimony must respond when called. BURSEVI (author): One woman may forget and the other remind her; reminder is the real purpose, while possible error is named as its cause, as in preparing a weapon to repel a possible enemy. ALUSI-FULL (بعض المحققين): Some exacting grammarians prefer an implicit dual pronoun after the fa: then the two women remind one another. ELMALILI (author): He generalizes that women’s retention is weaker and forgetfulness more likely than men’s, while allowing individual exceptions and treating gender and the majority as the legal reference. ELMALILI (author): He attributes women’s alleged forgetfulness partly to greater sensitivity and emotional impressions, which can weaken recall even in intelligent people. ELMALILI (author): He says modesty and reserve predominate in women and should do so, and that even a small engagement diminishes their distinct worth and leaves fewer reminders of events. ELMALILI (author): He treats women’s comparatively lower retention of external events as a consequence of their sex-specific nature, while saying a woman who later recalls an event fully can testify. ELMALILI (author): Two women can confer before testifying and remind one another without outside prompting, strengthening their recall and preserving both their dignity and the right entrusted to them. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The two women provide a safeguard against confusion or forgetting, which the author describes as more common among women by ordinary disposition; ḍalāl here means forgetfulness. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The author prefers a compound-cause account: the wording concisely expresses both avoiding loss when one woman forgets and gaining the benefit of the second woman’s reminder, better than al-Zamakhsharī’s account.

question: Does the provision imply women are intrinsically deficient?

positions.position: The rule reflects an intrinsic weakness in women's memory or judgment
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Al-Razi explains the two-women provision by saying a second woman can prompt the first if she forgets, which he attributes to women’s bodily temperament. BAYDAWI-FULL (author): The verse's explanation implies women's lesser reason and memory; it expresses reminder through its cause, like preparing a weapon to repel an enemy if one comes. IBNKATHIR-FULL (author): Witnesses accompany writing for additional assurance. In financial matters, one man and two women may testify; Ibn Kathir connects this arrangement to a hadith describing women's testimony as half a man's and explaining their lesser reason and religious practice. ALUSI-FULL (author): The two-woman provision explains the testimony rule: if one forgets, the other reminds her; al-Alusi attributes forgetfulness to women’s temperaments.

positions.position: It addresses usual social experience, not intrinsic inferiority
positions.reasons: ASAD-NOTES (author): The two-women provision does not question women’s moral or intellectual ability; Asad, citing ‘Abduh, attributes it to women’s usual lack of experience with business procedures and greater risk of mistakes. STUDYQURAN (author): The verse does not demand an inference of female inferiority; its described transaction allows two women to arrange a sale and use two men as witnesses. STUDYQURAN (author): Because women of the time generally lacked experience with complex finance, two women could make testimony more practical and protect them from bullying or manipulation, rather than indicting their reliability.

positions.position: The rationale is disputed between inherent and contextual explanations.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): He attributes women’s alleged forgetfulness partly to greater sensitivity and emotional impressions, which can weaken recall even in intelligent people. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): Financial testimony requires either two men or one man and two women, as a precaution to protect rights rather than because women are intellectually or morally deficient; the second woman helps the first remember, and a woman counts as one witness.
