question: What does تضل mean here?

positions.position: A woman forgets part of her testimony
positions.reasons: MAJAZ (author): أن تضل إحداهما means that one of the two forgets. IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB (author): أن تضل means that one woman forgets the testimony and the other reminds her; Moses' phrase uses ضالّ for forgetful. | mentions 26:20 IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL (author): Ḍalāl can mean forgetting: the forgetful person turns away from a matter and its recollection. TAB-FULL (الأعمش): Al-Aʿmash reads إن with kasra, puts تضل in the conditional jussive, and raises فتذكر as its response, yielding an independent statement about one witness reminding the other if she forgets. TAB-FULL (author): Al-Ṭabarī rejects Ibn ʿUyaynah's “making her male” interpretation: it contradicts the exegetes and misunderstands error in testimony as forgetfulness, when the forgetful witness needs reminding. IBNABIHATIM (سعيد بن جبير): The woman’s error means that she forgets her testimony. FARISI-HUJJA (author): Since Abu Ubayda glosses ضلال as forgetting, the natural opposite in context is remembering or reminding; this supports the ordinary reading of the clause. BAQILLANI (author): Reports of codex differences do not prove denial: a memorizer might err or forget a few letters, but the author rejects a broader claim against Ibn Masʿud. THALABI (author): Here tadilla means to forget, as in verses that pair ضلال with not knowing or forgetting and describe losing something in the earth. | mentions 20:52, 26:20, 32:10 MAWARDI-FULL (author): The woman may err or forget; Sibawayh identifies forgetting as one meaning. WAHIDI-BASIT (ابن عباس وجميع أهل التفسير والمعاني): Ibn ʿAbbās and exegetes and language scholars take taḍilla as forget, since the forgetful turns away from recall; 26:20 and al-Farazdaq’s verse illustrate it, while Abū ʿAmr says the root means disappearance. | mentions 26:20 WAHIDI-BASIT (author): Because the clause also says fatudhakkira, the interpretation of an taḍilla as the stated purpose fails: fear of forgetting makes sense, but fear of reminding does not. DAMGHANI (author): Ḍalāl can mean forgetting; one of the two women may forget. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): The purpose clause does not mean that testimony is taken in order for a woman to err; two women are appointed so one can remind the other if she forgets. Sibawayh compares this construction to preparing a prop for a wall if it leans. IBNATIYYA-FULL (أبو عبيد): Abu Ubayd glosses taḍilla as ‘forget’; the author says a witness’s error is forgetting part and remembering part, whereas total forgetfulness is not called straying from testimony. TABRISI (الربيع والسدي والضحاك وأكثر المفسرين): Most commentators take تضل as one woman forgetting the testimony she and the other woman heard; the light reading likewise means prompting her to recall it. IBNJAWZI-NUZHA (author): A Qur'anic use of ضل is forgetting, as in the case of one witness needing the other to remind her. RAZI-FULL (author): Ḍalāl in the clause can mean forgetting, as in the verse about what vanished from people, or failing to find one’s way; Abu ʿAmr says its root sense is disappearance. NASAFI-FULL (author): Writing a deferred debt is recommended because it better guards against forgetfulness and denial. SAMIN-DURR (ابن كثير وأبو عمرو): They lighten the kāf and read فتذكر with accusative rāʾ from أذكرته, meaning to make someone recall after forgetting; ضلال means forgetting, supported by 26:20 and al-Farazdaq. | mentions 26:20 BURHAN (author): The two women serve to ensure reminder, not to cause error; since forgetting triggers the other’s reminder, the cause is put in place of the intended outcome. BURHAN (سيبويه والبصريون): For this verse, neither “lest one err” nor “for fear of error” makes error a sensible purpose of testimony; the intended purpose is reminder if one forgets, with error as its trigger, like preparing a prop to support a wall if it leans. ALUSI-FULL (سعيد بن جبير والضحاك والربيع والسدي): These early authorities are reported as using ضل for a person who forgets, supporting the ordinary reading of the verse. ELMALILI (author): Requiring at least two witnesses removes suspicion and the possibility of error or forgetfulness, displaying the strength of their retention and justice. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The two women provide a safeguard against confusion or forgetting, which the author describes as more common among women by ordinary disposition; ḍalāl here means forgetfulness. IBNASHUR-FULL (أبو القاسم المغربي): Abū al-Qāsim al-Maghribī reads the first one as one of the two testimonies and takes ḍalāl as loss through forgetting, then assigns the second one to a woman. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): Because ordinary borrowing is necessary and abuse led to usury, the Qur'an permits loans and other lawful deferred contracts after forbidding interest; writing, witnesses, collateral, and trust help ensure timely full repayment and prevent forgetting or denial. STUDYQURAN (Q, R, Ṭ): To err means to forget an aspect of the contract.

positions.position: Ḍalāl here means forgetting or losing track of testimony.

FARISI-HUJJA (author): In 20:52, لا يضل ربي means the book does not go astray from my Lord. Here أن is accusative and attaches to one of the previously proposed implied verbs. | mentions 20:52 WAHIDI-BASIT (author): The purpose clause an taḍilla attaches to an implied command to seek one man and two women; it may attach to an implicit verb or to a supplied predicate. JISHUMI (author): Ḍalāl originally means destruction; Arabic says water was lost in milk, and the Qurʾan also uses it for the criminals' ruin. | mentions 54:47 JISHUMI (author): Another proposed root sense of ḍalāl is going away so completely that one cannot be found, as in the question about being lost in the earth. | mentions 32:10 IBNATIYYA-FULL (الباقون): The other readers use an open an in an taḍilla and make fataḏakkara accusative; Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr lighten its ذ and ك, while the others geminate them. question: How is إن or أن تضل read?

positions.position: Kasra إن gives a conditional clause
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (الأعمش): Al-Aʿmash reads إن with kasra, puts تضل in the conditional jussive, and raises فتذكر as its response, yielding an independent statement about one witness reminding the other if she forgets. ZAJJAJ (author): With kasra on إن, the clause is conditional: if one forgets, the remembering woman reminds her; فتذكر is indicative in this reading. THALABI (الأعمش وحمزة): Al-Aʿmash and Hamza read إن with kasra and فتذكر in the nominative, construing the clause conditionally or as a new beginning. JISHUMI (حمزة): Ḥamza reads the hamza of إن with kasra and فتذكر with indicative mood and shadda; he construes the phrase conditionally and as a new clause after the conditional fa. BAGHAWI-FULL (حمزة): Hamza reads in tadhilla with kasra and fa-tadhakkara in the nominative, construing the phrase as a conditional continuation; the following verb is resumed after the conditional fa. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): For Hamza’s reading, an is conditional and the fa-clause is its answer; Sibawayh treats the raised verb as an adjective of the two women, though the author has reservations. The majority accusative coordinates with the verb governed by an. TABRISI (حمزة): Ḥamza alone reads إن تضل with kasra, as a conditional particle whose جواب is فتذكر. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (author): Hamza reads in tadhilla with kasra; here dalāl means forgetfulness, according to Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, al-Rabiʿ, Muqatil, and others. RAZI-FULL (حمزة): Hamza reads إن with kasra and فتذكر as a raised, doubled form, taking the construction as conditional; the jussive of تضل is obscured by its doubled consonant. QURTUBI-FULL (حمزة): Ḥamza reads the particle with kasra as a conditional; the following clause answers it and the phrase describes the witnesses. | mentions 5:95 BAYDAWI-FULL (حمزة): Hamza reads an taḍilla conditionally, with fa-tudhakkira in the indicative. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الأعمش، حمزة): They read in tadhilla with a kasra as a conditional particle and fa-tudhakkiru with doubled dhāl and a jussive response. SAMIN-DURR (author): Hamza reads إن تضل as a conditional particle; others read أن تضل as an accusative verbal noun, with a causal lām understood. SAMIN-DURR (حمزة): Hamza reads فتذكر with doubled kāf and nominative rāʾ as the conditional answer, understood as فهي تذكر. NASHR (author): Within the two-kasra class, three loci are disputed: للنبي إن أراد and بيوت النبي except in Nafi’s reading, and من الشهداء أن تضل in Hamza’s reading. NASHR (author): The differing-hamza class has one locus, من الشهداء أن, except for Hamza’s reading, as already noted in the two-kasra discussion. NASHR (author): For the fifth class, early authorities mostly replace the softened second hamza with a pure kasra waw; later authorities mostly use a between-between sound. Al-Dani says the latter is better by analogy, the former stronger in transmission. NASHR (حمزة): Ḥamza reads the hamza in أن تضل with kasra. ALUSI-FULL (حمزة): Hamza reads an tadilla as a conditional clause and فتذكر in the indicative; its syntax is discussed in the next segment. ELMALILI (author): The verse's readings differ on the forms of an tadilla and fa-tudhakkira; Hamza reads with the hamza's kasra, while Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, and Yaqub use a still zā and an ungeminated kāf. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Ḥamza reads in tadhilla with kasra as a conditional, and raises tadhakkiru as the predicate of an omitted subject after fa; the author compares this syntax with Qur’an 5:95. | mentions 5:95

positions.position: Open أن gives a purpose clause with subjunctive verbs
positions.reasons: SIBAWAYH (author): In ‘أن تضل إحداهما,’ the preposition is omitted; the clause is treated like a verbal noun, as if it said ‘لأن تضل إحداهما.’ TAB-FULL (author): Most Hijaz, Medina, and some Iraqi reciters read “an taḍilla” with open أن and subjunctive verbs, meaning the second woman reminds the first if she errs; the wording places the reminder after the error for its intended sense. TAB-FULL (author): Al-Ṭabarī prefers the widely transmitted open-أن reading with a doubled kāf and subjunctive verbs: one woman reminds the other if she errs; فتذكر is coordinated with تضل and أن stands where كي would. IBNMUJAHID (حمزة): Hamza alone reads إن تضل with kasra and فتذكر with doubled kāf and indicative ending; the others use open أن and a subjunctive verb, except Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr, who lighten the verb. IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA (author): Kasra in إن تضل makes a conditional clause with a jussive verb; fatḥa in أن تضل treats it as a complement after an understood li, meaning lest one err. FARISI-HUJJA (author): Hamza alone reads إن تضل with kasra and فتذكر geminated in the nominative; the others open أن and use accusative فتذكر, with Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr lightening its kāf. FARISI-HUJJA (أبو الحسن): Abu al-Hasan supplies فليكن رجل وامرأتان; Abu Ali calls this a good analysis because it gives أن تضل an implied verb that raises the indefinite and governs the clause. FARISI-HUJJA (author): A third attachment is possible: أن تضل may depend on the predicate of an implied nominal clause, in addition to the implied command to witness or the verb فليشهد. FARISI-HUJJA (author): Under Hamza's conditional reading, the clause and response describe the two women; the lām in لأن تضل is jussive, opened to resolve adjacent sukūns, though kasra is also analogically possible. | mentions 22:41 WAHIDI-BASIT (author): The purpose clause an taḍilla attaches to an implied command to seek one man and two women; it may attach to an implicit verb or to a supplied predicate. WAHIDI-BASIT (author): Because the clause also says fatudhakkira, the interpretation of an taḍilla as the stated purpose fails: fear of forgetting makes sense, but fear of reminding does not. WAHIDI-BASIT (حمزة): Ḥamza reads in taḍilla with kasra and fatudhakkira in the indicative; inna is conditional, taḍilla is jussive with a joining fatḥa, and the fāʾ introduces the apodosis. KASHSHAF-FULL (author): Readings have fatadhakkara light or doubled, fatadhākarā, and Hamza’s conditional in tidilla with indicative fatadhakkaru. IBNATIYYA-FULL (حمزة): Hamza alone reads inna tadilla with kasra on inna and fatḥa then kasra on the verb, and fataḏakkara with fatḥa on the ذ and nominative rāʾ; al-Aʿmash shares this reading. IBNATIYYA-FULL (الباقون): The other readers use an open an in an taḍilla and make fataḏakkara accusative; Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr lighten its ذ and ك, while the others geminate them. RAZI-FULL (سائر القراء): Other readers use accusative أن, parsed either as لأن تضل with an elided preposition or as a purpose clause. QURTUBI-FULL (سيبويه): Under Ḥamza's conditional reading, Sībawayh parses the following verb as a new clause; with the open particle it is an object of purpose with an omitted governor. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): With open an, the clause is a purpose-cause: the possibility of forgetting is expressed as the reason for the other to remind, carried by meaning like preparing a prop for a wall that may lean. SAMIN-DURR (author): Two economical estimates are رجل وامرأتان يشهدون لأن تضل or فليشهد رجل; each supplies the needed predicate or verb. SAMIN-DURR (أبو جعفر): Abu Ja'far reports that al-Abbas estimated كراهة أن تضل; Abu Ja'far calls it mistaken because it makes the desired reminder something disliked. SAMIN-DURR (author): Nominative فتذكر is coordinated to أن تضل in the readings with أن; only Hamza raises the rāʾ, and the readers divide into three combinations of إن/أن, light/doubled kāf, and case. SAMIN-DURR (author): With أن, the verb is subjunctive and the lām of purpose is omitted: لأن تضل or إرادة أن تضل; its fatha differs from the junction fatha in Hamza's jussive reading. BURHAN (الكوفيون): The Kufans explain an before a future verb as لئلا, “lest,” in examples such as أن تضل إحداهما فتذكر. NASHR (الباقون): The other readers read the hamza in أن تضل with fatḥa. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): A text opens a relationship with truth rather than stating a final truth; readers in each era give it contemporary language and fill it with meaning according to general purposes.

positions.position: The readings differ between a purpose clause and a condition.
positions.reasons: MAJAZ (author): أن تضل إحداهما means that one of the two forgets. IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB (author): أن تضل means that one woman forgets the testimony and the other reminds her; Moses' phrase uses ضالّ for forgetful. | mentions 26:20 FARISI-HUJJA (author): أن تضل cannot attach directly to استشهدوا شهيدين; the following alternative of one man and two women signals an omitted command to call those witnesses. SAMIN-DURR (الجرجاني): Al-Jurjani estimates مخافة أن تضل and cites Amr's verse; the author says this works alone, but فتذكر makes it mistakenly mean fearing that she reminds.

question: Why is error stated before reminding?

positions.position: Forgetting is the cause, reminder the intended result
positions.reasons: SIBAWAYH (author): Mentioning possible error explains the reason for the reminder, as preparing support for a wall explains the cause without intending it to lean. SIBAWAYH (author): In 2:282, فتذكر is subjunctive because witnessing is commanded so that one woman may remind the other; error is a cause, not the intended aim. IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB (author): أقسط means more just; the record strengthens testimony because it reminds witnesses of all they witnessed. ZAJJAJ (سيبويه والخليل وجميع النحويين الموثوق بعلمهم): The reliable grammarians take أن as purpose: appoint two women so one can remind the other; forgetting is mentioned because it causes the reminder. ZAJJAJ (سيبويه): Sibawayh explains that the cause of reminding is mentioned as its purpose, like preparing a beam to support a wall if it begins to lean. FARISI-HUJJA (author): The testimony is called so one woman may forget and the other remind her; as Sibawayh explains, forgetting is the cause that makes reminding necessary, not the intended outcome. THALABI (author): The author rejects that reading of the rationale because the reminder is conjoined to forgetting, not to male remembrance. WAHIDI-BASIT (author): An is accusative with a purpose sense: call two women as witnesses so that one can remind the other. WAHIDI-BASIT (سيبويه والبصريون): Sibawayh and the Basran grammarians explain that the verse names forgetting because it causes the needed reminder, as preparing a support because a wall may lean. WAHIDI-BASIT (author): Because the clause also says fatudhakkira, the interpretation of an taḍilla as the stated purpose fails: fear of forgetting makes sense, but fear of reminding does not. WAHIDI-BASIT (أبو عمرو بن العلاء): Abū ʿAmr distinguishes the readings: geminated means reminding after forgetting; light means one woman reminds the other because the two together stand in a man’s place. WAHIDI-BASIT (author): Written records make testimony more reliable because they remind witnesses, instead of leaving them to impressions; aqwam means more fully upright, and adnā means closer to removing doubt about amount and term. WAHIDI-WAJIZ (author): Writing is fairest before God, makes testimony more reliable because the record reminds witnesses, and best prevents doubt about amount or due date. JISHUMI (سيبويه): Sibawayh explains that straying is stated before reminding because it causes the reminder; the connected actions function as one purpose, as in propping a wall because it is leaning. JISHUMI (author): Jishumi rejects the ‘make her like a man’ gloss because the preceding condition that one may err indicates that reminder means recalling the testimony. BAGHAWI-FULL (author): Writing is most equitable because God commanded it, strengthens testimony by reminding witnesses, and most nearly prevents doubt. KASHSHAF-FULL (author): ‘Lest one err’ means fail to recall the testimony; purpose is phrased by its cause and effect, like preparing a prop for a leaning wall or a weapon for an approaching enemy. KASHSHAF-FULL (author): The cause-effect construction works because the two are closely linked; intent to remind is expressed as intent that one err. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): The purpose clause does not mean that testimony is taken in order for a woman to err; two women are appointed so one can remind the other if she forgets. Sibawayh compares this construction to preparing a prop for a wall if it leans. TABRISI (author): The particle أن is accusative here, with the sense “because one woman may forget, then the other remind her.” TABRISI (سيبويه): Sībawayh says testimony is requested so one woman may remind the other; possible forgetfulness is the reason for reminding, like shoring a wall because it may lean. BAYDAWI-FULL (author): Witnesses must be people whose uprightness is known; one woman may remind the other if she forgets, with reminder the real rationale and forgetting its trigger. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Pairing Allah with Lord reminds the debtor that God nurtures, repairs, and favors him; Allah comes first because divine authority precedes the reminder of favors. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): With open an, the clause is a purpose-cause: the possibility of forgetting is expressed as the reason for the other to remind, carried by meaning like preparing a prop for a wall that may lean. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): He agrees with al-Zamakhsharī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya: the reading fails linguistically because the verb is not recorded with that causative sense, and logically because both women's testimony, not one woman's reminder, would make the equivalent. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (النحاس عن علي بن سليمان عن أبي العباس): Abū al-ʿAbbās analyzes it as “for fear that one forget”; Abū Jaʿfar rejects this because it would make the purpose that the other woman remind her. SAMIN-DURR (سيبويه): Sibawayh explains that error causes reminder, so cause and result are treated as interchangeable; the purpose is that one woman remind the other, as in preparing a prop for a leaning wall. SAMIN-DURR (أبو جعفر): Abu Ja'far reports that al-Abbas estimated كراهة أن تضل; Abu Ja'far calls it mistaken because it makes the desired reminder something disliked. SAMIN-DURR (author): Because أذكرته is causative and takes two objects, the omitted second is testimony: one woman reminds the other of her testimony after forgetting. SAMIN-DURR (author): The repeated إحداهما rather than a pronoun preserves ambiguity because either woman may forget and remind; the generic wording means if one forgets, the other reminds. BURHAN (author): The two women serve to ensure reminder, not to cause error; since forgetting triggers the other’s reminder, the cause is put in place of the intended outcome. BURHAN (سيبويه والبصريون): For this verse, neither “lest one err” nor “for fear of error” makes error a sensible purpose of testimony; the intended purpose is reminder if one forgets, with error as its trigger, like preparing a prop to support a wall if it leans. BIQAI-FULL (author): The future term creates risk of forgetting, which explains the emphasis on writing; hand-to-hand trade is exempt because it is immediately exchanged and unlikely to be disputed. BURSEVI (author): One woman may forget and the other remind her; reminder is the real purpose, while possible error is named as its cause, as in preparing a weapon to repel a possible enemy. ALUSI-FULL (السيوطي): Al-Suyuti treats Salim as one of Abu Bakr's commissioned collectors, but Alusi calls this an error because Salim died at Yamama, before Abu Bakr ordered the collection. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Although the wording appears to make forgetting the cause, the practical aim is preventing loss of the testimony; remembering is the consequence that completes the causal explanation. | mentions 2:266 IBNASHUR-FULL (الزمخشري): Al-Zamakhsharī explains the wording as stressing reminder so strongly that the sentence names its enabling cause, comparing prepared timber to brace a leaning wall and weapons to repel an enemy. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The author prefers a compound-cause account: the wording concisely expresses both avoiding loss when one woman forgets and gaining the benefit of the second woman’s reminder, better than al-Zamakhsharī’s account. IBNASHUR-FULL (التفتازاني): Al-Taftāzānī notes that the repetition is not an ordinary replacement of a pronoun because the woman who reminds is not the forgetful one, and asks for the rhetorical reason.

question: How is فتذكر read and derived?

positions.position: The doubled form is an intensive reminder verb
positions.reasons: SIBAWAYH (author): Nouns longer than three letters follow doubled-consonant rules of four-letter verbs: shift a vowel onto a preceding quiescent consonant, retain an existing vowel, and leave preceding alif unchanged; afʿal forms assimilate too. SIBAWAYH (author): A dual nūn can drop and therefore differs from the inseparable doubled consonant after alif; separated doubled consonants do not undergo the same alteration. SIBAWAYH (author): A doubled verb has two identical consonants at its end, as in رددت and وددت; this is the morphological class of the verse's مضارّ form. SIBAWAYH (أهل الحجاز): The Hijaz dialect keeps the doubled consonants separate when the verb ending is quiescent, moving the preceding consonant to avoid two sukūns together. SIBAWAYH (author): If the consonant before the first of the doubled pair is quiescent, it takes that consonant’s vowel; a now-unneeded alif of connection is deleted. SIBAWAYH (author): With an alif before the doubled consonants and no alif of connection, the form remains unchanged; لا تضار is one of Sibawayh’s examples. TAB-FULL (author): Al-Ṭabarī prefers the widely transmitted open-أن reading with a doubled kāf and subjunctive verbs: one woman reminds the other if she errs; فتذكر is coordinated with تضل and أن stands where كي would. TAB-FULL (ابن زيد): Ibn Zayd says the two forms are synonymous dialects and that he reads فتذكر with a doubled kāf. IBNMUJAHID (حمزة): Hamza alone reads إن تضل with kasra and فتذكر with doubled kāf and indicative ending; the others use open أن and a subjunctive verb, except Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr, who lighten the verb. IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA (author): فتذكر may be doubled or light and jussive, indicative, or subjunctive: it can continue the conditional, begin a clause after fa, or be governed by the open أن. FARISI-HUJJA (author): Hamza alone reads إن تضل with kasra and فتذكر geminated in the nominative; the others open أن and use accusative فتذكر, with Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr lightening its kāf. FARISI-HUJJA (ابن كثير وأبو عمرو): Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read فتذكر lightly, using the hamzated causative pattern; the other readers geminate it, using the intensive pattern, and both are valid. THALABI (ابن كثير وأبو عمرو ويعقوب وأبو حاتم وقتيبة): Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, Yaqub, Abu Hatim, and Qutayba read فتذكر without doubling; the remaining readers double the consonant. THALABI (عمر وأبي وابن مسعود ومجاهد): Umar, Ubayy, Ibn Masʿud, and Mujahid read ولا يضارر with the doubled consonants made explicit, supporting the interpretation that the writer or witness is not to be harmed. WAHIDI-BASIT (author): Fatudhakkira is read with either gemination or a light consonant; gemination makes dhakara transitive to a second object, supported by 51:55, 88:21 and a poem, while the light form uses hamza-transitivity and omits the object, meaning the testimony. | mentions 51:55, 88:21 WAHIDI-BASIT (أبو عمرو بن العلاء): Abū ʿAmr distinguishes the readings: geminated means reminding after forgetting; light means one woman reminds the other because the two together stand in a man’s place. KASHSHAF-FULL (author): Readings have fatadhakkara light or doubled, fatadhākarā, and Hamza’s conditional in tidilla with indicative fatadhakkaru. TABRISI (حمزة): Ḥamza reads فتذكر with doubled dhāl and indicative mood. TABRISI (الباقون): The remaining readers read فتذكر with doubled dhāl and subjunctive mood. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (author): Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read fatudhakkira with a light kaf and accusative ra; Hamza reads it with a doubled kaf and nominative ra; the rest use doubled kaf and accusative ra. RAZI-FULL (نافع وابن عامر وعاصم والكسائي): Nafiʿ, Ibn ʿAmir, ʿAsim, and al-Kisaʾi read فتذكر with doubling and the subjunctive; Hamza doubles it with the indicative, while Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr use the lighter form. RAZI-FULL (حمزة): Hamza reads إن with kasra and فتذكر as a raised, doubled form, taking the construction as conditional; the jussive of تضل is obscured by its doubled consonant. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الجمهور): Most readers use subjunctive an and coordinate fa-tudhakkira; Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr lighten the kāf, while others double it. SAMIN-DURR (الأصمعي): Al-Asma'i transmits from Abu Amr two readings of meaning: doubled فتذكر recalls after forgetting, while light فتذكر makes the second woman a reminder by joining her testimony. SAMIN-DURR (author): Nominative فتذكر is coordinated to أن تضل in the readings with أن; only Hamza raises the rāʾ, and the readers divide into three combinations of إن/أن, light/doubled kāf, and case. SAMIN-DURR (أبو جعفر وعمرو بن عبيد): Abu Jaʿfar and ʿAmr b. ʿUbayd read the doubled rāʾ sākin in connected speech; the author notes the three-consonant cluster is weak, tolerated by lengthening and by analogy to pause. SAMIN-DURR (author): أمل and أملى both mean dictating; some call them dialects, others derive the yāʾ as a replacement for a doubled consonant, with repetition underlying both forms. | mentions 5:54 SAMIN-DURR (حمزة): Hamza reads فتذكر with doubled kāf and nominative rāʾ as the conditional answer, understood as فهي تذكر. BURHAN (ابن مالك): Ibn Malik says the Qur’an is mostly in the Hijazi dialect, with a few Tamimi forms: assimilation is Tamimi, while preserving doubled consonants, as in فليملل and يحلل, is common in Hijaz. | mentions 59:4, 5:54, 3:31, 3:125, 4:115, 8:13, 58:5, 19:75, 20:27, 20:31 NASHR (ابن كثير والبصريان): Ibn Kathīr and the two Basran readers pronounce فتذكر without gemination. NASHR (الباقون): The other readers pronounce فتذكر with gemination. BIQAI-FULL (أبو الحسن الحرالي): Al-Harali says the readings with light and doubled consonants distinguish women who forget once from those who repeatedly forget; either may forget different details, allowing mutual correction. DURR-FULL (الحسن): Al-Hasan recited the verb for reminding with a doubled consonant. ALUSI-FULL (author): Imlāl means dictating to a scribe; the form alternates with imlāʾ through sound changes involving the doubled consonant and final hamza. SAMARRAI-ASRAR-MUH (author): The doubled form يُضَارّ can be read as active or passive; spelling the consonant without assimilation would distinguish the two forms. | mentions 8:13, 5:54

positions.position: The light and doubled forms both express making someone remember.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (الأعمش): Al-Aʿmash reads إن with kasra, puts تضل in the conditional jussive, and raises فتذكر as its response, yielding an independent statement about one witness reminding the other if she forgets. FARISI-HUJJA (author): The second object of فتذكر إحداهما الأخرى is omitted; the meaning is that one woman reminds the other of the testimony they undertook. WAHIDI-BASIT (author): Because the clause also says fatudhakkira, the interpretation of an taḍilla as the stated purpose fails: fear of forgetting makes sense, but fear of reminding does not. JISHUMI (الباقون): The other readers use fatḥ on أن and read فتذكر in connection with the preceding clause, with نصب either as the object of the verb or after an understood preposition أن. TABRISI (حمزة): Ḥamza alone reads إن تضل with kasra, as a conditional particle whose جواب is فتذكر. SAMIN-DURR (الجرجاني): Al-Jurjani estimates مخافة أن تضل and cites Amr's verse; the author says this works alone, but فتذكر makes it mistakenly mean fearing that she reminds. SAMIN-DURR (بعضهم): An eccentric interpretation takes فتذكر to mean making the other woman a male witness, so their joint testimony equals a man's. BURHAN (الكوفيون): The Kufans explain an before a future verb as لئلا, “lest,” in examples such as أن تضل إحداهما فتذكر. NASHR (الباقون): The other readers read the r in فتذكر with fatḥa. ITQAN (ابن هشام): Ibn Hisham prefers the conditional analysis because both particles occur in the same syntactic position and the following فـ in فتذكر supports it. ALUSI-FULL (ابن كثير ويعقوب وأبو عمرو والحسن): These readers recite فتذكر with a still dhal and kasra on kaf.

positions.position: The verb's case is indicative under a condition
positions.reasons: SIBAWAYH (أهل الكوفة): The Kufans read فتذكر with indicative mood. ZAJJAJ (author): With kasra on إن, the clause is conditional: if one forgets, the remembering woman reminds her; فتذكر is indicative in this reading. THALABI (الأعمش وحمزة): Al-Aʿmash and Hamza read إن with kasra and فتذكر in the nominative, construing the clause conditionally or as a new beginning. WAHIDI-BASIT (حمزة): Ḥamza reads in taḍilla with kasra and fatudhakkira in the indicative; inna is conditional, taḍilla is jussive with a joining fatḥa, and the fāʾ introduces the apodosis. JISHUMI (حمزة): Ḥamza reads the hamza of إن with kasra and فتذكر with indicative mood and shadda; he construes the phrase conditionally and as a new clause after the conditional fa. JISHUMI (author): In Ḥamza’s reading, تضل is jussive in the conditional though its doubling obscures the form; فتذكر is indicative as the clause after the conditional fa begins anew. NASHR (حمزة): Ḥamza reads the r in فتذكر in the nominative. ALUSI-FULL (حمزة): Hamza reads an tadilla as a conditional clause and فتذكر in the indicative; its syntax is discussed in the next segment.

positions.position: The light form is the causative reminder verb
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (سفيان بن عيينة): Some readers of the light-kāf form interpret the two women's testimony together as equivalent to one man's, so each woman makes the other a “male” witness; this is reported from Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah. TAB-FULL (آخرون): Other readers of the light-kāf form take it to mean ordinary remembering after forgetfulness. JISHUMI (نافع وعاصم والكسائي وابن عامر): Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim, al-Kisāʾī, and Ibn ʿĀmir read فتذكر with shadda and نصب; Ḥamza uses shadda and رفع, while Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr use a light form with نصب. TABRISI (ابن كثير وأبو عمرو وقتيبة): Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, and Qutayba read فتذكر lightly and in the subjunctive. SAMIN-DURR (ابن كثير وأبو عمرو): They lighten the kāf and read فتذكر with accusative rāʾ from أذكرته, meaning to make someone recall after forgetting; ضلال means forgetting, supported by 26:20 and al-Farazdaq. | mentions 26:20 SAMIN-DURR (حميد بن عبد الرحمن ومجاهد): They read فتذكر with light kāf and nominative rāʾ. DURR-FULL (مجاهد): Mujahid recited the same verb with a light consonant.

positions.position: The verb's case is subjunctive under open أن
positions.reasons: SIBAWAYH (author): In 2:282, فتذكر is subjunctive because witnessing is commanded so that one woman may remind the other; error is a cause, not the intended aim. THALABI (author): The common reading has إن with fatḥa and فتذكر accusative, linked to the preceding clause through an understood causal preposition: one woman may err so the other reminds her. BURHAN (author): The Maliki shaykh prefers not to combine different canonical readings in one verse; combining forms where one reading depends on the other, including this phrase with فتذكر in the accusative, is prohibited under the same ruling.

positions.position: A mutual form means the women remind each other
positions.reasons: THALABI (زيد بن أسلم): Zayd ibn Aslam reads فتذكر as mutual reminding. SAMIN-DURR (زيد بن أسلم): Zayd ibn Aslam reads فتذاكر, the reciprocal form of mutual reminding. BIQAI-FULL (author): Written debts make evidence more upright and reduce doubt; the record can also settle men's uncertainty, just as mutual reminding addresses women's lapses.

question: Does فتذكر mean reminding or male equivalence?

positions.position: One woman reminds the other of forgotten testimony
positions.reasons: MUQATIL (author): For a debt, use two acceptable male witnesses or one man and two women; if one woman forgets, the other reminds her, and a summoned witness should serve when free. IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB (author): أن تضل means that one woman forgets the testimony and the other reminds her; Moses' phrase uses ضالّ for forgetful. | mentions 26:20 TAB-FULL (الأعمش): Al-Aʿmash reads إن with kasra, puts تضل in the conditional jussive, and raises فتذكر as its response, yielding an independent statement about one witness reminding the other if she forgets. TAB-FULL (الربيع): Al-Rabīʿ explains that one woman may forget and the other reminds her. TAB-FULL (السدي): Al-Suddī says one woman may forget the testimony and the other reminds her. TAB-FULL (الضحاك): Al-Ḍaḥḥāk likewise interprets the clause as one woman forgetting and the other reminding her. ZAJJAJ (بعض أهل اللغة): For the majority’s open أن reading, some grammarians posit a condition moved forward: appoint two women so the remembering one can remind the forgetful one. ZAJJAJ (سيبويه والخليل وجميع النحويين الموثوق بعلمهم): The reliable grammarians take أن as purpose: appoint two women so one can remind the other; forgetting is mentioned because it causes the reminder. IBNABIHATIM (مقاتل بن حيان): The other woman reminds her companion of the testimony. IBNABIHATIM (سعيد بن جبير): The reminding woman is the one who retained her testimony. FARISI-HUJJA (author): The testimony is called so one woman may forget and the other remind her; as Sibawayh explains, forgetting is the cause that makes reminding necessary, not the intended outcome. FARISI-HUJJA (author): The second object of فتذكر إحداهما الأخرى is omitted; the meaning is that one woman reminds the other of the testimony they undertook. FARISI-HUJJA (سفيان بن عيينة): Sufyan ibn Uyayna interprets the phrase as one woman making the other a reminder, but Abu Ali judges this weak because women still need a man for a valid testimony. THALABI (author): The common reading has إن with fatḥa and فتذكر accusative, linked to the preceding clause through an understood causal preposition: one woman may err so the other reminds her. THALABI (author): The author rejects that reading of the rationale because the reminder is conjoined to forgetting, not to male remembrance. MAWARDI-FULL (قتادة والسدي والضحاك وابن زيد): One woman reminds the other if she forgets. WAHIDI-BASIT (عامة المفسرين): Most exegetes understand the other woman to remind her after she forgets. WAHIDI-BASIT (أبو عمرو بن العلاء): Abū ʿAmr distinguishes the readings: geminated means reminding after forgetting; light means one woman reminds the other because the two together stand in a man’s place. WAHIDI-BASIT (المفسرون): Exegetes reject the male-equivalence interpretation: women without a man still cannot testify, forgetting should be paired with its opposite, remembering, and equal male status would apply across all legal rulings. WAHIDI-WAJIZ (author): Witnesses are two free adult men of the believers, acceptable for their merit and religion; if one woman forgets, the other reminds her of the testimony. JISHUMI (الربيع والسدي والضحاك وابن زيد): Al-Rabīʿ, al-Suddī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ibn Zayd, and most exegetes take ‘go astray’ as forget, so one woman reminds the other of the testimony. JISHUMI (author): Jishumi rejects the ‘make her like a man’ gloss because the preceding condition that one may err indicates that reminder means recalling the testimony. BAGHAWI-FULL (author): The majority read an tadhilla in the subjunctive, coordinated with fa-tadhakkara, meaning one woman may forget her testimony and the other remind her of the hearing. BAGHAWI-FULL (سفيان بن عيينة): He interprets the wording as making one woman the equivalent of a male witness, but the author prefers the reminder interpretation because it is coordinated with forgetting. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): The purpose clause does not mean that testimony is taken in order for a woman to err; two women are appointed so one can remind the other if she forgets. Sibawayh compares this construction to preparing a prop for a wall if it leans. TABRISI (author): The particle أن is accusative here, with the sense “because one woman may forget, then the other remind her.” TABRISI (سيبويه): Sībawayh says testimony is requested so one woman may remind the other; possible forgetfulness is the reason for reminding, like shoring a wall because it may lean. RAZI-FULL (سفيان بن عيينة): Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna interprets the second woman as making the first a male-equivalent witness, rather than reminding her of forgotten testimony. QURTUBI-FULL (سفيان بن عيينة وأبو عمرو بن العلاء): Ibn ʿUyayna and Abū ʿAmr understand the lighter reading of the reminder verb as returning a woman's testimony to memory, so two women's testimony totals a man's. QURTUBI-FULL (author): Al-Qurṭubī finds the lighter reminder reading less apt: a reminder naturally answers forgetfulness, and the doubled reading means one woman alerts the other when she forgets. BAYDAWI-FULL (author): Witnesses must be people whose uprightness is known; one woman may remind the other if she forgets, with reminder the real rationale and forgetting its trigger. NASAFI-FULL (author): The two-witness clause explains that one woman may forget the testimony and the other remind her; Ḥamza reads the verb with nominative and gemination under the conditional, while Makki and Baṣri read it accusatively from dhikr. SAMIN-DURR (author): Because أذكرته is causative and takes two objects, the omitted second is testimony: one woman reminds the other of her testimony after forgetting. SAMIN-DURR (الأصمعي): Al-Asma'i transmits from Abu Amr two readings of meaning: doubled فتذكر recalls after forgetting, while light فتذكر makes the second woman a reminder by joining her testimony. SAMIN-DURR (المفسرون وأهل اللسان): Exegetes and linguists reject the male-equivalence interpretation: forgetting pairs naturally with reminding, it does not fit the testimony rule's male witness, and it would imply wider legal equivalence. SAMIN-DURR (author): The repeated إحداهما rather than a pronoun preserves ambiguity because either woman may forget and remind; the generic wording means if one forgets, the other reminds. IBNKATHIR-FULL (author): If one woman forgets, the other reminds her; another reading intensifies the verb. Ibn Kathir rejects the claim that having two women together makes them equivalent to a man and prefers the reminder interpretation. BURHAN (author): The two women serve to ensure reminder, not to cause error; since forgetting triggers the other’s reminder, the cause is put in place of the intended outcome. BURHAN (سيبويه والبصريون): For this verse, neither “lest one err” nor “for fear of error” makes error a sensible purpose of testimony; the intended purpose is reminder if one forgets, with error as its trigger, like preparing a prop to support a wall if it leans. BIQAI-FULL (author): One woman may lose or forget some testimony, so the other reminds her; the verse makes this the reason two women stand in place of one man. BIQAI-FULL (author): The reference to reminding implies that testimony without recall is barred; the verse also uses reciprocal omission, with one side understood from the other. DURR-FULL (سعيد بن جبير): The witnesses should be two free Muslim men or one man and two women; one woman may forget and the other remind her, and witnesses who hold testimony must respond when called. DURR-FULL (ابن مسعود): Ibn Masud's reading says one woman may err and the other remind her. BURSEVI (author): One woman may forget and the other remind her; reminder is the real purpose, while possible error is named as its cause, as in preparing a weapon to repel a possible enemy. ALUSI-FULL (author): The two-woman provision explains the testimony rule: if one forgets, the other reminds her; al-Alusi attributes forgetfulness to women’s temperaments. ALUSI-FULL (author): Putting the explicit object before the subject foregrounds reminding the woman who forgot; repeating the noun also avoids assigning forgetfulness to one particular woman. ALUSI-FULL (author): Ibn Masud’s reading, transmitted by al-Aʿmash, has her remind her; other grammarians say the canonical wording intensifies ambiguity about which woman forgets. ELMALILI (author): If neither woman forgot, their evidentiary position is stronger; the mutual reminder need not happen in court, where it could prevent acceptance of testimony. ELMALILI (author): On Hamza’s reading, if one woman forgets or errs, the other reminds her. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The author prefers a compound-cause account: the wording concisely expresses both avoiding loss when one woman forgets and gaining the benefit of the second woman’s reminder, better than al-Zamakhsharī’s account. IBNASHUR-FULL (التفتازاني): Al-Taftāzānī notes that the repetition is not an ordinary replacement of a pronoun because the woman who reminds is not the forgetful one, and asks for the rhetorical reason. STUDYQURAN (author): Commentators differ over whether the reminded woman becomes legally equal to a man or the two women together equal one man; the latter view was more widely accepted. IBNATIYYA-FULL (أبو عمرو بن العلاء وسفيان بن عيينة): They interpret the light form as making the other woman’s testimony count as a man’s testimony; the author rejects this as distant and inelegant, saying remembrance is the fitting opposite of straying and the implied object is testimony.

positions.position: The two women together count like a male witness
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-BASIT (سفيان بن عيينة): Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna instead interprets it as making the other woman a male witness, so their joint testimony counts as a man’s; this is also attributed to Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ and reported through a narration. RAZI-FULL (أبو عمرو بن العلاء): Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlaʾ also transmits the male-equivalent reading, explaining that the second woman’s testimony joins the first to make one man’s testimony. SAMIN-DURR (بعضهم): An eccentric interpretation takes فتذكر to mean making the other woman a male witness, so their joint testimony equals a man's.

turns_on: Whether the lighter verb means recall or male equivalence.

question: Why is إحداهما repeated?

positions.position: Repetition leaves either woman able to forget or remind.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (author): The repeated إحداهما may put the subject before its object and avoid separating verb and subject, or may clarify that a testimony is lost rather than a person straying. BURHAN (author): Repeating إحداهما instead of using a pronoun gives the noun greater importance and balances the two clauses; the author calls this rare structural or semantic parallelism, beyond mere sound-patterning. BURHAN (author): The repeated إحداهما may refer to the same woman or another; in 2:282, if the second is an object, definite nouns identify the same referent, while if it is subject they may match by kind. Most grammarians treat an unmarked first noun as subject, unlike al-Zajjaj’s view on دعواهم. | mentions 21:15 IBNASHUR-FULL (التفتازاني): Al-Taftāzānī notes that the repetition is not an ordinary replacement of a pronoun because the woman who reminds is not the forgetful one, and asks for the rhetorical reason. TABATABAI (author): “Lest one of them err” elliptically means fearing that one woman will err; repeating “one of them” distinguishes the initially unspecified woman from the one who reminds after the other errs.

positions.position: Repetition makes either woman the possible forgetter or reminder
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): The repeated إحداهما rather than a pronoun preserves ambiguity because either woman may forget and remind; the generic wording means if one forgets, the other reminds. SAMIN-DURR (أبو البقاء): Abu al-Baqa gives two reasons for repeating the apparent noun: preserve role ambiguity, or replace a pronoun whose reference would make the forgetter also the reminder. ALUSI-FULL (شهاب الدين الغزنوي): In the Khafaji anecdote, the judge answers that repeating one of them preserves ambiguity; a pronoun would wrongly identify a particular woman as the one subject to the ruling. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Repeating one of them instead of a pronoun lets either woman be subject or object without changing the meaning; an implicit pronoun would still have an unambiguous antecedent despite its different grammatical role. IBNASHUR-FULL (الخفاجي): Al-Khafājī says the repetition conveys generality: either woman may forget or remind, so neither is merely a secondary reminder rather than a witness in her own right.

positions.position: The first occurrence refers to a testimony, not a woman
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (حسين بن علي المغربي): Al-Maghribi takes the first one of them as one of the two testimonies and the second as one of the two women, so one woman recalls the forgotten testimony. IBNASHUR-FULL (أبو القاسم المغربي): Abū al-Qāsim al-Maghribī reads the first one as one of the two testimonies and takes ḍalāl as loss through forgetting, then assigns the second one to a woman.

positions.position: Repetition makes each clause independent and emphatic
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The author says repetition makes each clause stand alone like a maxim: forgetting explains why one woman is insufficient, and the second woman can keep the first woman’s testimony from failing altogether.

turns_on: The notes offer different readings, referents, grounds, or applications.

question: When must summoned witnesses respond?
words: وَلَا يَأْبَ ٱلشُّهَدَآءُ إِذَا مَا دُعُوا۟

positions.position: The summons requires an answer from a witness when testimony is needed.
positions.reasons: MUQATIL (author): For a debt, use two acceptable male witnesses or one man and two women; if one woman forgets, the other reminds her, and a summoned witness should serve when free. ABDURRAZZAQ (قتادة): Qatada says a witness must not refuse when called to give testimony. AKHFASH (author): فرجل وامرأتان means the witnesses to be summoned are one man and two women. IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB (author): The writer must not be made to record what was not dictated, nor the witness to testify without being summoned; another view says they may refuse a summons. TAB-FULL (الضحاك): Al-Ḍaḥḥāk includes witnesses who were formally engaged and scribes who wrote a record: when called to adjudicate a right, they must answer and report what they were entrusted with. TAB-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās also describes harm as compelling a person despite there being enough other witnesses, simply because the caller invokes the command to answer summonses. TAB-FULL (أبو سليمان المرعشي): A seller who failed to document or witness a debt and was later denied it had sinned, so his prayer against the debtor would not be answered. TAB-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās says a Muslim whose testimony is needed must give it and may not refuse when summoned. ZAJJAJ (author): If two men are unavailable, one man and two women may witness; ‘whom you approve’ means people whose standing or judgment you approve, implying some witnesses are not acceptable. FARISI-HUJJA (author): The testimony is called so one woman may forget and the other remind her; as Sibawayh explains, forgetting is the cause that makes reminding necessary, not the intended outcome. THALABI (عامر): Amir says a witness remains free to decline until he has actually testified. THALABI (طاوس والحسن وقتادة وابن زيد): On the active reading, a writer must not alter the dictated record and a witness must not invent testimony or refuse to establish what he saw. MAWARDI-FULL (ابن عباس وقتادة والربيع): Witnesses must answer a summons to have their testimony recorded in the document. MAWARDI-FULL (مجاهد والشعبي وعطاء): Witnesses must answer a summons to give testimony before a judge. WAHIDI-BASIT (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās glosses those whom you approve as people of virtue and religion, like the just witnesses in 65:2; this implies some witnesses should not be accepted. | mentions 65:2 WAHIDI-BASIT (الزجاج): Al-Zajjāj chooses the first interpretation because fisq suits a false witness or person who alters writing, not someone who merely summoned a busy witness; defenders of the second read fisq as sin and disobedience. WAHIDI-WAJIZ (author): The ban on harming a scribe or witness forbids altering records, false testimony, and refusing to testify; doing so is sinful. WAHIDI-WAJIZ (author): Witnesses are two free adult men of the believers, acceptable for their merit and religion; if one woman forgets, the other reminds her of the testimony. JISHUMI (ابن مسعود ومجاهد): Ibn Masʿud and Mujahid are associated with the fatḥa reading, meaning a witness must not be summoned while occupied in order to harm him. JISHUMI (عطاء وطاووس والحسن وقتادة وابن زيد): The writer must not be harmed by being forbidden to write or made to add or subtract from what was dictated; the witness must not be made to refuse or testify to what he does not know. JISHUMI (author): The passive reading means not to burden a writer or witness when called for an important need; another person should be summoned if possible. BAGHAWI-FULL (الحسن): He says a witness must answer if no substitute exists; where another is available, the witness may choose whether to do so. KASHSHAF-FULL (author): If two men are unavailable, one man and two women may witness; Abū Ḥanīfa accepts women’s testimony with men except in ḥudūd and retaliation. KASHSHAF-FULL (author): Witnesses must not refuse when summoned to give testimony. IBNATIYYA-FULL (أبو عبيد): Abu Ubayd glosses taḍilla as ‘forget’; the author says a witness’s error is forgetting part and remembering part, whereas total forgetfulness is not called straying from testimony. IBNATIYYA-FULL (الحسن وقتادة وطاوس وابن زيد): They say “do not harm a scribe or witness” prohibits a writer from adding to or subtracting from what was dictated and a witness from altering testimony; Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and ʿAṭāʾ also understand it to prohibit their refusal. IBNATIYYA-FULL (ابن عباس ومجاهد والضحاك والسدي وطاوس): They say a claimant harms a scribe or witness by demanding work when that person is busy or excused, then shaming him for refusing; the word's reciprocal sense encompasses these readings and the preceding ones. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): If harm means falsification by a writer or witness, fisq is the legal commission of grave sins and invalidating rights; if it means mistreatment or refusal, fisq means departing from what is right, though disobeying God's command approaches the legal sense too. TABRISI (author): If two men are unavailable, the witness set is one man and two women whose outward probity and trustworthiness the parties accept; this makes justice a condition of testimony. TABRISI (author): The wording requires witnesses acceptable to the parties, since people cannot know whom God approves except from outward reliability and integrity. TABRISI (مجاهد وعطاء وسعيد بن جبير): One reported view says summoned witnesses must not refuse to give testimony they know without doubt, provided doing so causes them no harm. TABRISI (قتادة والربيع): Qatāda and al-Rabīʿ say the witnesses must not refuse when summoned to establish and carry the testimony. TABRISI (الحسن وقتادة وعطاء وابن زيد): With kasra on the first rāʾ, the prohibition addresses the writer and witness: do not change dictated terms, testify to matters not requested, or refuse to testify. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (الزجاج): Al-Zajjaj prefers the debtor’s guardian: accepting the claimant’s dictation would leave no reason for writing and witnesses, and would simply accept the claimant’s word; Qadi Abu Yaʿla agrees. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, ʿIkrima, al-Suddi, al-Rabiʿ, al-Farra, and Muqatil say a scribe or witness must not be burdened with a summons while busy; al-Rabiʿ describes a requester insisting despite an available alternative. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (الزجاج): Al-Zajjaj argues that falsifying a document or testimony is the sort of harm called transgression in the next clause; merely summoning a busy person would not make one sinful. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (عطاء): A third view from ʿAta and others says the harm is the scribe refusing to write or the witness refusing to testify. RAZI-FULL (author): Al-Razi says the sounder reading of the phrase forbidding witnesses to refuse is a ban on withholding testimony when the rights-holder needs it. QURTUBI-FULL (author): He rejects slave testimony because the address concerns transacting believers, while slaves do not own such assets independently; he also invokes the later restriction on witnesses refusing a summons. QURTUBI-FULL (author): Witnesses must directly know what they attest: probable inference may suffice for ordinary acts such as accepting a gift or recognizing a spouse by voice, but not testimony about another's admission, sale, slander, or seizure. QURTUBI-FULL (author): Al-Qurṭubī calls those accusations mistaken: the verse does not negate the Prophet's ruling by an oath and one witness, and an exclusive reading would also invalidate claims proved when a defendant refuses to swear, contrary to consensus. QURTUBI-FULL (القاضي أبو محمد عبد الوهاب): Among jurists accepting oath-plus-witness, its use is limited by consensus to property and related rights, not bodily rights; property rights are lower because women's testimony is accepted there. QURTUBI-FULL (author): The verse indicates that witnesses go to the judge when summoned, a practice established across legal traditions and reflected in a proverb. QURTUBI-FULL (author): An enslaved person is excluded from the witness class because he cannot independently answer a summons, just as he lacks independent authority in other duties. QURTUBI-FULL (ابن عباس ومجاهد وعطاء): Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and ʿAṭāʾ interpret the prohibition as forbidding a scribe or witness from refusing when asked to serve. BAYDAWI-FULL (author): Lā yuḍārr has two readings: scribes and witnesses must not refuse, distort, or alter testimony, or others must not harm them by disrupting duties, demanding extra travel, or withholding their fees and expenses. BAYDAWI-FULL (author): Witnesses are sought for the debt; men from your community means Muslims, which most scholars require, while Abu Hanifa accepts non-Muslims' testimony among themselves. NASAFI-FULL (author): Two witnesses are sought from believing men; Islam, freedom, and adulthood are conditions, while the author's school accepts non-Muslims testifying among themselves. NASAFI-FULL (author): If two men are unavailable, one man and two women may witness; male testimony with women is accepted outside fixed punishments and retaliation. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): “Seek two witnesses” is a request for testimony or equivalent to “make two witnesses”; shahīd is intensive, suggesting experienced witnesses whose repeated use indicates acceptance and integrity. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Some accept a mute witness through gestures and some reject the testimony; deaf witnesses are rejected for spoken claims but accepted for other sensory matters. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (ابن أبي ليلى، أبو حنيفة، أبو يوسف، محمد): They accept upright witnesses from sectarian groups except the Khaṭṭābiyya among the Rāfiḍa; Muḥammad rejects Kharijites but accepts Ḥarūriyya because he distinguishes their treatment of Muslims' property. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (ابن أبي ليلى، مالك): Ibn Abī Laylā rejects a poor witness because poverty may prompt desire for money; Mālik rejects beggars in substantial matters but accepts testimony in trivial ones. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الشافعي): One report rejects a witness whose usual conduct is sinful or indecent; another accepts one whose usual conduct is obedience and who has committed no major sin. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الحسن، ابن شبرمة، محمد، أبو يوسف، مالك، الليث، الشافعي): They differ over investigating witnesses: al-Ḥasan accepts unless impeached; Ibn Shubrumah investigates if challenged; Muḥammad and Abū Yūsuf always investigate; Mālik requires private inquiry; al-Layth lets the opponent produce discrediting evidence; al-Shāfiʿī adds public attestation after private clearance. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): An active reading forbids a writer altering the document or a witness concealing, changing, or withholding testimony; al-Zajjāj prefers this. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and ʿAṭāʾ also explain harm as refusing with excuses about being busy. IBNKATHIR-FULL (قتادة): He recounts Abu Sulayman al-Mar'ashi's warning: a seller who grants credit without writing or witnesses and is later cheated has wronged himself by disobeying God, so his plea is not answered. IBNKATHIR-FULL (مجاهد وأبو مجلز): If invited to take testimony, one may choose; after having witnessed, one must respond when called to testify. IBNKATHIR-FULL (ابن عباس): Another interpretation forbids burdening or harming the writer and witness: a person summons them, and they explain that they are occupied, but he insists that they were commanded to answer; Ibn Abbas says the caller may not harm them. Similar views are attributed to many early authorities. BIQAI-FULL (author): The phrase your men implies Muslim witnesses and, by the verse's wording and conditions, free witnesses; the witness must be reliable and accepted. DURR-FULL (ابن عباس): Debt should be witnessed to prevent denial or forgetting; someone who refuses a needed request to testify despite holding evidence disobeys, while a requester must not burden a scribe or witness when another is available. DURR-FULL (سعيد بن جبير): The witnesses should be two free Muslim men or one man and two women; one woman may forget and the other remind her, and witnesses who hold testimony must respond when called. BURSEVI (author): Two male witnesses are sought to carry testimony about the transaction; they are called witnesses in anticipation of giving testimony later. ALUSI-FULL (author): If active, the verse forbids witnesses and scribes to refuse, distort, add, or subtract; if passive, it forbids burdening them, withholding the fee, or requiring costly travel. ELMALILI (author): Where men can know the matter, women should not be made witnesses; if no man is available and a woman must be called, two women should serve for one man. ELMALILI (author): The witnesses must be people whose testimony is accepted and whose justice and reliability are known; a random pairing is not valid. ELMALILI (author): The command not to harm a scribe or witness can mean they must not harm rights-holders by refusing a request or falsifying or altering the writing or testimony. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The parties are commanded because they may neglect to secure witnesses, while witnesses are forbidden because they may refuse; each rule addresses the likely lapse and implies its opposite. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Harm includes parties burdening a scribe or witness with hardship, loss, or exposure to punishment, and witnesses causing a party to lose a right or suffer the burden of answering. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT (author): The verse forbids writers and witnesses from harming others by suppressing, refusing, or distorting testimony, and forbids others from coercing them into the same harms.

positions.position: The ban concerns accepting an initial call to witness
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (عطاء): ʿAṭāʾ is also reported to say that an invitation to give new testimony is a recommendation that may be accepted or declined. TAB-FULL (قتادة): Qatāda says the clause forbids refusing an initial request to witness rights; he recounts a man calling through a large encampment with no one answering, and reads the verse as testifying for one person against another. TAB-FULL (السدي): Al-Suddī says an available witness should not refuse an initial request to come forward and testify. ZAJJAJ (الحسن): Al-Hasan says witnesses must not refuse when summoned to begin giving testimony. THALABI (author): Jurists disagree whether writing is obligatory; Ibn Jurayj says a borrower should write and a seller obtain witnesses, the view chosen by al-Tabari and supported by a prophetic report that begins by naming three unanswered supplications. WAHIDI-BASIT (طاوس والحسن وقتادة وابن زيد): One reading prohibits harming a scribe or witness through falsifying or altering the record, bearing false testimony, or refusing to testify; the active form has the writer and witness as agents. WAHIDI-WAJIZ (author): Witnesses must not refuse when summoned to bear or give testimony; parties should not let irritation keep them from recording a small or large debt through its due date. JISHUMI (author): Some reject interpreting the call as bearing testimony because the people have not yet become witnesses; Jishumi answers that the command to seek two witnesses makes them witnesses. BAGHAWI-FULL (author): One view says witnesses are called to undertake testimony; some therefore make answering obligatory, while al-Hasan requires it only when no one else is available, and others recommend it in every case. KASHSHAF-FULL (وقيل): Another interpretation is that they are summoned to bear testimony; they may be called witnesses before bearing it because the imminent is named as present. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAtiyya, Qatada, and al-Rabiʿ say witnesses are called to bear testimony and have it recorded. BAYDAWI-FULL (author): Witnesses must not refuse to give or undertake testimony; they are called witnesses in advance because the expected event is treated as imminent, and mā is extra. NASAFI-FULL (author): The active reading forbids a scribe or witness to refuse, distort, add, or omit; the passive forbids burdening them, rushing them from duties, withholding the scribe's fee, or making a witness bear travel costs. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (أبو حنيفة، إياس بن معاوية، بلال بن أبي بردة، عمر بن عبد العزيز، شريح، أبو هريرة، محمد): Reports reject witnesses for miserliness, sea-trading, eating clay, plucking or hiding the beard, answering a disparaging nickname, slave dealing, frivolity, effeminacy, or flying pigeons; Shurayḥ's anecdote illustrates the nickname ruling. IBNKATHIR-FULL (قتادة والربيع بن أنس): They interpret 'when called' as a summons to undertake testimony, which witnesses must accept; this makes taking testimony a communal obligation. BURSEVI (author): Witnesses should not refuse when summoned to give or bear testimony. ELMALILI (author): A summons to bear or give testimony must not be refused: testimony is a collective duty, and becomes individually obligatory when nobody else can meet the need or particular people are required. IBNASHUR-FULL (قتادة): Qatāda, al-Rabīʿ ibn Sulaymān, and a report from Ibn ʿAbbās understand the omitted object as being called to bear witness at the transaction; refusing to bear it is forbidden all the more.

positions.position: The ban concerns delivery of testimony already held
positions.reasons: MUJAHID (مجاهد): The witnesses must not refuse when called if they had already witnessed the transaction. MAJAZ (author): A witness who has already testified must not refuse a summons; before witnessing, the person may choose not to testify. TAB-FULL (عطاء): ʿAṭāʾ says those summoned are people who already testified; an initial invitation may be declined because witnesses are plentiful, unlike the scribe's binding duty to write. TAB-FULL (ابن زيد): Ibn Zayd says a witness who has testified must answer a summons to deliver and perform that testimony. TAB-FULL (قتادة): Qatāda says al-Ḥasan interpreted the verse as requiring a person who already has testimony to perform it when summoned. TAB-FULL (مجاهد): Mujāhid generally takes the command to concern carrying out testimony already given or held, not refusing a summons to perform it. TAB-FULL (مجاهد): Mujāhid also distinguishes existing testimony, which must be performed, from a new invitation to witness, which one may accept or decline. ZAJJAJ (غير الحسن): Another view applies the command only to witnesses already holding testimony who are summoned to deliver it; those not yet witnesses may choose whether to accept an initial request. IBNABIHATIM (عامر): A person who has already witnessed must attend when summoned, but one not yet a witness may choose whether to testify; Mujahid, Saʿid, Rabiʿa, and Zayd ibn Aslam report similarly. THALABI (مجاهد وعطاء وعكرمة وسعيد بن جبير والضحاك والسدي): Mujahid and these scholars say the prohibition concerns establishing testimony already witnessed: a witness must not refuse when called to give it. BAGHAWI-FULL (مجاهد وعطاء وعكرمة وسعيد بن جبير): They understand the command as requiring witnesses to attend and deliver testimony they already accepted. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): When necessity or a real risk of losing a right arises, the recommendation approaches obligation; if delay will certainly destroy the right, testimony is obligatory, especially when it was already acquired and the summons is to deliver it, as a trust owed. RAZI-FULL (author): Al-Razi favors testimony performance: the witnesses are already called witnesses, and the command is obligatory for all, whereas accepting testimony is not required of everyone. QURTUBI-FULL (الشافعي وابن أبي ليلى وأبو يوسف): They accept testimony after blindness when the witness already knew the person before losing sight, analogizing the impairment to absence or death; al-Qurṭubī sees no reason to reject testimony previously borne while sighted and accepts public knowledge for lineage. QURTUBI-FULL (مجاهد): Mujāhid interprets the summons as a request to give testimony already held; he and others say an initial invitation to witness may be declined. NASAFI-FULL (author): Witnesses are called witnesses before they testify because the anticipated event is treated as already actual; the first command is obligatory in principle and the second recommended. IBNKATHIR-FULL (الجمهور): The majority interprets the summons as one to give testimony already borne; a witness must answer when personally required, otherwise the duty is communal. DURR-FULL (سعيد بن جبير): The witnesses who must not refuse are those who already hold testimony. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Those invited are called witnesses in anticipation: their invitation itself signals that they are already committed to accept the witnessing role.

positions.position: It covers both undertaking and delivering testimony
positions.reasons: ABDURRAZZAQ (الحسن): Al-Hasan says the prohibition covers both withholding testimony one already has and refusing to testify when summoned. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): He prefers al-Hasan’s inclusive reading: the verse recommends both forms of assistance. With ample witnesses and no danger to the right, a summoned person may decline for even a slight excuse; otherwise declining without excuse earns neither sin nor reward. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (ابن عطية): Ibn ʿAṭiyya combines both readings: assistance is recommended when witnesses are plentiful, nearly obligatory in necessity, and obligatory if delay would destroy the right, especially when summoned to perform testimony already borne. BIQAI-FULL (author): Witnesses must not refuse either to bear testimony when called or to give it after bearing it; the added ma makes the summons emphatic. ALUSI-FULL (ابن عباس والحسن): Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan are cited for interpreting the witnesses’ refusal as refusal either to give testimony or to undertake it.
