question: Is the summons duty individual, communal, or advisory?

positions.position: Responding is individually obligatory when needed
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): Al-Ṭabarī says an initial request to witness is obligatory only when no other suitable witness is available, by broader duties to preserve a fellow Muslim's right, not by this verse itself. TAB-FULL (الحسن والشعبي): Al-Ḥasan and al-Shaʿbī treat witnessing at sale as recommended or optional, citing the permission to rely on trust. | mentions 2:283 TAB-FULL (author): Al-Ṭabarī rules that witnessing every purchase and sale is an obligatory duty, because divine commands bind unless evidence shows a recommendation; he rejects abrogation by the trust clause. | mentions 2:283 TAB-FULL (الشعبي): Al-Shaʿbī says answering an initial request is optional when others are available, but obligatory if no other witness can be found. ZAJJAJ (author): The author argues that the next command not to tire of writing reinforces that giving testimony from the outset is obligatory. NAHHAS (الفراء): Some say recording deferred debts and witnessing sales are recommendations, by analogy with commands that grant permission after a prohibition. | mentions 2:282 NAHHAS (عبد الله بن عمر): Ibn Umar says witnessing is obligatory for every sale, large or small, citing the command to witness sales. | mentions 2:282 THALABI (الشعبي): The debt record, witnesses, and pledge were initially obligatory, then the trust clause abrogated that requirement. | mentions 2:283 THALABI (الشعبي): Al-Shaʿbi says accepting a witness role is optional when another witness is available and obligatory when the person is the only one. THALABI (آخرون): Other scholars treat witnessing sales as recommended, leaving the parties free to call witnesses or not. MAWARDI-FULL (الضحاك وداود بن علي): Witnessing sales is obligatory. MAWARDI-FULL (الحسن والشعبي ومالك والشافعي): Witnessing sales is recommended. WAHIDI-BASIT (عطاء وابن جريج وإبراهيم وابن جرير): A group, chosen by Ibn Jarīr, treat writing and witnessing deferred debts as obligatory to protect wealth and deter denial; Ibrāhīm says even a tiny handful of greens should be documented. WAHIDI-BASIT (آخرون): Others say writing, witnesses, or collateral were initially obligatory but were abrogated by the trust clause in 2:283, which permits leaving documentation when the parties trust each other. | mentions 2:283 WAHIDI-BASIT (قتادة والربيع): Qatāda and al-Rabīʿ say the ban on refusing applies when asked to undertake testimony; al-Shaʿbī makes it obligatory only if no one else can do so. WAHIDI-WAJIZ (author): An immediate exchange of goods is exempt from writing because the risks of delayed payment are absent; witnessing spot sales is also no longer obligatory under the abrogated ruling. DAMGHANI (author): The two women witnesses are unidentified women, not a named individual or pair. JISHUMI (الشعبي): Al-Shaʿbī reports that writing, witnessing, and pledging were once obligatory and were abrogated by the following verse’s allowance when parties trust each other; Jishumi prefers the view that writing is recommended as a means of securing rights. | mentions 2:283 JISHUMI (الحسن والشافعي): Al-Ḥasan and al-Shāfiʿī regard witnessing sales as recommended, which Jishumi says is the jurists’ position. JISHUMI (author): If the verse concerns bearing testimony, that duty is variously described as communal obligation, recommendation, or permission; if giving testimony, it is communal when others can do it and individual when no substitute exists. JISHUMI (الضحاك): Al-Ḍaḥḥāk considers witnessing a sale obligatory. JISHUMI (author): Writing and witnessing are guidance and recommendation, not obligation, since a creditor may waive the right itself and need not document it as a precaution. BAGHAWI-FULL (author): Some consider writing obligatory, but most deem the command recommendatory; al-Shaʿbi says writing, witnessing, and pledging were obligatory then abrogated by the trust provision. | mentions 2:283 BAGHAWI-FULL (الشعبي): Al-Shaʿbi holds that writing, witnessing, and pledging were initially obligatory and that the instruction to fulfill a trusted deposit abrogated all three. | mentions 2:283 BAGHAWI-FULL (author): One view says witnesses are called to undertake testimony; some therefore make answering obligatory, while al-Hasan requires it only when no one else is available, and others recommend it in every case. BAGHAWI-FULL (الضحاك): He considers witnessing a binding command for both small and large transactions, cash or credit; Abu Saʿid al-Khudri leaves it to mutual trust, while others call it recommended. | mentions 2:283 KASHSHAF-FULL (الضحاك): Al-Ḍaḥḥāk considers witnessing obligatory even for a bunch of greens. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): The sound view is that witnessing makes a transaction prudent while mutual trust leaves room; no abrogation follows, because documentation is recommended as a precaution for rights people may waive, and 2:283 instructs debtors to repay when trusted. | mentions 2:283 IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): He prefers al-Hasan’s inclusive reading: the verse recommends both forms of assistance. With ample witnesses and no danger to the right, a summoned person may decline for even a slight excuse; otherwise declining without excuse earns neither sin nor reward. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): When necessity or a real risk of losing a right arises, the recommendation approaches obligation; if delay will certainly destroy the right, testimony is obligatory, especially when it was already acquired and the summons is to deliver it, as a trust owed. IBNATIYYA-FULL (الحسن والشعبي): Al-Ḥasan, al-Shaʿbī, and others say witnessing a transaction is recommended; Ibn ʿAmr and al-Ḍaḥḥāk say it is obligatory, followed by Ibn ʿUmar's practice and ʿAṭāʾ, with al-Ṭabarī preferring obligation. IBNATIYYA-FULL (القاضي أبو محمد): Ibn ʿAṭiyya finds obligation untenable: witnessing tiny sales is burdensome, while larger dealings may rely on social trust or customary practice. He prefers recommendation unless an excuse prevents it. TABRISI (الحسن وجميع الفقهاء): Al-Ḥasan and the jurists regard witnessing sales as recommended; the Ẓāhirīs make it obligatory. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (author): Witnessing is recommended for transactions where it is customary. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (الجمهور): The majority treat writing debts and witnessing sales or debts as recommended, so the command remains operative without abrogation. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (ابن عمر): A group including Ibn ʿUmar, Abu Musa, Mujahid, Ibn Sirin, and others regard writing and witnessing as obligatory. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (القاضي أبو يعلى): Qadi Abu Yaʿla says a witness must attend to perform testimony only if no one else can testify; both bearing and performing it are communal duties like jihad. RAZI-FULL (author): Al-Razi favors testimony performance: the witnesses are already called witnesses, and the command is obligatory for all, whereas accepting testimony is not required of everyone. RAZI-FULL (author): If the witness is uniquely available, giving testimony is an individual duty; if many can testify, it is a communal duty. RAZI-FULL (عطاء وابن جريج والنخعي والطبري): ʿAtaʾ, Ibn Jurayj, al-Nakhaʿi, and al-Tabari hold that writing and witnessing deferred debts are obligatory; al-Nakhaʿi even requires witnessing a tiny vegetable purchase. RAZI-FULL (الشافعي وأبو حنيفة): Al-Shafiʿi and Abu Hanifa reject an enslaved person as a witness, reasoning that the command to attend testimony cannot be obligatory for slaves. QURTUBI-FULL (author): Seeking witnesses is recommended, not obligatory, as al-Qurṭubī explains later. QURTUBI-FULL (ابن عطية): Ibn ʿAṭiyya treats assistance as recommended when witnesses are plentiful, increasingly urgent when rights may be lost, and obligatory when delay will destroy a right. QURTUBI-FULL (author): Al-Qurṭubī rejects the view that testimony already held is merely recommended: it is obligatory when a right risks loss, supported by Qurʾānic commands and the Prophet's call to aid the wronged. | mentions 65:2, 43:86 QURTUBI-FULL (الطبري): Al-Ṭabarī reads the witnessing command as covering small and large sales; Abū Mūsā, Ibn ʿUmar, and others hold it obligatory, and ʿAṭāʾ demands witnesses for tiny purchases. QURTUBI-FULL (الشعبي والحسن): Al-Shaʿbī and al-Ḥasan treat witnessing as recommendation and guidance rather than a binding duty; Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and other jurists are also said to hold this. QURTUBI-FULL (ابن عطية): Ibn ʿAṭiyya finds mandatory witnessing impractical for small sales and sometimes socially awkward; he treats it as recommended for its usual benefit unless an excuse intervenes. QURTUBI-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās says the debt verse is established, not abrogated, and writing, pledges, and witnesses are alternative means of securing debt; witnessing is recommended like pledging. | mentions 2:283 NASAFI-FULL (author): Witnesses are called witnesses before they testify because the anticipated event is treated as already actual; the first command is obligatory in principle and the second recommended. NASAFI-FULL (author): Witnessing sales is recommended for immediate and deferred exchanges as a precaution, or the command concerns immediate trade alone, where testimony suffices without writing. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (ابن عطية): Ibn ʿAṭiyya combines both readings: assistance is recommended when witnesses are plentiful, nearly obligatory in necessity, and obligatory if delay would destroy the right, especially when summoned to perform testimony already borne. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (أبو موسى الأشعري، ابن عمر، الضحاك، ابن المسيب، جابر بن زيد، مجاهد، عطاء، إبراهيم، الشعبي، النخعي، داود بن علي): They hold witnessing obligatory; al-Ḍaḥḥāk requires it even for greens and ʿAṭāʾ for any price. Al-Ṭabarī says an unwitnessed sale defies God's Book. IBNKATHIR-FULL (قتادة والربيع بن أنس): They interpret 'when called' as a summons to undertake testimony, which witnesses must accept; this makes taking testimony a communal obligation. IBNKATHIR-FULL (الجمهور): The majority interprets the summons as one to give testimony already borne; a witness must answer when personally required, otherwise the duty is communal. IBNKATHIR-FULL (الجمهور): The majority treats witnessing sales as guidance and recommendation, not obligation; the report of the Prophet's disputed horse purchase and Khuzaima's extraordinary testimony supports this. BIQAI-FULL (author): Witnesses should be present whenever parties trade, immediately or later, whether for business or another purpose; this instruction is guidance, not an obligation. ALUSI-FULL (author): The command to seek witnesses is considered recommended or obligatory according to the broader disagreement over these commands. ELMALILI (author): A summons to bear or give testimony must not be refused: testimony is a collective duty, and becomes individually obligatory when nobody else can meet the need or particular people are required. ELMALILI (author): The majority of exegetes regard witnessing a sale here as a recommendation for precaution. ELMALILI (author): Although giving testimony is especially important, necessity can make both accepting and giving testimony individually obligatory. IBNASHUR-FULL (جمهور السلف): The majority of early authorities interpret the command to obtain two witnesses as obligatory. IBNASHUR-FULL (مالك): The later majority of jurists, including Mālik, Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Shāfiʿī, and Aḥmad, regard witnessing as recommended; the discussion continues at the command to witness sales. IBNASHUR-FULL (ابن الحاجب): Ibn al-Ḥājib says bearing witness is a communal duty when needed, while giving testimony from a distance of two barīd is an individual duty and cannot be replaced by an oath. IBNASHUR-FULL (أبو حنيفة): The author applies the earlier disagreement about scribes: accepting the request to bear witness becomes individual when designated, and giving testimony is individually obligatory if it causes no bodily or financial harm; Abū Ḥanīfa makes performance communal unless uniquely required, subject to court integrity, proximity, admissibility, and a claimant’s request. IBNASHUR-FULL (أبو موسى الأشعري): Abū Mūsā, Ibn ʿUmar, Abū Saʿīd, Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, Mujāhid, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿAṭāʾ, Ibn Jurayj, al-Nakhaʿī, Jābir ibn Zayd, Dāwūd, and al-Ṭabarī take witnessing at sales as obligatory. IBNASHUR-FULL (مالك): Al-Ḥasan and al-Shaʿbī, followed by Mālik, Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Shāfiʿī, and Aḥmad, regard witnessing as recommended; they cite the Prophet’s sales without witnesses.

positions.position: Responding is recommended or optional when others can serve
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (عطية العوفي): ʿAṭiyya al-ʿAwfī treats the rule as a recommendation for a man or woman invited to give new testimony, not as an obligation. TAB-FULL (عطاء): ʿAṭāʾ is also reported to say that an invitation to give new testimony is a recommendation that may be accepted or declined. WAHIDI-BASIT (الفراء): Al-Farrāʾ regards writing and witnesses as recommendation and permission like the commands in 5:2 and 62:10: documenting is good but leaving it is harmless. | mentions 5:2, 62:10 WAHIDI-BASIT (أبو عبيد): Abū ʿUbayd says scholars in the Ḥijāz and Iraq agree that sale witnesses are not mandatory and that buyers can choose; they treat the following trust clause as abrogating the obligation. | mentions 2:283 JISHUMI (author): Taking witnesses is guidance and recommendation in ordinary transactions; most jurists require witnesses for marriage, though Malik does not. BAYDAWI-FULL (author): Witness the sale in particular or every sale as safer; most imams recommend the commands, while some require them and debate whether they remain effective or are abrogated. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (ابن عباس، قتادة، الربيع؛ عطاء، الحسن؛ الشعبي): Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, and al-Rabīʿ read the summons as initial bearing; ʿAṭāʾ and al-Ḥasan consider it advisory, while al-Shaʿbī requires it when no other witness exists. BURSEVI (author): Witness sales either in this particular transaction or generally as a precaution; the majority take the verse’s commands as recommendations. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): When a cash transaction is immediately completed, the writing requirement is lifted though witnesses remain recommended, because disputes can arise even without a term.

JISHUMI (author): Some say the command that a scribe not refuse was abrogated by the instruction not to harm a scribe or witness; the adopted practice is the first view, communal obligation. STUDYQURAN (author): The testimony stipulation is particular to this circumstance and addresses social or communal difficulties; the approval of witnesses also suggests competence in this specialized area.

positions.position: The duty's force varies with need and available witnesses.

question: What incident illustrates refusal to witness?

positions.position: Reports describe people refusing a request to serve as witnesses.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (قتادة): Qatāda says the clause forbids refusing an initial request to witness rights; he recounts a man calling through a large encampment with no one answering, and reads the verse as testifying for one person against another. TAB-FULL (الربيع): Al-Rabīʿ reports the same setting: people summoned in a large gathering would not follow the caller to testify. THALABI (قتادة والربيع): Qatada and al-Rabiʿ report that people once refused when asked to witness in a large neighborhood, prompting this verse. KASHSHAF-FULL (قتادة): Qatāda says a verse was revealed after a man visited a large gathering and nobody followed him, illustrating refusal to respond. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (قتادة): Qatāda relates an occasion of revelation in which a man passed through a large gathering at Ḥirāʾ and no one accompanied him. DURR-FULL (قتادة): Qatada reports the same occasion: people in a large neighborhood ignored a man's call to testify, so the verse was revealed. ELMALILI (author): Qatada relates that the verse was revealed after a man went from camp to camp seeking a witness and no one paid attention.

question: What does تسأموا mean?

positions.position: Saʾama means growing weary or irritated.
positions.reasons: MUQATIL (author): Do not tire of recording even a small amount through its due date: writing better records the term and protects property, is just, reliable for testimony, and less likely to create doubt. AKHFASH (author): تسأم is from the verb سئمت, with the listed verbal nouns سآمة, سأمة, سآما, and سأما. IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB (author): ولا تسأموا means do not grow tired. TAB-FULL (author): Do not grow weary of recording a small or large debt until its term; a written record keeps track of both the due date and amount. question: What is meant by أدنى ألا ترتابوا?

question: What is the scope of the cash-trade exception?

positions.position: Immediate trade is exempt from writing only
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): Al-Ṭabarī rules that recording a fixed-term debt and the scribe's duty to write are binding unless proof establishes recommendation; the trust exception applies when writing or a scribe is unavailable, so it does not abrogate the ordinary rule. | mentions 2:283 IBNABIHATIM (السدى): The exemption from writing refers to transactions between people present in the same town. IBNABIHATIM (سعيد بن جبير): The exception from writing applies to immediate trade. THALABI (author): The exemption from writing applies to the cash transaction, while witnesses are still commanded when a sale takes place. WAHIDI-WAJIZ (author): An immediate exchange of goods is exempt from writing because the risks of delayed payment are absent; witnessing spot sales is also no longer obligatory under the abrogated ruling. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (author): The exception is an immediate exchange in which each party must deliver what it contracted for at once; ʿAsim reads tijāratan in the accusative, treating the funds as the commerce, and writing is waived to avoid burden in ordinary purchases. RAZI-FULL (author): The exception for immediate trade may be connected to the debt-writing command or to the writer’s duty, or disconnected as a separate concession; ease and immediate exchange explain the concession. RAZI-FULL (أكثر المفسرين): Most exegetes say immediate trade is exempt from writing but remains subject to witnessing, which is easier and avoids later memory failure. BAYDAWI-FULL (author): The exception covers present trade managed hand to hand, whether exchanging debt or goods, where writing is less necessary to prevent dispute and forgetfulness. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): The exception is disconnected because immediate sales are not deferred debts; writing may be omitted because it protects against uncertainty about amount, description, and term. Other views connect the exception to the debt or writing command. SAMIN-DURR (مكي ابن أبي طالب): Makki b. Abi Talib calls the exception disconnected; the author prefers this reading as the apparent sense, permitting omission of writing and witnesses for immediate trade. BIQAI-FULL (author): The exemption from writing applies to cash trade, because merchandise circulates and is not held by one person for long. ALUSI-FULL (author): The cash-trade exception is best read as a detached exception from the writing command: immediate exchange of both countervalues permits leaving the transaction unwritten. ALUSI-FULL (author): Other analyses make the exception detached from both writing and witnessing, or attach it to both; al-Alusi favors the first analysis. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The connected-exception reading takes immediate trade to mean a debt due soon and exempts that debt from writing, but the author considers this remote. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The explicit statement that there is no blame restates the exception and signals a concession; writing nevertheless remains preferable.

positions.position: Immediate trade is exempt from both writing and witnesses
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA (author): أن in إلا أن تكون تجارة عن تراض منكم is accusative and governed by لا تأكلوا through إلا; both exceptions are disconnected. Sibawayh reports an accusative reading of تجارة. | mentions 4:29 ALUSI-FULL (أبو حيان): The Dur al-Masun allows a connected exception from witnessing: cash trade is exempt from witnessing in every case.
SAMIN-DURR (أبو البقاء): Abu al-Baqa treats the trade exception as connected: from all transactions requiring testimony, it excludes the case of present trade.

positions.reasons: IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The immediate-trade exception qualifies the general range of transactions; it may be a disconnected exception because an immediate cash sale is not a debt.

question: How is تجارة حاضرة read and parsed?

positions.position: Nominative تجارة: kāna is complete or takes the trading clause as predicate
positions.reasons: FARRA (author): In إلا أن تكون تجارة حاضرة تديرونها, تديرونها may be accusative or nominative; an indefinite noun can take a verbal predicate in either position. FARRA (author): When the noun is overt, as in فإن كن نساء, the predicate can still be nominative or accusative, as in the cited trade construction. TAB-FULL (author): Most Hijaz, Iraqi, and other reciters raise تجارة حاضرة; some Kufans use the accusative, which is grammatically possible, but al-Ṭabarī prefers the widespread nominative reading. TAB-FULL (بعض نحويي البصرة): Some Basran grammarians treat kāna here as a complete verb meaning “exist” or “occur,” with تجارة حاضرة as its subject and no predicate. TAB-FULL (author): Al-Ṭabarī says the complete-verb analysis is grammatically possible but less apt; تديرونها بينكم can be the predicate in the accusative or follow the indefinite تجارة حاضرة in the nominative. IBNMUJAHID (عاصم): Asim alone reads إلا أن تكون تجارة حاضرة with both words accusative; the other readers use nominative, though Abu Bakr hesitates about Ibn Amir. FARISI-HUJJA (author): Asim alone reads تجارة منصوب; the rest read it nominative, though Abu Bakr is unsure about Ibn Amir. WAHIDI-BASIT (أبو الحسن الأخفش): Al-Akhfash supplies an implicit kāna; it may take a predicate or be complete, with the complete verb preferred because it requires fewer omitted words, though either reading implies testimony by one man and two women. JISHUMI (author): For the nominative reading, one analysis supplies تقع: unless a trade occurs. JISHUMI (author): Another nominative analysis makes تجارة the subject of كان and the following clause its predicate, meaning a trade circulating among you. BAGHAWI-FULL (author): The other readers use the nominative either with kāna meaning occur, or with trade as its subject and your exchanging it as its predicate; this is hand-to-hand trade without a term, which need not be written. KASHSHAF-FULL (author): Trade is read nominative with kāna complete or incomplete, or accusative in an excepted construction illustrated by poetry. IBNATIYYA-FULL (عاصم): ʿĀṣim reads tijāratan in the accusative; the other readers read it in the nominative, though Abū ʿAlī is unsure about Ibn ʿĀmir. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): With nominative, kāna means “occur” and needs no predicate; with accusative, its event sense is absent and an omitted subject or predicate is supplied, such as “unless the transaction is a trade.” TABRISI (author): With the nominative reading, كان means “occur” or “happen,” so the phrase means that a present trade occurs. TABRISI (عاصم): ʿĀṣim alone reads تجارة حاضرة in the accusative; the others read it nominative. RAZI-FULL (author): An takuna may use kāna for occurrence, or incomplete kāna with تجارة حاضرة as its subject and تديرونها as predicate; al-Farraʾ gives the latter parse. RAZI-FULL (عاصم): ʿAsim reads تجارة in the accusative, while the other readers use the nominative. BAYDAWI-FULL (عاصم): Asim reads tijāratan in the accusative as a predicate with an omitted subject; the other readers make it nominative, either with tadīrūnahā as predicate or as a complete verb. NASAFI-FULL (author): Other readings analyze يكون as complete, meaning an immediate transaction occurs, or as incomplete with تجارة حاضرة as its subject and تديرونها as predicate. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (عاصم، الباقون): ʿĀṣim reads “trade, present” in the accusative, with kāna incomplete; others use nominative and a complete verb. SAMIN-DURR (author): ʿAsim reads ‘trade’ and its adjective in the accusative; in al-Nisaʾ the two other Kūfan readers agree, while the rest read both nominative. | mentions 4:29 SAMIN-DURR (author): With nominative, kāna may be complete, meaning a trade occurs; ‘you circulate it’ is then an adjectival clause, a more idiomatic order. SAMIN-DURR (الفراء): Alternatively, kāna is incomplete: ‘trade’ is its subject and ‘you circulate it’ its predicate; al-Farraʾ and others adopt this. NASHR (الباقون): The other readers read both words in تجارة حاضرة in the nominative. ALUSI-FULL (author): Other grammarians make the implied subject refer to the transaction and treat trade as a verbal noun; most readers use the nominative, with trade as subject and the clause as predicate, or take kāna as complete. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Most readers vocalize tijāratun as nominative with kāna complete; ʿĀṣim reads it accusative with kāna incomplete and an understood noun repeated as predicate. QIRAAT-ER (author): Nominative tijāratun makes kāna complete, meaning that a present trade exists, rather than taking an accusative predicate; both are canonical. QIRAAT-ER (author): Nominative ḥāḍiratun agrees with the nominative tijāratun reading and the complete-verb analysis of kāna.

positions.position: Accusative تجارة: kāna has an omitted subject
positions.reasons: AKHFASH (author): تكون in إلا أن تكون تجارة حاضرة can mean 'occur'; alternatively it can take an accusative predicate with an implied subject, تلك. TAB-FULL (بعض الناس): Some assume the accusative reading requires the masculine form يكون, as though its sense were “unless it be a trade.” ZAJJAJ (author): Most readers raise تجارة: the exception means ‘unless a cash trade takes place’; ʿĀṣim’s accusative reading means ‘unless the debt transaction is a cash trade.’ NAHHAS (الأخفش): Al-Akhfash construes تجارة as the subject of تكون; others take تديرونها as its predicate. FARISI-HUJJA (author): أن in إلا أن تكون تجارة عن تراض منكم is accusative and governed by لا تأكلوا through إلا; both exceptions are disconnected. Sibawayh reports an accusative reading of تجارة. | mentions 4:29 THALABI (عاصم): Asim reads the immediate-trade exception in the accusative as a predicate of kāna with its subject omitted; the syntax is explained further in the next segment. THALABI (author): The majority reading raises tijāra under either an existential sense of kāna or as its subject, with تديرونها بينكم as predicate. WAHIDI-BASIT (عاصم): ʿĀṣim reads tijāratan ḥāḍiratan in the accusative; Abū Isḥāq understands an implied present debt transaction. JISHUMI (عاصم): Asim reads تجارة in the accusative as the predicate of كان, with an omitted subject: unless the trade is a trade. BAGHAWI-FULL (عاصم): Asim reads tijāratan ḥāḍiratan in the accusative, supplying an omitted subject: the trade or transaction is a present trade. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (author): The exception is an immediate exchange in which each party must deliver what it contracted for at once; ʿAsim reads tijāratan in the accusative, treating the funds as the commerce, and writing is waived to avoid burden in ordinary purchases. RAZI-FULL (الزجاج): Al-Zajjaj parses the accusative by supplying مداينة as the subject, while Abu ʿAli al-Farisi objects that a debt transaction cannot be immediate trade. NASAFI-FULL (عاصم): ʿĀṣim reads the phrase so تجارة is the noun of كان or an appositional clarification of trade. SAMIN-DURR (الزجاج): For ʿAsim’s accusative reading, al-Zajjaj supplies an omitted subject for kāna, estimating ‘debt transaction.’ NASHR (عاصم): ʿĀṣim reads both words in تجارة حاضرة in the accusative. ALUSI-FULL (عاصم): Asim reads tijaratan in the accusative as the predicate of kāna, with an implicit subject referring to trade.

positions.position: The case of tijāra depends on how kāna is parsed.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Abu Jaafar reads tijāratan hāḍiratan with an ungeminated rāʾ; Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read furuhun with both rāʾ and hāʾ vocalized and without the alif.

question: What does no blame for leaving it unwritten mean?

positions.position: No blame means omission is permitted without sin
positions.reasons: IBNABIHATIM (سعيد بن جبير): No blame means no hardship or difficulty. THALABI (قوم): Writing the debt is recommended and discretionary: documenting it is good, but leaving it carries no blame. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): For most exegetes, “no blame” means no harm in omitting writing because writing is not obligatory; those who require it interpret the phrase as “no sin.” SAMIN-DURR (أبو البقاء): Abu al-Baqa says the fāʾ in ‘there is no blame’ signals that the following clause depends on the preceding one. ELMALILI (author): The exception is a fully cash, hand-to-hand commercial transaction; in that case leaving it unwritten causes no blame. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The explicit statement that there is no blame restates the exception and signals a concession; writing nevertheless remains preferable.

positions.position: Omitting a written record of immediate trade incurs no blame.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR-FULL (author): An immediate cash trade may go unwritten because no harm results from omitting a record. ALUSI-FULL (author): There is no harm or sin in omitting written records for immediate exchanges, because they are less exposed to dispute and forgetfulness or because writing them is burdensome.

question: Must sales be witnessed?

positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (الضحاك): Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says immediate cash sales may go unwitnessed, but deferred sales must be written and witnessed while the parties are settled. IBNABIHATIM (الضحاك): All sales deferred for a short or long term must be written and witnessed until their due date. NAHHAS (عبد الله بن عمر): Ibn Umar says witnessing is obligatory for every sale, large or small, citing the command to witness sales. | mentions 2:282 MAWARDI-FULL (الضحاك وداود بن علي): Witnessing sales is obligatory. WAHIDI-BASIT (عطاء وابن جريج وإبراهيم وابن جرير): A group, chosen by Ibn Jarīr, treat writing and witnessing deferred debts as obligatory to protect wealth and deter denial; Ibrāhīm says even a tiny handful of greens should be documented. JISHUMI (الضحاك): Al-Ḍaḥḥāk considers witnessing a sale obligatory. BAGHAWI-FULL (الضحاك): He considers witnessing a binding command for both small and large transactions, cash or credit; Abu Saʿid al-Khudri leaves it to mutual trust, while others call it recommended. | mentions 2:283 KASHSHAF-FULL (الضحاك): Al-Ḍaḥḥāk considers witnessing obligatory even for a bunch of greens. IBNATIYYA-FULL (الحسن والشعبي): Al-Ḥasan, al-Shaʿbī, and others say witnessing a transaction is recommended; Ibn ʿAmr and al-Ḍaḥḥāk say it is obligatory, followed by Ibn ʿUmar's practice and ʿAṭāʾ, with al-Ṭabarī preferring obligation. TABRISI (الحسن وجميع الفقهاء): Al-Ḥasan and the jurists regard witnessing sales as recommended; the Ẓāhirīs make it obligatory. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (ابن عمر): A group including Ibn ʿUmar, Abu Musa, Mujahid, Ibn Sirin, and others regard writing and witnessing as obligatory. RAZI-FULL (عطاء وابن جريج والنخعي والطبري): ʿAtaʾ, Ibn Jurayj, al-Nakhaʿi, and al-Tabari hold that writing and witnessing deferred debts are obligatory; al-Nakhaʿi even requires witnessing a tiny vegetable purchase. QURTUBI-FULL (الطبري): Al-Ṭabarī reads the witnessing command as covering small and large sales; Abū Mūsā, Ibn ʿUmar, and others hold it obligatory, and ʿAṭāʾ demands witnesses for tiny purchases. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (أبو موسى الأشعري، ابن عمر، الضحاك، ابن المسيب، جابر بن زيد، مجاهد، عطاء، إبراهيم، الشعبي، النخعي، داود بن علي): They hold witnessing obligatory; al-Ḍaḥḥāk requires it even for greens and ʿAṭāʾ for any price. Al-Ṭabarī says an unwitnessed sale defies God's Book. DURR-FULL (سعيد بن جبير): Witness a sale whether deferred or immediate; harming the scribe or witness in violation of the command is disobedience, and one must fear God. IBNASHUR-FULL (أبو موسى الأشعري): Abū Mūsā, Ibn ʿUmar, Abū Saʿīd, Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, Mujāhid, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿAṭāʾ, Ibn Jurayj, al-Nakhaʿī, Jābir ibn Zayd, Dāwūd, and al-Ṭabarī take witnessing at sales as obligatory. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Witnesses are also required for a sale without debt when it is not ordinary immediate commerce, completing the categories of debt, credit sales, immediate trade, and immediate noncommercial sales. TAB-FULL (author): Al-Ṭabarī rules that witnessing every purchase and sale is an obligatory duty, because divine commands bind unless evidence shows a recommendation; he rejects abrogation by the trust clause. | mentions 2:283

TAB-FULL (الحسن والشعبي): Al-Ḥasan and al-Shaʿbī treat witnessing at sale as recommended or optional, citing the permission to rely on trust. | mentions 2:283 TAB-FULL (الشعبي): Al-Shaʿbī says the parties may choose whether to witness their sale. NAHHAS (الفراء): Some say recording deferred debts and witnessing sales are recommendations, by analogy with commands that grant permission after a prohibition. | mentions 2:282 THALABI (آخرون): Other scholars treat witnessing sales as recommended, leaving the parties free to call witnesses or not. MAWARDI-FULL (الحسن والشعبي ومالك والشافعي): Witnessing sales is recommended. JISHUMI (الحسن والشافعي): Al-Ḥasan and al-Shāfiʿī regard witnessing sales as recommended, which Jishumi says is the jurists’ position. JISHUMI (author): Writing and witnessing are guidance and recommendation, not obligation, since a creditor may waive the right itself and need not document it as a precaution. KASHSHAF-FULL (الحسن): Al-Ḥasan says one may choose whether to witness a sale. IBNATIYYA-FULL (القاضي أبو محمد): Ibn ʿAṭiyya finds obligation untenable: witnessing tiny sales is burdensome, while larger dealings may rely on social trust or customary practice. He prefers recommendation unless an excuse prevents it. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (author): Witnessing is recommended for transactions where it is customary. QURTUBI-FULL (ابن عطية): Ibn ʿAṭiyya finds mandatory witnessing impractical for small sales and sometimes socially awkward; he treats it as recommended for its usual benefit unless an excuse intervenes. NASAFI-FULL (author): Witnessing sales is recommended for immediate and deferred exchanges as a precaution, or the command concerns immediate trade alone, where testimony suffices without writing. IBNKATHIR-FULL (الجمهور): The majority treats witnessing sales as guidance and recommendation, not obligation; the report of the Prophet's disputed horse purchase and Khuzaima's extraordinary testimony supports this. ITQAN (author): Commands can remind of favor, express wonder or equal treatment, give practical guidance as in witnessing sales, show contempt, warn, or honor the addressee. BURSEVI (author): Witness sales either in this particular transaction or generally as a precaution; the majority take the verse’s commands as recommendations. ELMALILI (author): The majority of exegetes regard witnessing a sale here as a recommendation for precaution. IBNASHUR-FULL (مالك): The later majority of jurists, including Mālik, Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Shāfiʿī, and Aḥmad, regard witnessing as recommended; the discussion continues at the command to witness sales. IBNASHUR-FULL (مالك): Al-Ḥasan and al-Shaʿbī, followed by Mālik, Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Shāfiʿī, and Aḥmad, regard witnessing as recommended; they cite the Prophet’s sales without witnesses. QURTUBI-FULL (الشعبي والحسن): Al-Shaʿbī and al-Ḥasan treat witnessing as recommendation and guidance rather than a binding duty; Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and other jurists are also said to hold this. QURTUBI-FULL (ابن العربي): Ibn al-ʿArabī says only al-Ḍaḥḥāk is reported to require witnessing; the Prophet made and recorded sales without witnesses and pledged his armor without them. QURTUBI-FULL (طارق بن عبد الله المحاربي): Ṭāriq ibn ʿAbd Allāh recounts selling a camel to a man later identified as the Prophet; the Prophet sent word for the sellers to take dates and eat until satisfied, without witnesses at the sale. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The author answers the argument from unwitnessed sales by limiting those cases to contexts of mutual trust and refers to the following trust provision; he also rejects Ibn ʿAṭiyya’s earlier rationale. | mentions 2:283 STUDYQURAN (author): Women may conduct sales and loans for themselves, including transactions without witnesses; the witness provision therefore serves another purpose. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): The sound view is that witnessing makes a transaction prudent while mutual trust leaves room; no abrogation follows, because documentation is recommended as a precaution for rights people may waive, and 2:283 instructs debtors to repay when trusted. | mentions 2:283 IBNJAWZI-ZAD (الجمهور): The majority treat writing debts and witnessing sales or debts as recommended, so the command remains operative without abrogation. QURTUBI-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās says the debt verse is established, not abrogated, and writing, pledges, and witnesses are alternative means of securing debt; witnessing is recommended like pledging. | mentions 2:283

positions.position: Witnessing a sale is urged as a safeguard.
positions.reasons: MUQATIL (author): An immediate cash trade with no term may go unwritten; sales should be witnessed, but a scribe or witness should not be pressured when occupied if another can be found. TAB-FULL (author): Even when cash trades need not be written, both parties should have witnesses for every sale, large or small, immediate or deferred, to prevent either buyer or seller from losing a right through denial and lack of proof. IBNABIHATIM (مجاهد): For a cash sale, take witnesses without writing; for a deferred sale, write and take witnesses. IBNABIHATIM (سعيد بن جبير): Witness all sales to protect one’s rights, whether payment is deferred or immediate; Jabir ibn Zayd, Mujahid, ʿAta, and al-Dahhak agree. THALABI (author): The exemption from writing applies to the cash transaction, while witnesses are still commanded when a sale takes place. KASHSHAF-FULL (author): Witness any sale, immediate or deferred, as a precaution against disputes; alternatively, witnessing alone can suffice for immediate trade without writing. QURTUBI-FULL (الشافعي): Al-Shāfiʿī classifies sales as documented with witnesses, secured by a pledge, or based on trust, reading the verse as evidence for these forms. QURTUBI-FULL (ابن عمر): Ibn ʿUmar would obtain witnesses for cash sales and write down deferred sales. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Witnessing all sales, immediate or deferred, is safer against disagreement; another interpretation limits the command to present trade. DURR-FULL (جابر بن زيد): Jabir ibn Zayd bought a whip and had witnesses, following the command to witness sales. DURR-FULL (الضحاك): Al-Dahhak likewise says to witness a sale even of a small bundle of greens. ALUSI-FULL (author): Witness when you make the specified sale, or, according to a broader reading, whenever a sale is made. ELMALILI (author): For any sale, including a cash sale, make it openly in the presence of witnesses rather than secretly; this precaution protects property and legal security. STUDYQURAN (author): Forward contracts could span years, and women might be less socially available to witness them over time; spot sales need no written contract because delivery and payment are simultaneous.

positions.position: The trust clause abrogated the sales-witness duty
positions.reasons: IBNABIHATIM (الحسن): Al-Hasan says the command to witness sales was abrogated by the clause allowing trusted dealings; al-Shaʿbi reports similarly. | mentions 2:283 WAHIDI-WAJIZ (author): After prohibiting usury, God permits forward-credit sales and commands writing and witnessing deferred debts to protect property; the trust exception in 2:283 abrogates this command. | mentions 2:283 WAHIDI-WAJIZ (author): An immediate exchange of goods is exempt from writing because the risks of delayed payment are absent; witnessing spot sales is also no longer obligatory under the abrogated ruling. JISHUMI (الشعبي): Al-Shaʿbī reports that writing, witnessing, and pledging were once obligatory and were abrogated by the following verse’s allowance when parties trust each other; Jishumi prefers the view that writing is recommended as a means of securing rights. | mentions 2:283 BAGHAWI-FULL (author): Some consider writing obligatory, but most deem the command recommendatory; al-Shaʿbi says writing, witnessing, and pledging were obligatory then abrogated by the trust provision. | mentions 2:283 BAGHAWI-FULL (الشعبي): Al-Shaʿbi holds that writing, witnessing, and pledging were initially obligatory and that the instruction to fulfill a trusted deposit abrogated all three. | mentions 2:283 IBNATIYYA-FULL (قوم): Some say witnessing is abrogated by the trust exception in 2:283; al-Mahdawī records this view and Makkī attributes it to Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī. | mentions 2:283 QURTUBI-FULL (النحاس): Al-Ḥasan, al-Ḥakam, and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd are reported to say that the mutual-trust clause abrogated witnessing sales. | mentions 2:283 BAYDAWI-FULL (author): Witness the sale in particular or every sale as safer; most imams recommend the commands, while some require them and debate whether they remain effective or are abrogated. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الجحدري، الحسن، عبد الرحمن بن يزيد، الحكم): They say the witnessing command was abrogated by the permission to trust one another. IBNKATHIR-FULL (الشعبي والحسن): They say the command to witness sales was abrogated by the option to trust one another and return the entrusted property in 2:283. | mentions 2:283

turns_on: Whether the command binds, recommends, or was superseded by trust.

question: Who may harm whom under ولا يضار?

positions.position: The prohibition prevents harm connected with writing or testimony.
positions.reasons: ABDURRAZZAQ (قتادة): Qatada says a scribe is harmed by being made to write what was not dictated, and a witness by being made to attest what he did not witness. ABDURRAZZAQ (عمر): Ikrima reports Umar reciting the verb with a doubled r, as ‘ولا يضارر كاتب ولا شهيد.’ AKHFASH (author): ولا يضار can be parsed as a prohibition or as an indicative statement; compare لا تضار والدة بولدها, though that form was not read in the indicative. | mentions 2:233 TAB-FULL (author): On the first interpretation, the underlying form is ولا يضارر; the two identical rāʾ letters assimilate, with fatḥa used despite the jussive because it is the lightest vowel. TAB-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās glosses the harm as summoning a writer or witness who has a need, only for them to be told to ignore it and come anyway. TAB-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās also describes harm as compelling a person despite there being enough other witnesses, simply because the caller invokes the command to answer summonses. TAB-FULL (عمر): ʿUmar is reported to have read the phrase with an unassimilated doubled rāʾ, ولا يضارر. TAB-FULL (ابن مسعود): Ibn Masʿūd is reported to have read the phrase as ولا يضارر. TAB-FULL (الضحاك): Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says callers must not harm writers or witnesses who explain they have a need; the caller should seek another person instead. TAB-FULL (ابن طاوس): Ibn Ṭāwūs says the writer or witness should not be harmed when saying “I have a need; let me go” by a claimant insisting “write for me.” TAB-FULL (author): Fusūq here means sin and disobedience: whoever harms the scribe or witness has disobeyed God and committed what is forbidden. TAB-FULL (الضحاك): Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says the original obligation to write was abrogated by the prohibition on harming a scribe or witness. ZAJJAJ (author): The view under discussion also bars summoning a witness when his attendance would harm him. IBNABIHATIM (قتادة): Do not harm the scribe by making him write what was not dictated, or the witness by making him testify to what was not requested; Zayd ibn Aslam agrees. IBNABIHATIM (سعيد بن جبير): Harming the scribe or witness, or doing what was forbidden, is transgression; Ibn ʿAbbas reports similarly. NAHHAS (أبو إسحاق): Abu Ishaq prefers taking ولا يضار as a prohibition on the writer or witness causing harm, since the next clause calls such conduct sinful. NAHHAS (المفضل): Al-Mufaddal reports al-Aʿmash reading ولا يضار with kasra on rāʾ; kasra or fatḥa resolves the meeting of two sukūns, with fatḥa lighter. NAHHAS (عمر بن الخطاب وابن عباس وابن أبي إسحاق): Umar, Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Abi Ishaq read ولا يضارر with kasra on the first rāʾ. THALABI (الضحاك): Al-Dahhak says the command originally bound writers and witnesses, then the prohibition on harming them abrogated it. THALABI (author): An acceptable witness must meet ten conditions: freedom, adulthood, Islam, uprightness, knowledge of the matter, no personal gain or avoidance of harm, few errors, proper social conduct, no excessive leniency, and no adverse testimony from his slave. THALABI (author): The prohibition has assimilated doubled rāʾ letters from yudār ir, with fatḥa resolving the two adjacent sukūns. THALABI (عمر وأبي وابن مسعود ومجاهد): Umar, Ubayy, Ibn Masʿud, and Mujahid read ولا يضارر with the doubled consonants made explicit, supporting the interpretation that the writer or witness is not to be harmed. THALABI (أبو جعفر): Abu Jaʿfar reads ولا يضار in a light, jussive form with one rāʾ. THALABI (الحسن): Al-Hasan reads ولا يضار with a doubled rāʾ and kasra. MAWARDI-FULL (الضحاك): The command is abrogated by the later command not to harm a scribe or witness. MAWARDI-FULL (طاووس والحسن وقتادة): Harming a scribe or witness includes writing terms not dictated or testifying to what was not witnessed. MAWARDI-FULL (ابن عباس ومجاهد وعطاء): Harming a scribe or witness includes preventing a scribe from writing or a witness from testifying. WAHIDI-BASIT (الفراء): Al-Farrāʾ regards writing and witnesses as recommendation and permission like the commands in 5:2 and 62:10: documenting is good but leaving it is harmless. | mentions 5:2, 62:10 JISHUMI (أبو جعفر): Abu Jaʿfar reads يضار in the jussive with a light, ungeminated rāʾ. JISHUMI (الحسن): Al-Hasan reads يضار with a kasra and a geminated rāʾ. JISHUMI (الحسن، وقتادة، وابن زيد): The kasra reading of يضارر is associated with al-Hasan, Qatada, and Ibn Zayd. JISHUMI (author): The forbidden conduct is understood as harming the writer and witness or doing what was prohibited and disobeying what was commanded; it is departure from God’s obedience. BAGHAWI-FULL (author): Suspicion bars an enemy's testimony against an enemy and testimony for one's parents or children; it also bars a witness whose testimony gains benefit or averts harm for himself. BAGHAWI-FULL (author): Examples of self-interest are an heir testifying against his benefactor's killer and a defendant accusing a witness of wrongdoing to ward off harm. IBNATIYYA-FULL (عمر بن الخطاب وابن مسعود ومجاهد): They read the verb with the letters separated and the first rāʾ fatḥa, meaning a claimant may initiate harm to the scribe or witness; al-Ṭabarī reports and explains this reading accordingly. IBNATIYYA-FULL (عكرمة): ʿIkrima reads the first rāʾ with kasra and makes “scribe” and “witness” accusative, so that the rights-holder is forbidden to begin harming them. IBNATIYYA-FULL (ابن محيصن): Ibn Muḥayṣin reads the geminated verb with rafʿ; after Ibn Mujāhid questions it, Abū al-Fatḥ explains it as a negative statement meaning the scribe ought not to be harmed, supported by poetry. Ibn ʿAṭiyya finds it close to the earlier analysis. TABRISI (author): One analysis derives لا يضار from doubled ر, with the writer and witness forbidden to depart from the truth. TABRISI (author): The first interpretation of لا يضار is clearer; Abū Jaʿfar's doubled quiescent rāʾ is unusual and explained by treating connected recitation like pause. TABRISI (الضحاك): Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says writing was originally obligatory but was abrogated by the ban on harming a scribe or witness. TABRISI (author): The verse threatens that harming a scribe or witness in writing or testimony is a departure from God's commands; fear God, who teaches what is needed and knows all. TABRISI (أبو جعفر): Abū Jaʿfar reads لا يضار with a doubled, quiescent rāʾ; the remaining readers use the doubled rāʾ in the accusative form. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (author): Abu Jaʿfar reads yuḍār with a light ra and sukun. RAZI-FULL (الزجاج): Al-Zajjaj prefers the reading that writers and witnesses must not harm the claimant, while the opposing reading points to the plural address and the ensuing plural verb. | mentions 2:283 RAZI-FULL (author): Another view says the writer’s duty was obligatory but later abrogated by the prohibition on harming writers and witnesses. | mentions 2:282 QURTUBI-FULL (الربيع والضحاك): They say the order to write was abrogated by the prohibition against harming a writer or witness; al-Qurṭubī calls this remote because a universal obligation was never established and paid document-writing is permitted. NASAFI-FULL (author): Harming the scribe or witnesses is sinful conduct; fear God in this duty. BURHAN (author): The author lists Qur’anic denunciations as signs that an act is forbidden, including calling it injustice, wrongful appropriation, sin, or fisq, as in the ban on harming scribes and witnesses. NASHR (author): The preceding discussion gives a lightened r in يضار and reports Abū Jaʿfar's sukūn there, with disagreement transmitted from him. DURR-FULL (سعيد بن جبير): Witness a sale whether deferred or immediate; harming the scribe or witness in violation of the command is disobedience, and one must fear God. ELMALILI (author): Hamza also reads the relevant form with rāʾ in the nominative, whereas readings other than Asim's use the nominative for wa-la yudārra. IBNASHUR-FULL (الضحاك): Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, with a report from ʿAṭāʾ, regards the scribe’s duty as abrogated by the ban on harming a scribe or witness; the author objects that writing is not ordinarily harm except in rare cases such as great distance. | mentions 2:282 IBNASHUR-FULL (أبو حنيفة): The author applies the earlier disagreement about scribes: accepting the request to bear witness becomes individual when designated, and giving testimony is individually obligatory if it causes no bodily or financial harm; Abū Ḥanīfa makes performance communal unless uniquely required, subject to court integrity, proximity, admissibility, and a claimant’s request. QIRAAT-ER (author): Abu Jaʿfar and Yaʿqub quiesce the final rāʾ in yuḍār; the source treats it as phonetic, with the same morphological analysis.

positions.position: Scribes and witnesses must not harm parties through distortion or refusal
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (ابن زيد): Ibn Zayd says the scribe harms people by changing what was dictated, while a witness harms them by altering testimony and thereby voiding their rights. TAB-FULL (عطاء): ʿAṭāʾ offers another interpretation: the writer and witness must not be harmed by having to withhold the knowledge or testimony they possess. TAB-FULL (الربيع): Al-Rabīʿ reports that after the duty not to refuse writing was revealed, people pressured busy scribes and witnesses despite being able to find others; this harassment occasioned the prohibition on harming them. IBNABIHATIM (الحسن): Harming a witness includes concealing or distorting testimony. THALABI (الحسن): Al-Hasan makes writing obligatory when refusing would harm the creditor because no other writer is available, but optional when another can do it. THALABI (الربيع بن أنس): Al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas reports that people sometimes pressured busy writers and witnesses by invoking the command, even when alternatives existed, so the verse prohibited harming them. WAHIDI-BASIT (الحسن): Al-Ḥasan limits the duty to cases where no other scribe is available, because refusal would harm the creditor. WAHIDI-BASIT (طاوس والحسن وقتادة وابن زيد): One reading prohibits harming a scribe or witness through falsifying or altering the record, bearing false testimony, or refusing to testify; the active form has the writer and witness as agents. WAHIDI-WAJIZ (author): The ban on harming a scribe or witness forbids altering records, false testimony, and refusing to testify; doing so is sinful. WAHIDI-WAJIZ (author): A just scribe writes without altering amount or term and must not refuse when asked; this was first obligatory for writer and witness, then abrogated by the prohibition on harming them. JISHUMI (author): Some say the command that a scribe not refuse was abrogated by the instruction not to harm a scribe or witness; the adopted practice is the first view, communal obligation. JISHUMI (author): On the active reading, the underlying form is yudārir with kasra; the writer and witness are the agents. JISHUMI (عطاء وطاووس والحسن وقتادة وابن زيد): The writer must not be harmed by being forbidden to write or made to add or subtract from what was dictated; the witness must not be made to refuse or testify to what he does not know. KASHSHAF-FULL (author): Ḍārr may be active or passive; ʿUmar’s and Ibn ʿAbbās’s readings clarify it. The ban covers refusing, falsifying, adding, or omitting testimony, or harming witnesses through coercion, unpaid work, and travel costs. IBNATIYYA-FULL (الربيع والضحاك): Al-Rabīʿ and al-Ḍaḥḥāk, as transmitted by al-Mahdawī, say the prohibition on a scribe refusing was abrogated by the command not to cause harm in 2:282. | mentions 2:282 IBNATIYYA-FULL (الحسن وقتادة وطاوس وابن زيد): They say “do not harm a scribe or witness” prohibits a writer from adding to or subtracting from what was dictated and a witness from altering testimony; Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and ʿAṭāʾ also understand it to prohibit their refusal. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): If harm means falsification by a writer or witness, fisq is the legal commission of grave sins and invalidating rights; if it means mistreatment or refusal, fisq means departing from what is right, though disobeying God's command approaches the legal sense too. TABRISI (الحسن): Al-Ḥasan says refusal is obligatory to avoid only when there is no alternative scribe and refusal would harm the creditor; otherwise the scribe has latitude. TABRISI (مجاهد وعطاء وسعيد بن جبير): One reported view says summoned witnesses must not refuse to give testimony they know without doubt, provided doing so causes them no harm. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (عطاء): A third view from ʿAta and others says the harm is the scribe refusing to write or the witness refusing to testify. RAZI-FULL (أكثر المفسرين والحسن وطاوس وقتادة): Most exegetes, al-Hasan, Tawus, and Qatada read ولا يضار as forbidding the writer or witness from harming the rights-holder through falsification, omission, or ineffective testimony. QURTUBI-FULL (الحسن): He makes writing obligatory only where refusal would harm the creditor because no substitute writer is available; otherwise the writer has latitude. NASAFI-FULL (عمر): ʿUmar reads يضارر in the active voice; Ibn ʿAbbās reads يضار in the passive. NASAFI-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās reads the passive form ولا يضار, while ʿUmar's active form is ولا يضارر. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الربيع والضحاك): Al-Rabīʿ and al-Ḍaḥḥāk say the ban on a scribe refusing was abrogated by the later ban on harming a scribe or witness. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): An active reading forbids a writer altering the document or a witness concealing, changing, or withholding testimony; al-Zajjāj prefers this. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and ʿAṭāʾ also explain harm as refusing with excuses about being busy. SAMIN-DURR (الزجاج): On the active reading, the scribe and witness are forbidden to harm the beneficiary by altering or withholding documentation; al-Zajjaj prefers it because such conduct is clearly sinful. SAMIN-DURR (ابن عباس ومجاهد وطاووس): Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Tawus are reported to explain the active reading as the scribe or witness harming the party entitled to the record. BURHAN (author): The stronger reading is that a scribe or witness must not be harmed, including by concealing the writing or testimony; another reading forbids callers from burdening them at harmful times. DURR-FULL (الضحاك): Al-Dahhak says the obligation not to refuse was abrogated by the prohibition on harming a scribe or witness. BURSEVI (author): If active, the prohibition bars a scribe from refusing or altering the document and a witness from withholding testimony; if passive, it bars others from harming them while occupied or withholding their fee. ALUSI-FULL (عمر): Umar’s uncontracted reading with kasra supports the active interpretation of the prohibition against harming a scribe or witness. ELMALILI (author): The command not to harm a scribe or witness can mean they must not harm rights-holders by refusing a request or falsifying or altering the writing or testimony. ELMALILI (author): Alternatively, on the passive reading, scribes and witnesses themselves must not be harmed by excessive demands, interruption of important work, or denial of a scribe’s fee. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): Parties must not inconvenience or harm scribes and witnesses, even with unnecessary calls, pressure, or threats to distort the record; the verse forbids such conduct and calls them to fear God. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT (author): The verse forbids writers and witnesses from harming others by suppressing, refusing, or distorting testimony, and forbids others from coercing them into the same harms.

positions.position: The wording encompasses harm in both directions
positions.reasons: FARRA (author): ولا يضار الكاتب والشاهد means do not summon either while occupied. IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB (مجاهد والكلبي): Mujāhid and al-Kalbī explain لا يضار as not bothering a writer by distracting him from his trade or work. NAHHAS (ابن مسعود): Ibn Masʿud reads ولا يضارر with fatḥa on the first rāʾ; both readings explain the text and do not replace the codex reading. MAWARDI-FULL (author): A just scribe must neither add a term to harm the debtor nor omit one to harm the creditor. WAHIDI-BASIT (الضحاك): Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says the command initially imposed an obligation on scribe and witness, later abrogated by the ban on harming either one. JISHUMI (author): The scribe records the debt or sale between the parties with fairness, neither adding nor subtracting nor harming either without their knowledge. JISHUMI (author): The verse prescribes fair drafting of contract terms and documents and forbids harming either party. BAGHAWI-FULL (الضحاك): He says the writer's and witness's duties were binding, then abrogated by the ban on harming either. IBNATIYYA-FULL (ابن عباس ومجاهد والضحاك والسدي وطاوس): They say a claimant harms a scribe or witness by demanding work when that person is busy or excused, then shaming him for refusing; the word's reciprocal sense encompasses these readings and the preceding ones. TABRISI (author): A just scribe records the debt or sale accurately, without changing its terms, amount, or anything that harms either party without consent. RAZI-FULL (عمر وابن عباس): The ambiguity comes from assimilation in يضارر: the subject may inflict harm or suffer it; Umar’s kasra and Ibn ʿAbbas’s fatḥa with explicit pronunciation preserve both readings. | mentions 2:233 QURTUBI-FULL (author): The reciprocal form encompasses both kinds of harm: dishonest additions and omissions wrongfully affect people and property, while imposing on busy witnesses violates God's command. BAYDAWI-FULL (author): Lā yuḍārr has two readings: scribes and witnesses must not refuse, distort, or alter testimony, or others must not harm them by disrupting duties, demanding extra travel, or withholding their fees and expenses. BIQAI-FULL (author): The prohibition on harming a scribe or witness covers both causing harm and suffering harm; the author says both readings make sense. ITQAN (ابن قتيبة): Ibn Qutayba’s first variation type changes case or vowel without changing meaning or form, illustrated by two readings of ولا يضار كاتب. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The verb yaḍārr can be active or passive, allowing the ban to cover either scribes and witnesses harming the parties or the parties harming them; the wording deliberately carries both compatible rules. ASAD-NOTES (author): A scribe or witness must not be harmed by being held responsible for the contract’s consequences or either party’s failure to perform. SAMARRAI-ASRAR-MUH (author): The verse forbids both a writer or witness harming others by withholding or distorting testimony and others pressuring them into changing or withholding it.

positions.position: Parties must not burden or mistreat scribes and witnesses
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (مجاهد): Mujāhid says a requester harms a busy scribe or witness by insisting “fear God, you were commanded” when other people can be found; they need not interrupt their work or feel pressured. MAWARDI-FULL (عكرمة والضحاك والسدي والربيع): Harming them may mean summoning a busy, excused scribe or witness. WAHIDI-BASIT (ابن مسعود وعطاء ومجاهد): Ibn Masʿūd, ʿAṭāʾ, and Mujāhid instead say not to summon a busy scribe or witness when attending would harm him; on this reading the verb is passive. JISHUMI (ابن مسعود ومجاهد): Ibn Masʿud and Mujahid are associated with the fatḥa reading, meaning a witness must not be summoned while occupied in order to harm him. JISHUMI (author): On the passive reading, the writer and witness are the objects of harm. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (ابن عباس، مجاهد، طاووس، الضحاك، السدي): Under the passive reading, they say others must not harm the writer or witness by burdening them, disrupting their work, or making unreasonable demands. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الطبري): Al-Ṭabarī prefers the passive reading, supported by ʿUmar's unassimilated reading: the opening addresses transaction parties, not writers and witnesses, and the warning fits parties forbidden to cause harm. SAMIN-DURR (author): On the passive reading, no one may harm the scribe or witness; its context concerns those receiving the writing and testimony, and the consequence would otherwise address two people. IBNKATHIR-FULL (ابن عباس): Another interpretation forbids burdening or harming the writer and witness: a person summons them, and they explain that they are occupied, but he insists that they were commanded to answer; Ibn Abbas says the caller may not harm them. Similar views are attributed to many early authorities. DURR-FULL (الربيع): When people pressed a busy scribe to write despite other available scribes, God revealed the prohibition against harming a scribe or witness. ITQAN (author): The verse can mean that the scribe and witness must not wrong the claimant, or that the claimant must not harm them by imposing undue work or coercing them. ALUSI-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbas’s uncontracted reading with fatha supports the passive interpretation, forbidding others to harm the scribe or witness. ALUSI-FULL (الربيع): Al-Rabiʿ reports that requesters sometimes forced busy scribes to write and would not let them decline; this occasion explains the command not to harm them. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Harm includes parties burdening a scribe or witness with hardship, loss, or exposure to punishment, and witnesses causing a party to lose a right or suffer the burden of answering.

question: How is يضار read and analyzed?

positions.position: The unassimilated or unusual vocalizations clarify the form
positions.reasons: SIBAWAYH (author): The form radd stays unassimilated in faʿala because quiescing the ending would still leave gemination, while the first radical is inherently quiescent. SIBAWAYH (author): Forms such as ṭabb and khāf follow the three-letter verbal pattern; the lack of an unassimilated tabbab confirms that faʿal is assimilated. SIBAWAYH (قوم): Some speakers preserve the unassimilated faʿil form, as in ḍafaf, because this pattern can be sound in the qult class. SIBAWAYH (author): Tāʾ and dāl assimilate to one another because they share a place and differ mainly in voicing; unassimilated speech is possible but laborious. TAB-FULL (author): On the first interpretation, the underlying form is ولا يضارر; the two identical rāʾ letters assimilate, with fatḥa used despite the jussive because it is the lightest vowel. TAB-FULL (عمر): ʿUmar is reported to have read the phrase with an unassimilated doubled rāʾ, ولا يضارر. NAHHAS (المفضل): Al-Mufaddal reports al-Aʿmash reading ولا يضار with kasra on rāʾ; kasra or fatḥa resolves the meeting of two sukūns, with fatḥa lighter. NAHHAS (عمر بن الخطاب وابن عباس وابن أبي إسحاق): Umar, Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Abi Ishaq read ولا يضارر with kasra on the first rāʾ. NAHHAS (ابن مسعود): Ibn Masʿud reads ولا يضارر with fatḥa on the first rāʾ; both readings explain the text and do not replace the codex reading. THALABI (author): The prohibition has assimilated doubled rāʾ letters from yudār ir, with fatḥa resolving the two adjacent sukūns. THALABI (أبو جعفر): Abu Jaʿfar reads ولا يضار in a light, jussive form with one rāʾ. THALABI (الحسن): Al-Hasan reads ولا يضار with a doubled rāʾ and kasra. JISHUMI (أبو جعفر): Abu Jaʿfar reads يضار in the jussive with a light, ungeminated rāʾ. JISHUMI (الحسن): Al-Hasan reads يضار with a kasra and a geminated rāʾ. JISHUMI (الحسن، وقتادة، وابن زيد): The kasra reading of يضارر is associated with al-Hasan, Qatada, and Ibn Zayd. IBNATIYYA-FULL (عمر بن الخطاب وابن مسعود ومجاهد): They read the verb with the letters separated and the first rāʾ fatḥa, meaning a claimant may initiate harm to the scribe or witness; al-Ṭabarī reports and explains this reading accordingly. IBNATIYYA-FULL (أبو جعفر بن القعقاع وعمرو بن عبيد): They read the geminated rāʾ with sukūn in the jussive; Abū al-Fatḥ calls it questionable but explains it as treating connected speech like a pause. IBNATIYYA-FULL (عكرمة): ʿIkrima reads the first rāʾ with kasra and makes “scribe” and “witness” accusative, so that the rights-holder is forbidden to begin harming them. TABRISI (author): The first interpretation of لا يضار is clearer; Abū Jaʿfar's doubled quiescent rāʾ is unusual and explained by treating connected recitation like pause. TABRISI (أبو جعفر): Abū Jaʿfar reads لا يضار with a doubled, quiescent rāʾ; the remaining readers use the doubled rāʾ in the accusative form. RAZI-FULL (عمر وابن عباس): The ambiguity comes from assimilation in يضارر: the subject may inflict harm or suffer it; Umar’s kasra and Ibn ʿAbbas’s fatḥa with explicit pronunciation preserve both readings. | mentions 2:233 ABUHAYYAN-FULL (عمر، ابن عباس، مجاهد، ابن أبي إسحاق): Their reading is reported with the first rāʾ unassimilated and either kasra or fatḥa; unassimilated pronunciation is Ḥijāzī and assimilation Tamīmī. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (ابن القعقاع، عمرو بن عبيد، عكرمة، ابن محيصن): Their variants include a jussive rāʾ, an unassimilated verb with accusative kātiban, and a raised doubled rāʾ used as a negative form that strengthens the prohibition. SAMIN-DURR (أبو جعفر وعمرو بن عبيد): Abu Jaʿfar and ʿAmr b. ʿUbayd read the doubled rāʾ sākin in connected speech; the author notes the three-consonant cluster is weak, tolerated by lengthening and by analogy to pause. SAMIN-DURR (عكرمة): ʿIkrima reads the form with both rāʾs separated and the first kasra; the implied subject is the rights-holder, who must not coerce the scribe or witness. SAMIN-DURR (عكرمة): In a report from Miqsam, ʿIkrima reads doubled rāʾ with kasra, reflecting the original meeting of two sukūns. NASHR (ابن كثير والبصريان): Ibn Kathir and the two Basrans read the rāʾ with ḍamma; the other readers use fatḥa. The author gives no semantic distinction here. NASHR (أبو جعفر): Abu Jaʿfar has two transmitted forms: some routes lighten and silence the rāʾ, while other routes double it with fatḥa; all retain the alif’s lengthening at the meeting of two sukūns. NASHR (author): The preceding discussion gives a lightened r in يضار and reports Abū Jaʿfar's sukūn there, with disagreement transmitted from him. ITQAN (جمال الدين بن مالك): Ibn Malik says the Quran is in Hijazi speech except a few Tamimi forms, including assimilation of jussive verbs; Hijazi unassimilated forms are common, as in وليملل. | mentions 11:87, 20:81 ELMALILI (author): Hamza also reads the relevant form with rāʾ in the nominative, whereas readings other than Asim's use the nominative for wa-la yudārra. QIRAAT-ER (author): Abu Jaʿfar and Yaʿqub quiesce the final rāʾ in yuḍār; the source treats it as phonetic, with the same morphological analysis.

positions.position: The active form forbids scribes and witnesses to wrong parties
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (author): On the active reading, the underlying form is yudārir with kasra; the writer and witness are the agents. KASHSHAF-FULL (author): Ḍārr may be active or passive; ʿUmar’s and Ibn ʿAbbās’s readings clarify it. The ban covers refusing, falsifying, adding, or omitting testimony, or harming witnesses through coercion, unpaid work, and travel costs. BAYDAWI-FULL (author): Lā yuḍārr has two readings: scribes and witnesses must not refuse, distort, or alter testimony, or others must not harm them by disrupting duties, demanding extra travel, or withholding their fees and expenses. NASAFI-FULL (عمر): ʿUmar reads يضارر in the active voice; Ibn ʿAbbās reads يضار in the passive. NASAFI-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās reads the passive form ولا يضار, while ʿUmar's active form is ولا يضارر. NASAFI-FULL (author): The active reading forbids a scribe or witness to refuse, distort, add, or omit; the passive forbids burdening them, rushing them from duties, withholding the scribe's fee, or making a witness bear travel costs. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): The warning addresses writer and witness under an active reading, the parties under the passive reading, or everyone regarding all commands and prohibitions. SAMIN-DURR (عمر وابن عباس ومجاهد وابن أبي إسحاق): Al-Dani reports these authorities reading the first rāʾ with kasra, supporting the active interpretation. BURSEVI (author): If active, the prohibition bars a scribe from refusing or altering the document and a witness from withholding testimony; if passive, it bars others from harming them while occupied or withholding their fee. ALUSI-FULL (author): If active, the verse forbids witnesses and scribes to refuse, distort, add, or subtract; if passive, it forbids burdening them, withholding the fee, or requiring costly travel. ALUSI-FULL (author): Al-Alusi rejects making the صيغة carry both active and passive meanings at once. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The verb yaḍārr can be active or passive, allowing the ban to cover either scribes and witnesses harming the parties or the parties harming them; the wording deliberately carries both compatible rules. SAMARRAI-ASRAR-MUH (author): The doubled form يُضَارّ can be read as active or passive; spelling the consonant without assimilation would distinguish the two forms. | mentions 8:13, 5:54 SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT (author): The undiacritized form يُضارّ can be active or passive; spelling the assimilated consonant separately would distinguish يُضارِر from يُضارَر. | mentions 8:13, 2:217

positions.position: Assimilation permits active and passive analyses of yuḍārr.
positions.reasons: FARRA (author): ولا يضار الكاتب والشاهد means do not summon either while occupied. ABDURRAZZAQ (عمر): Ikrima reports Umar reciting the verb with a doubled r, as ‘ولا يضارر كاتب ولا شهيد.’ AKHFASH (author): ولا يضار can be parsed as a prohibition or as an indicative statement; compare لا تضار والدة بولدها, though that form was not read in the indicative. | mentions 2:233 IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB (مجاهد والكلبي): Mujāhid and al-Kalbī explain لا يضار as not bothering a writer by distracting him from his trade or work. TAB-FULL (ابن مسعود): Ibn Masʿūd is reported to have read the phrase as ولا يضارر. NAHHAS (أبو إسحاق): Abu Ishaq prefers taking ولا يضار as a prohibition on the writer or witness causing harm, since the next clause calls such conduct sinful. THALABI (عمر وأبي وابن مسعود ومجاهد): Umar, Ubayy, Ibn Masʿud, and Mujahid read ولا يضارر with the doubled consonants made explicit, supporting the interpretation that the writer or witness is not to be harmed. TABRISI (author): One analysis derives لا يضار from doubled ر, with the writer and witness forbidden to depart from the truth. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (author): Abu Jaʿfar reads yuḍār with a light ra and sukun. RAZI-FULL (أكثر المفسرين والحسن وطاوس وقتادة): Most exegetes, al-Hasan, Tawus, and Qatada read ولا يضار as forbidding the writer or witness from harming the rights-holder through falsification, omission, or ineffective testimony. ITQAN (ابن قتيبة): Ibn Qutayba’s first variation type changes case or vowel without changing meaning or form, illustrated by two readings of ولا يضار كاتب.

positions.position: The passive form forbids parties to burden scribes and witnesses
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الطبري): Al-Ṭabarī prefers the passive reading, supported by ʿUmar's unassimilated reading: the opening addresses transaction parties, not writers and witnesses, and the warning fits parties forbidden to cause harm. SAMIN-DURR (عمر وابن عباس ومجاهد وابن أبي إسحاق): Al-Dani reports these authorities reading the first rāʾ with fatḥa, matching the passive interpretation.

question: What is فسوق بكم?

positions.position: Fusūq is sin, disobedience, or transgression
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): Fusūq here means sin and disobedience: whoever harms the scribe or witness has disobeyed God and committed what is forbidden. TAB-FULL (الضحاك): The verse calls it transgression whenever people do other than what God commanded. TAB-FULL (ابن عباس): He glosses fusūq as disobedience. TAB-FULL (الربيع): He also glosses fusūq as disobedience. IBNABIHATIM (مقاتل بن حيان): Failing to follow God’s instructions in the debt verse is sin and disobedience; al-Dahhak reports similarly. IBNABIHATIM (سعيد بن جبير): Harming the scribe or witness, or doing what was forbidden, is transgression; Ibn ʿAbbas reports similarly. IBNABIHATIM (ابن عباس): Transgression means disobedience; Mujahid, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, ʿAta ibn Dinar, and al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas report similarly. THALABI (author): The prohibited harm is disobedience and departure from God's command; the passage closes by commanding reverence and affirming God's knowledge. question: What does the Adam-David written-gift report recount?

positions.position: The report presents a written, witnessed gift from Adam to David.

IBNKATHIR-FULL (ابن عباس): A Prophetic report says Adam first denied an agreement: God showed him his descendants, including David, gave David forty years from Adam's thousand-year lifespan, and documented and witnessed the gift; Adam later denied it until shown the record. DURR-FULL (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): A report says Adam was the first to deny: God drew future descendants from Adam's back, showed them to him, and Adam saw David shining and asked who he was.
