question: What do the cited works report about Quranic collection and readings generally?

positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): A good-chain Ibn Abi Dawud report from Abd Khayr says Ali called Abu Bakr the person with the greatest merit in the codices and the first to collect God's Book in the stated official sense. ALUSI-FULL (author): Calling Abu Bakr the first collector does not conflict with al-Qarmani's statement that Umar first collected it, since the intended collection differs. ALUSI-FULL (أبو بريدة): Abu Burda's strange, disconnected report says Salim, freedman of Abu Hudhayfa, first collected the Quran in a codex, swearing not to wear his cloak until finishing. ALUSI-FULL (أنس): Alusi rejects saying Uthman first collected the Quran: al-Bukhari's report from Anas says Uthman standardized one reading in year 25 when Hudhayfa feared Syrian and Iraqi differences could divide the community. ALUSI-FULL (أنس): At Hudhayfa's urging, Uthman borrowed Hafsa's sheets, appointed Zayd and three Qurashis to copy them, directed Qurashi wording in disputes, returned the sheets, sent copies to regions, and burned other codices. ALUSI-FULL (سويد بن غفلة): A sahih Ibn Abi Dawud chain from Suwayd ibn Ghafala quotes Ali asking people to speak only well of Uthman, since he acted on the codices with the group's agreement; another report says Ali would have done the same. ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi calls the report that Ibn Masud threatened to treat Uthman's codex as they treated his a lie, along with claims that Uthman mistreated him. ALUSI-FULL (زيد بن ثابت): In al-Bukhari's report, after the Yamama deaths Umar feared further losses among Quran reciters would cause the Quran to be lost and urged Abu Bakr to collect it. ALUSI-FULL (زيد بن ثابت): Abu Bakr initially questioned doing what the Prophet had not done, but Umar persisted, saying collection was good, until God opened Abu Bakr's heart to the proposal. ALUSI-FULL (زيد بن ثابت): Abu Bakr chose Zayd as young, intelligent, trusted, and a former revelation scribe; Zayd found collection as burdensome as moving a mountain, then accepted after Abu Bakr pressed him. ALUSI-FULL (زيد بن ثابت): Zayd collected from palm stalks, flat stones, and men's memories; he found the end of al-Tawba only with Khuzayma al-Ansari, and the sheets later passed from Abu Bakr to Umar to Hafsa. | mentions 9:128 ALUSI-FULL (أبو بكر): A disconnected Ibn Abi Dawud report with trustworthy transmitters says Abu Bakr instructed Umar and Zayd to write any Quran text presented by two witnesses; Alusi supposes they attested its writing before the Prophet or its final-year review.

BURHAN (البيهقي): Al-Bayhaqi says Abu Bakr first gathered the Qur'an in one codex; Uthman later copied it into multiple codices when reading disagreements threatened to spread. BURHAN (زيد بن ثابت): Zayd reports that arrangement occurred in the Prophet's lifetime, the codex collection under Abu Bakr, and copying into codices under Uthman, drawing on both written materials and companions' memorization. BURHAN (author): The work was done with consultation and approval of the companions; ʿAli approved Uthman's effort and praised its result. BURHAN (القاضي أبو بكر): Al-Baqillani says Uthman aimed to unify people on readings established from the Prophet and discard unsupported forms, not to perform Abu Bakr's initial collection. BURHAN (القاضي أبو بكر): The Uthmanic codex excluded additions, omissions, glosses, and abrogated recitations, to prevent later corruption and doubt. BURHAN (أنس): Anas's report in al-Bukhari says Hudhayfa, alarmed by Syrian-Iraqi recitation disputes during campaigns in Armenia and Azerbaijan, urged Uthman to act before divisions resembled those among Jews and Christians. BURHAN (عثمان): Uthman borrowed Hafsa's sheets and appointed Zayd with three Quraysh members to copy them, instructing the Quraysh members to choose Quraysh speech if they disagreed with Zayd. BURHAN (عثمان): After copying, Uthman returned Hafsa's sheets, sent a codex to each region, and ordered other Qur'anic written materials burned.

ITQAN (ابن حجر): Ibn Hajar prefers the first account: writing on leather and palm stalks came first, then those materials were gathered into sheets under Abu Bakr, as several sound reports indicate. ITQAN (الحاكم): Al-Hakim calls the ordering of surahs in ʿUthman’s time the third collection of the Qur’an. ITQAN (حذيفة بن اليمان): During the Armenia and Azerbaijan campaign, Hudhayfa alarmed ʿUthman about recitation disputes among Syrian and Iraqi forces and urged him to protect the community from division. ITQAN (عثمان): ʿUthman borrowed Hafsa’s sheets and ordered Zayd and three Quraysh scribes to make codices, directing them to use Quraysh speech if they disagreed with Zayd. ITQAN (عثمان): After copying, ʿUthman returned Hafsa’s sheets, sent a codex to each region, and ordered other Qur’anic sheets and codices burned. ITQAN (سالم بن عبد الله ابن عمر): A report in Ibn Wahb’s Muwatta says Abu Bakr collected the Qur’an on sheets after Zayd first refused, then agreed when ʿUmar helped persuade him. ITQAN (ابن شهاب): After the losses at Yamama, Abu Bakr feared part of the Qur’an would be lost; people brought what they had and it was collected on paper under Abu Bakr, the first to gather it in sheets. ITQAN (زيد بن ثابت): In ʿUmarah ibn Ghaziyya’s version, Zayd says Abu Bakr had him write on leather and palm stalks, then ʿUmar put the material into one sheet kept with him.

IBNATIYYA-FULL (حذيفة بن اليمان): Ḥudhayfa reports that, after transmitters and non-Arab readers spread across regions, Iraqi and Syrian groups disputed their readings in the Armenia campaign; some disavowed others’ recitations. IBNATIYYA-FULL (حذيفة بن اليمان): On returning to Medina, Ḥudhayfa urged ʿUthmān to act on the Book before the community split like Jews and Christians; ʿUthmān agreed to intervene. IBNATIYYA-FULL (عثمان بن عفان): ʿUthmān appointed capable, learned, eloquent men to prepare a codex, choosing among transmitted variants the best-known Prophetic readings and most eloquent language. IBNATIYYA-FULL (عثمان بن عفان): ʿUthmān instructed the scribes to use Quraysh’s language when they differed. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): The community followed the selected codex and set aside variant codices to prevent further division and preserve unity. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): Ibn Masʿūd resisted replacing his codex, so it was left; scholars nevertheless barred reciting from it to prevent confusion, since explanatory notes were reportedly mistaken for Qurʾān.

NASHR (أبو عبيد القاسم بن سلام): Abū ʿUbayd lists Companion transmitters of reading forms: numerous Muhājirūn including Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, and Ibn Masʿūd, and Anṣār including Ubayy, Muʿādh, Zayd, and Anas. NASHR (أبو بكر الصديق): After the Prophet’s death and the wars against apostates and Musaylima, in which about five hundred Companions were killed, Abū Bakr was urged to compile the Qurʾan lest it be lost with them; he first hesitated because the Prophet had not ordered it. NASHR (زيد بن ثابت): Abū Bakr and the Companions agreed to collection, and Zayd ibn Thābit gathered the Qurʾan into sheets kept successively by Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, and Ḥafṣa. NASHR (عثمان): ʿUthmān borrowed Ḥafṣa’s sheets and appointed Zayd, Ibn al-Zubayr, Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ, and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥārith to copy them; in disagreement with Zayd, they were to write in Quraysh’s tongue because revelation came in it. NASHR (عثمان): ʿUthmān sent codices to Basra, Kufa, Syria, Mecca, Yemen, and Bahrain, left one in Medina, and kept the central copy for himself. NASHR (author): The community agreed on the contents of these codices and set aside divergent additions, omissions, and word substitutions that had been permitted but were not established by widespread transmission as Qurʾan.

TAB-FULL (زيد بن ثابت): Zayd reports that after Yamāma's losses, ʿUmar urged collecting the Qur'an; Abū Bakr initially refused because the Prophet had not done so, then accepted the proposal and assigned Zayd. TAB-FULL (زيد بن ثابت): Zayd says he gathered the Qur'an from parchment, shoulder blades, and palm stalks; the single sheet later passed from Abū Bakr to ʿUmar and Ḥafṣa. TAB-FULL (حذيفة بن اليمان): Ḥudhayfa warned ʿUthmān after seeing Syrians and Iraqis recite differently in Armenia and accuse each other's readings of unbelief. TAB-FULL (عثمان بن عفان): ʿUthmān commissioned Zayd and the eloquent Abān ibn Saʿīd to produce a codex, write what they agreed on, and refer disagreements to him. TAB-FULL (عثمان بن عفان): ʿUthmān borrowed Ḥafṣa's sheet, collated the codex without finding differences, returned it, ordered copies made, then after her death reclaimed and erased the sheet.

IBNKATHIR-FULL (حذيفة بن اليمان): During the Armenia and Azerbaijan campaigns, Ḥudhayfa heard Syrian and Iraqi Muslims differing in their recitations and warned ʿUthmān to act before the community divided over scripture as Jews and Christians had. IBNKATHIR-FULL (عثمان بن عفان): ʿUthmān borrowed Ḥafṣa’s pages and commissioned Zayd ibn Thābit, ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr, Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ, and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥārith to copy them into codices. IBNKATHIR-FULL (author): Ibn Kathir counts ʿUthmān’s unification of the community on one reading among his greatest merits; Abū Bakr and ʿUmar had earlier collected the Qur’an to prevent any part from being lost. IBNKATHIR-FULL (author): The Companions all agreed with ʿUthmān’s decision; Ibn Masʿūd initially showed anger because he was not among the codex copyists and told his followers to conceal their codices, but later returned to agreement. IBNKATHIR-FULL (علي بن أبي طالب): ʿAlī said that had ʿUthmān not taken this step, he would have done it himself.

ITQAN (ابن حجر): Ibn Hajar dates Uthman’s collection to 25 AH and says a later estimate around 30 AH was asserted without supporting evidence. ITQAN (أبو قلابة): Abu Qilaba reports that reading disputes in Uthman's time led to fights; Uthman ordered a standard codex, and when the committee disagreed, they consulted Companions on the Prophet’s recitation and recorded it. ITQAN (محمد بن سيرين): Ibn Sirin reports that Uthman assembled twelve Quraysh and Ansar to copy the codices from the sheets kept at Umar’s house; the committee delayed disputed passages, which Ibn Sirin thought allowed consultation of those last present at the final review. ITQAN (علي): Ali says Uthman’s codex decision had the Companions’ agreement and united Muslims after competing readings led some to declare another’s recitation nearly unbelief. ITQAN (ابن التين): Ibn al-Tin and others distinguish Abu Bakr’s collection, which guarded against loss by placing the Quran’s dispersed material in ordered sheets, from Uthman’s codex, which addressed escalating reading disputes.

IBNKATHIR-FULL (مصعب بن سعد): Musʿab b. Saʿd reports that ʿUthmān responded to reading disputes by collecting written Qurʾan fragments, checking each against the Prophet’s dictation, assigning Saʿīd to dictate and Zayd to write; Ibn Kathīr grades the chain ṣaḥīḥ. IBNKATHIR-FULL (كثير بن أفلح): Kathīr b. Aflah reports that ʿUthmān assembled twelve Qurashī and Anṣārī men, including Ubayy and Zayd, and brought the collected sheets; Ibn Kathīr calls this report ṣaḥīḥ. IBNKATHIR-FULL (author): Ibn Kathīr clarifies that the collected sheets were with Ḥafṣa; ʿUthmān used them to compile the codex, then returned them to her as promised rather than burning them. IBNKATHIR-FULL (author): After Ḥafṣa died, Marwān b. al-Ḥakam took and burned the sheets, adopting the rationale ʿUthmān had used for destroying other copies.

ITQAN (author): Al-Suyuti says the hadith about seven ahruf has roughly forty interpretations. ITQAN (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): Ubayy’s Muslim report likewise recounts successive easing from one to two and ultimately seven ahruf. ITQAN (أبو بكرة): In Abu Bakra’s Nasaʾi report, Michael’s silence signals that the fixed count has ended. ITQAN (author): A third view takes seven ahruf to mean seven readings; its objection is that few words, such as عبد الطاغوت and أف, have seven forms.

ITQAN (ابن سيرين): Ibn Sirin disliked writing the mushaf in mashq, explaining that it involves a deficiency. ITQAN (ابن مسعود): Ibn Masʿud said the best adornment of a gold-decorated mushaf is reciting it truthfully. ITQAN (عمر): ʿUmar rebuked and struck a man for writing a mushaf in very fine script, telling him to honor God’s Book; he was pleased to see a large mushaf. ITQAN (علي): Ali disliked making mushafs small.

BAQILLANI (author): If material was absent from Ibn Masʿud’s codex, he may have relied on communal memorization rather than denied its Qur’anic status; the reports are solitary and insufficient for such a claim. BAQILLANI (author): Ibn Masʿud may have written the qunut supplication on the back of his codex as a personal reminder, as people write prayers on their own copies. BAQILLANI (author): Had Ibn Masʿud rejected the two surahs, the Companions would have debated and publicized so grave a dispute; their agreement on the codex cannot be undone by isolated fabricated reports. | mentions 113:1, 114:1

IBNKATHIR-FULL (بعضهم): One view says ʿUthmān consolidated the community on one reading and final recension because variation risked division and mutual accusations of unbelief, then prohibited other readings despite the former concession. IBNKATHIR-FULL (الخطابي): A second view says the Qurʾan’s seven aḥruf do not mean every passage is recited in all seven; different passages may occur in different forms. Al-Khaṭṭābī gives 5:60 and 12:12 as examples. | mentions 5:60, 12:12 IBNKATHIR-FULL (القاضي الباقلاني): Al-Bāqillānī says ʿUthmān’s statement that it was revealed in Quraysh speech means most of it, not all: no proof establishes that every word is Qurashī, since Arabic includes all tribes; Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr agrees.

IBNASHUR-FULL (عبد الله ابن مسعود): When Abu Bakr sought a name for the written Quran, suggestions Injil and Sifr were rejected for their Christian and Jewish associations; Ibn Masud proposed Mushaf, a name he had seen used in Abyssinia. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Calling the revelation a book foretold miraculously that it would be written in codices, as shown by Quranic passages describing it as a revealed book. | mentions 6:92, 21:50 IBNASHUR-FULL (author): When Abu Bakr ordered a written codex, the collected text matched what Muslims had retained by heart with what had been written down.

IBNKATHIR-FULL (أنس بن مالك): Anas reports that ʿUthmān assigned Zayd, Saʿīd b. al-ʿĀṣ, Ibn al-Zubayr, and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. al-Ḥārith to copy codices, directing them to use Quraysh speech if they and Zayd differed in Qurʾanic Arabic. IBNKATHIR-FULL (عمر بن الخطاب): ʿUmar reportedly said only Qurashī or Thaqafī youths should dictate in the official codices; Ibn Kathīr grades the chain ṣaḥīḥ.

IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The Quran encourages extended recitation; Ibn Ashur reads ما تيسر as reciting as much as one can manage, with coherence and stylistic variety helping sustain it. | mentions 73:20 IBNASHUR-FULL (أبو بكر بن العربي): In Siraj al-Muridin, Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi calls the links among Quranic verses a great science, making them cohere like a single phrase.

TAB-FULL (author): Al-Ṭabarī argues the community could transmit some of the seven modes and omit the rest; they fulfilled their duty, and preserving every mode could have harmed Islam and its people.
THALABI (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): Uthman, Ibn Masud, and Ubayy report that the Prophet taught ten verses at a time and waited until they learned their knowledge and practice before proceeding.
BAGHAWI-FULL (author): The Qur'an is inimitable: creation cannot answer it or produce a sura like it, although God makes its recitation easy for people.
KASHSHAF-FULL (شريح وابن سيرين وعثمان البتي): Shurayḥ, Ibn Sīrīn, and ʿUthmān al-Battī allow testimony by enslaved people.
IBNKATHIR-FULL (مجاهد): Mujāhid says he recited the entire muṣḥaf to Ibn ʿAbbās three times, stopping at every verse to ask its interpretation.
BURHAN (الأزهري): Al-Azhari calls this the preferred view and cites Uthman's instruction to write in Quraysh speech when he and Zayd disagreed, since most revelation came in that language.
BURHAN (مالك): Malik permits reading variants such as Umar’s فامضوا and يعلمون/تعلمون, invoking the seven ahruf; he says disagreement is harmless and people once used separate codices.
BURHAN (الشيخ شهاب الدين): Shihab al-Din permits combining readings when they do not depend on one another, citing the seven ahruf as a concession; he sees no harm in such combinations.
BURHAN (إمام الحرمين): The Imam of the Two Sanctuaries says intending Qur'anic recitation in such phrases is sinful, while intending remembrance without intending recitation is not.
ITQAN (القاضي أبو بكر): Al-Qadi Abu Bakr says some jurists and theologians would establish Quranic status as a legal ruling, but not certainty, from an isolated report; the orthodox reject this.

YKHULI-TAJDID (author): The muṣḥaf’s arrangement does not preserve topical unity or chronology, Meccan and Medinan verses intermingle, and one subject appears in varied contexts; topical reading best enables deeper engagement.

turns_on: The notes offer different readings, referents, grounds, or applications.

question: What broader claims about Quranic eloquence accompany the verse?

positions.reasons: GHARNATI (author): The author invokes the Qurʾan’s exalted standing in the heavenly register as part of his praise of the divine gift of scripture. | mentions 43:4 GHARNATI (author): Muhammad is praised as the chosen prophet endowed with the Book and clear proofs that open the path for people of insight. GHARNATI (author): The cited warning says that only one who follows the Reminder and fears the Merciful unseen benefits from the Messenger’s warning. | mentions 36:11 GHARNATI (النبي): The Prophet says every prophet received signs sufficient for people to believe, while his own special gift was revelation, through which he hopes to have the most followers on Judgment Day. GHARNATI (author): The author says the Prophet had countless miracles besides the Qurʾan, but the Qurʾan is the clearest, wisest, most guiding, and most enduring miracle. GHARNATI (author): The Qurʾan joins proof and testimony with clarification of the path and the condition of each group, and remains directly observable to those who reflect. GHARNATI (author): Unlike other miracles known through later reports rather than direct observation, the Qurʾan remains pure and present for reflection across the ages.

BAQILLANI (author): Punning can be learned from books such as Kitab al-Ajnas and Kitab al-ʿAyn, and antithesis is easier; the eloquence at issue in Qur’anic inimitability cannot be acquired by study. BAQILLANI (author): Learnable capacities converge at a customary limit, like human strength; exceeding that limit breaks convention and can serve as a prophetic sign under the proper conditions. BAQILLANI (author): Exceptional lines or phrases may occur rarely in a poet’s or writer’s work, so a person may be famed for only one or two; if all speech sustained that level, it could be called miraculous. BAQILLANI (author): Humans can produce a fine word or phrase, but cannot compose a surah or equivalent or attain the Qur’an’s level of eloquence and oratory. BAQILLANI (author): Eloquence means conveying the self’s intended meaning with the best sense and strongest wording, reaching the utterance’s full purpose.

BAQILLANI (author): Speech becomes miraculous when it surpasses eloquence’s customary limit and reaches a level even the most accomplished practitioners cannot attain. BAQILLANI (author): The Qur’an differs from other speech in its genre and style and in exceeding the human limit of eloquence. BAQILLANI (السائل): An objection asks why a poet’s rare brilliant passage could not become the model for all his work through supreme mastery, just as the Qur’an might be exceptional speech. BAQILLANI (author): After a long challenge and repeated rebukes, the Qur’an alone holds the lead; everyone failed, some recognizing their incapacity without understanding its cause. BAQILLANI (author): Its rupture of customary human ability is a miracle and proof that the prophet who brought it is truthful in his claim and rightly guided.

BAQILLANI (author): An accomplished critic recognizes each speaker’s style and ranks speech accurately, including whether a writer excels in only certain genres or throughout. BAQILLANI (author): Poets may excel selectively in praise, invective, humor, or description; an expert knows each person’s limits and can identify their later work. BAQILLANI (author): Experts distinguish Abu Tammam from al-Buhturi except where the former drops artifice and adopts an easy, bookish style resembling the latter. BAQILLANI (author): He lists recognizable styles among al-Aʿsha, Imruʾ al-Qays, al-Nabigha, Zuhayr, Jarir, al-Akhtal, al-Baʿith, and al-Farazdaq.

BAQILLANI (السائل): An objection asks whether the Prophet’s exceptional eloquence could have produced the Qur’an, since he is reported to have called himself the most eloquent Arab. BAQILLANI (author): The Prophet did not challenge others to match his own speech; his difference from other eloquent people is an ordinary gradation like that between poets or orators. BAQILLANI (السائل): An objection invokes reports that Ibn Masʿud was uncertain whether the two protecting surahs or the qunut supplication belonged to the Qur’an. | mentions 113:1, 114:1 BAQILLANI (author): He calls this an infidel’s confusion: the Companions knew the Qur’an and its surah count, and no Qur’anic material could have been unknown to them.

BINTSHATI-IJAZ (الفخر الرازي): Al-Razi recast Jurjani's theory in a better order and style, while acknowledging that Jurjani established its principles and rules but left the topics poorly arranged and wrote at great length. BINTSHATI-IJAZ (ابن أبي الإصبع المصري): Ibn Abi al-Isba's Badi al-Qur'an organized rhetoric into 120 chapters seeking Qur'anic examples, but usually named a device and supplied examples without explaining their rhetorical force. BINTSHATI-IJAZ (السكاكي): Al-Sakkaki made rhetoric in Miftah al-Ulum an autonomous, rule-bound craft, separating it from the question of inimitability and from the syntactic meanings Jurjani had included in nazm. BINTSHATI-IJAZ (author): Later rhetoric concentrated on formal taxonomies of simile, metaphor, figurative language, metonymy, and embellishment, while Qur'anic examples were sparse beside examples from human speech.

BINTSHATI-IJAZ (author): The passage condemns people who relabel falsehood, degradation, shamelessness, error, and unbelief as utility, instinct, freedom, reason, and science, then call themselves scholars and reformers. BINTSHATI-IJAZ (author): A teacher may wear a turban and claim religious standing while carrying a destructive scientific ideology into the young; the reader should not be deceived by appearances. BINTSHATI-IJAZ (author): The passage depicts such a teacher as parasitic and socially destructive, weakening life and strength and leaving illness, harm, or constriction wherever he acts. BINTSHATI-IJAZ (author): The author says scholars unfairly burden the Qur'an with every scientific objection and shun it, like aircraft deluded by rising into the sky and mounting a campaign toward the sun.

BINTSHATI-IJAZ (بعض المتكلمين): A theologian's argument says either the Qur'an is inherently beyond human imitation, or people could imitate it but were prevented from doing so, making their failure miraculous. BINTSHATI-IJAZ (ابن كثير): Ibn Kathir finds the diversion argument unsatisfactory because the Qur'an is inherently miraculous, though useful as a concessive argument in debate. BINTSHATI-IJAZ (الرازي): Al-Razi uses this argument in his tafsir to explain the miraculousness of short suras such as al-Asr and al-Kawthar. | mentions 103:1, 108:1 BINTSHATI-IJAZ (author): The theoretical debate did not end rhetorical inquiry: later Mu'tazilites treated diversion as one aspect of inimitability, while non-Mu'tazilite surveyors soon focused on rhetorical inimitability.

YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Rhetoric studied the Qur’an’s inimitability, jurisprudence derived rulings by analogy with it, and kalām rationalized it and developed toward philosophy. YKHULI-TAJDID (أمين الخولي): Al-Khūlī treats the Qur’an’s psychological inimitability as its profound effect on the human psyche through sweetness of wording and meaning, sound, and rhythm. YKHULI-TAJDID (السكاكي): Al-Sakkākī’s view, as reported through Al-Khūlī, is that the Qur’an’s psychological inimitability is apprehended through artistic taste rather than described or explained. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): The Qur’an is miraculous literary art serving religious guidance: art voices the conscience, while religion addresses belief and the heart and disciplines human feeling.

BAQILLANI (author): The report derives qasida from accumulated marrow, as opposed to scattered marrow, and cites Labid’s stacked ostrich eggs as evidence for the sense of layered accumulation. BAQILLANI (بعض علماء هذه الصنعة): An unnamed master attributes such exceptional lines to deep command of the craft and broad knowledge, which can yield effects beyond calculation or classification. BAQILLANI (author): He reaffirms that speech equal in measure to a surah is miraculous.

BAQILLANI (author): What resembles sajʿ in the Qur’an is not necessarily sajʿ: ordinary sajʿ makes wording follow the cadence, whereas Qur’anic phrasing follows the meaning. BAQILLANI (author): When meaning is organized independently of cadence, the cadence is merely decorative rather than necessary to the meaning; he distinguishes this from meaning tied to sajʿ. BAQILLANI (author): Even if some passages combine the two patterns, a detailed treatment is outside the book’s scope; apparent non-sajʿ passages contain subtler benefits.

JURJANI-ASRAR (author): Jurjānī endorses al-Āmidī’s view that rain's fashioning and weaving of plants is literal, not metaphor; al-Āmidī praises al-Buḥturī's phrasing and calls Abū Tammām's explicit weaver comparison ugly. JURJANI-ASRAR (author): Jurjānī explains that explicit simile names both subjects, while implicit simile transfers the comparison's name to its subject; the same distinction lets actions be compared explicitly or called swimming and flight metaphorically. JURJANI-ASRAR (author): In the Abū Dulāma example, Jurjānī maps each mule leg's unstable or curved movement to a specific hand motion in kneading or baking dough.

JURJANI-ASRAR (معترض): An interlocutor objects that calling a brave man a lion does not transfer the word outside its meaning, since the intended comparison is courage, already associated with lions. JURJANI-ASRAR (author): Jurjānī replies that lion includes bodily shape and visible traits as well as courage; applying its name to a man strips away those literal traits and transfers the name by an imagined likeness. JURJANI-ASRAR (author): By contrast, attributing an action to spring is literal: the language predicates an act without asserting anything about the subject's nature, so no part of the word's meaning is displaced.

JURJANI-DALAIL (author): Coordinated clauses need related subjects and reports; pairing Abu al-Husayn’s generosity with the bitterness of separation is jarring because the ideas have no connection. JURJANI-DALAIL (author): When clauses concern one person, the conjunction clearly asserts both actions together; without it, the second statement could retract the first. JURJANI-DALAIL (author): Coordination inside a relative or similarly linked construction tightens the pairing further, so the actions cannot sensibly be understood apart.

JURJANI-DALAIL (author): With ‘not ... except’, placing the predicate after the subject restricts the predicate to that subject, while placing the predicate first restricts the subject to those bearing that predicate. JURJANI-DALAIL (author): ‘Zayd is nothing but standing’ excludes incompatible states such as sitting, but does not exclude unrelated qualities such as being tall, white, or learned; ‘no one is standing but Zayd’ is context-bound. JURJANI-DALAIL (author): The restriction denies that another, incompatible state replaces the named one, rather than denying all accompanying attributes; unlike ‘innamā’, ‘mā ... illā’ already excludes every contrary state.

JURJANI-DALAIL (author): A word is not eloquent in isolation: the same word can be excellent in one context and ordinary elsewhere because its merit appears only after it enters a composition. JURJANI-DALAIL (author): Though ordinary usage calls words eloquent rather than meanings, the claim that eloquence lies in meaning means that the merit behind an eloquent word ultimately returns to its meaning. JURJANI-DALAIL (author): Since a speaker cannot alter linguistic words or add a new formal quality to them, while eloquence is the speaker’s achievement, the merit must be in meaning.

JURJANI-DALAIL (القائلون): Critics argue that one meaning can be expressed in two ways, one eloquent and one not; this would give words an independent share in excellence. JURJANI-DALAIL (author): If the comparison concerns synonymous individual words, it misses the issue: Jurjānī is discussing eloquence produced by composition, not isolated vocabulary. JURJANI-DALAIL (author): If it concerns whole expressions, the same basic meaning can be plain or artistically fashioned, like a simple piece of jewelry versus an expertly crafted one.

JURJANI-DALAIL (author): The source of eloquence and inimitability is the arrangement of meanings, not the order of bare words; a word-focused account of the Qur’an’s merit collapses. JURJANI-DALAIL (author): Fasāḥa is attributed to a word because it names the quality by which that word signals rhetorical merit; the meaning itself is not directly described as eloquent. JURJANI-DALAIL (author): Older critics’ ‘noble’ or ‘restless’ word is shorthand for semantic fit with neighboring meanings: wording is called settled or awkward because of what it conveys in the composition.

IBNASHUR-FULL (فخر الدين الرازي): Al-Razi says the Quran is inimitable through arrangement and verse order as well as eloquent wording and noble meanings; al-Isfahani suggests this is what style-based claims mean. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Quranic prose uses balanced, near-rhyming endings without rhetorical necessity or the constraints of meter, giving it smooth and harmonious delivery. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The Quran’s prose form itself contributes to its inimitability; it gathers known Arabic styles and innovates new ones.

BINTSHATI-IJAZ (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas calls the most brazen person either someone who speaks without knowledge or someone who conceals knowledge God gave him. BINTSHATI-IJAZ (نجدة): Najda says they want Ibn Abbas to explain Qur'anic questions with Arabic evidence because God revealed the Qur'an in clear Arabic. BINTSHATI-IJAZ (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas invites them to ask whatever they wish; this transmission preserves 255 questions and closes with the completion of Ibn al-Azraq's questions.

KHATTABI (author): The elephant parody raises grand expectations but then dwells only on trunk and tail, omitting the creature’s intelligence, obedience, tusks, ears, and intricate design. KHATTABI (author): Analogy is judged by shared meanings rather than physical size: elephant and mosquito share animal functions and head and trunk features, while the mosquito’s wings offset its small body.

BAQILLANI (author): The Hudaybiyya treaty set a ten-year truce, returned Quraysh escapees who lacked a guardian’s permission, left Muslim defectors with Quraysh, allowed either side to join either pact, and set the Prophet’s delayed three-day Meccan visit and travel arms. BAQILLANI (author): Companions’ and other eloquent speakers’ sermons share the Prophet’s human style; their differences are bounded variations among eloquent people, unlike the Qur’an’s distinction.

JURJANI-ASRAR (author): In the travel poem, أطراف suggests both varied strands of conversation and the allusive gestures of companions; it conveys their lively ease, friendship, and pleasure on the journey home. JURJANI-ASRAR (author): The poet says the camels' necks because speed and slowness show especially in their necks and heads, whose movement reveals their spirited gait.

JURJANI-DALAIL (author): ‘You are the beloved’ presents love as a whole genus confined to one person, implying the speaker loves no one else; ‘Zayd, the one departing’ identifies a single known departure instead. JURJANI-DALAIL (author): Adding a habitual quality, as in ‘Zayd who goes about your need’, makes the description generic and restores the genus-like sense found in ‘you are the beloved’.

JURJANI-DALAIL (author): The commonplace thought that nature cannot change becomes newly striking in al-Mutanabbī’s line, where nature resists being carried away. JURJANI-DALAIL (author): An eloquent expression improves and adorns a shared underlying meaning, giving it a distinctive image that a plain paraphrase lacks.

JURJANI-DALAIL (author): A parable’s purpose is inferred from the combined sense, not from literal words: a ruler’s image of advancing one foot and drawing back the other means wavering over whether to pledge allegiance. JURJANI-DALAIL (author): The Prophet’s ‘green plants of dung heaps’ figures a beautiful woman of poor upbringing, just as ‘much ash in the pot’ figures generous hospitality; the inferred meaning, not the phrase, is the parable.

JURJANI-DALAIL (author): Jurjānī says scholars agree that nazm is indispensable to eloquent speech; without it, unusual meanings alone confer no rank or completeness. JURJANI-DALAIL (author): The composer must consider the different forms available within each grammatical category, such as alternative word orders and predicate forms.

BINTSHATI-IJAZ (author): The passage rejects calling Qur'anic endings saj' merely because they resemble rhyme: saj' subordinates wording to rhyme, whereas Qur'anic wording follows the meaning. BINTSHATI-IJAZ (author): Calling the Qur'an saj' would make it blameworthy by ordinary standards because saj' requires regular measures and a fixed pattern, unlike uneven Qur'anic endings.

JURJANI-ASRAR (author): Although tamthīl, simile, and metaphor are only three labels, explaining their divisions and fine distinctions requires extensive reading and thought; Jurjānī defends that detailed inquiry against dismissive critics.
BAGHAWI-FULL (author): The Qur'an is an inimitable, deep sea whose scholarly secrets and true meanings have no end.

IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): The clause puts the cause before the intended result because listeners naturally seek the cause of events; this anticipatory order is an especially eloquent, concise alternative to a follow-up question and answer.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): The verse varies address between direct presence and third-person reference, then shifts repeatedly to heighten its rhetorical movement.

BURHAN (بعضهم): Some parse رجلين as an explanatory circumstantial accusative with complete kāna; the author says this answers a question about parsing, not the rhetorical arrangement, and adds needless strain.
ITQAN (أهل البيان): Rhetoricians list coordination with لا or بل as a fourth construction of restriction and report no disagreement on it.

IBNASHUR-FULL (author): This scholarly dimension of inimitability belongs to the Quran as a whole, not every verse or sura separately; the challenge is only alluded to in the challenge to inconsistency. | mentions 4:82

IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Tafsir studies the Quran to clarify its meanings and guidance, instruction, manners, and reform of the community and its dealings with other peoples through linguistic and rhetorical evidence.

IBNASHUR-FULL (author): A poem in al-Ḥamāsa repeats al-luʾm in three lines to censure a tribe and its descendants, illustrating deliberate repetition; al-Jurjānī says taste can discern rhetorical effects that resist explanation.
BINTSHATI-IJAZ (author): The author concludes that sadad is narrower, chiefly denoting soundness and reform in speech or opinion, whereas adl is broader and most often appears in legal contexts.

RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): He used evolution to rebuild religious knowledge and Arabic language studies, disrupting traditional linguistic and rhetorical scholarship and opening new horizons in Azhar ethics.

positions.position: Declarative forms may express a demand or response.
positions.reasons: BURHAN (author): The passage lists declarative forms such as God's counter-maneuver, His making mockery, and like-for-like recompense as wording placed where a demand or response is intended.

question: What interpretive methods do the cited works discuss?

positions.reasons: YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Al-Khūlī’s approach to Qur’anic interpretation lies at the intersection of preserving intellectual origins and renewing them. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Although modern historical, archaeological, and anthropological research recovered ancient national origins, consciousness had already settled within the Qur’anic frame. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): The Qur’an became the center around which the heritage sciences arose, beginning with the linguistic disciplines because the Qur’an is a linguistic phenomenon. YKHULI-TAJDID (حسن حنفي): Ḥasan Ḥanafī contrasts an Islamic civilization formed around the Qur’an with Western Christian civilization, where the book emerged from tradition; the Gospels followed the Christian call rather than serving as its source. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): The author notes that seventeenth-century historical criticism, associated with Spinoza, Richard Simon, and Jean Astruc, examined alteration and change in sacred books. YKHULI-TAJDID (حسن حنفي): Ḥasan Ḥanafī identifies three distinguishing Qur’anic features: it is the final, complete revelation; preserved in writing; and revealed gradually over twenty-three years in response to human needs. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): The author links gradual, situation-responsive revelation to Al-Khūlī’s principle that the Qur’an is closely connected to human life, which grounds his literary school of interpretation. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Al-Khūlī’s literary approach challenges rigid, literal, static exegesis because that mode permits neither development nor renewal. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Interpretation is the starting point for intellectual work that renews the civilization, because the Qur’an anchors its origins and Muslim communal identity. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Al-Khūlī uses the psychological dimension to connect religion and literature and argues for reading the Qur’an topic by topic. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Topical interpretation is always colored by the historical period in which it is undertaken. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): The Qur’an uses taʾwīl, while legal theorists developed a specialized sense that later became common among theologians; Al-Khūlī considers tafsīr broader than taʾwīl. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Interpretive forms multiply because interpreters bring different cultural backgrounds to the text. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Hermeneutics has an older sense, the interpretation of sacred books, and a modern sense that developed into a major late-twentieth-century philosophical current. YKHULI-TAJDID (فيلهلم دلتاي): Dilthey’s hermeneutic position treats interpretation or understanding as a method for the social and historical sciences. YKHULI-TAJDID (مارتن هيدجر): Heidegger’s position treats interpretation as an ontological, existential event in which text and interpreter interact within the history of understanding. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): The author follows the Heideggerian line, treating hermeneutics as lived experience of texts and as dialogue that fuses text and reader across past and present. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Hermeneutics applies to religious, inherited, philosophical, and legal texts; in reading, text and reader, past and present, enter a reciprocal relation that keeps new understanding possible. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): A text gains particular content when a present-day reader speaks on its behalf; without the present’s participation, it becomes frozen and detached from reality. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): A writer’s work of classification ends when the text is produced, but reading, interpretation, and understanding remain open-ended tasks. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Hermeneutics became an independent discipline that both draws on and informs the human sciences; it engages theories of knowledge, being, and value, especially epistemology. YKHULI-TAJDID (هانز جيورج جادامر): Gadamer’s Truth and Method (1960) established hermeneutics as a powerful method, said to rival experimental science in importance for understanding the human reality of texts. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Hermeneutics developed schools and became a broad intellectual current with strong influence on cultural life and literary criticism. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): The author compares the Qur’an’s appearance in Arab civilization to philosophy’s appearance in the West: each was a decisive turn in outlook and method. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Hermeneutics rejects the gap between reader and text: meaning depends on the context of production and the recipient’s horizon, so it varies across times and places. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Interpretation makes the text living and renewable by placing responsibility on reading: the reader reshapes its raw material according to the cultural horizon of the present. YKHULI-TAJDID (أمين الخولي): Al-Khūlī argues that a reader’s personality, intellectual level, and mental horizon limit what the reader can understand from a text; Arabic’s rich resources permit many interpretive extensions. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): The author attributes the crisis of Islamic culture and Arab civilization to the failure of interpretation and renewal, followed by a long era of commentaries, glosses, and marginalia. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Renewing Qur’anic interpretation is necessary for the renewal and flourishing of Arab-Islamic thought, a goal pursued by Islamic thinkers since the Nahḍa began. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): The author concludes that Al-Khūlī substantially achieved this renewalist aim. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Pre-revelation cultural inheritances persisted in Egypt through Pharaonic customs and the Coptic calendar, and other Muslim countries also retained pre-Qur’anic inheritances. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Despite those inheritances, the Qur’an quickly gathered them into a new civilizational phase that shaped the later historical course. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): The Qur’an’s linguistic character makes authenticity a distinctive concern: language is the fabric of thought and consciousness, not a container for thought. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): The Qur’an’s linguistic force accompanied a kind of historical amnesia, as conquered peoples abandoned their national languages, which had embodied earlier social life and values. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Islam presented itself as a continuation, development, and refinement of earlier revealed religions, especially Judaism and Christianity.

RIFAI-KHULI (author): Classical tajdīd meant reviving neglected religious practice in its original form; Khuli instead defines renewal as development that discovers something new through ijtihād. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli rejected irrational claims that Arabic is uniquely perfect or complete: like other languages, it is a living social organism whose words die, arise, and develop through use. RIFAI-KHULI (author): Khuli traced the gap between written Classical Arabic and colloquial speech to early lexicographers privileging Bedouin usage and excluding common urban vocabulary. RIFAI-KHULI (author): The author reads this account as showing Arabic's inherited Bedouin worldview and limited urban vocabulary; Abbasid Arabic then borrowed and coined terms to cover city life's new realities. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli held that developing beliefs is possible and now necessary, both because life requires it and to protect religion's continued relevance and compatibility with thought and action. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): He urged a new approach to unseen matters, rejecting excessive attribution of phenomena to the unseen and detailed speculation that scientific-minded younger generations cannot absorb. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli opposed ahistorical readings of heritage: each tradition is shaped by the particular temporal and spatial conditions of its period and changes as those conditions change. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): He applied gradual progression to material and immaterial life alike: forms begin simply, compete, and develop as what is fit survives and becomes more complex. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli described Islamic beliefs as developing from simple early forms to more complex ones as Muslims moved from Bedouin life into civilization and encountered learning and other peoples' thought; he contrasted the clear creed of the salaf with the interpretive creed of later scholars. RIFAI-KHULI (author): Khuli departed from the revivalist reform program associated with al-Tahtawi, al-Afghani, and Muhammad Abduh, which relied on inherited principles to restore earlier glory. RIFAI-KHULI (author): The author regards Khuli's position as an early call for a new kalām: an age-responsive effort to interpret and justify belief, protecting faith from extremism and stagnation as well as defending it. RIFAI-KHULI (author): The author interprets Khuli's historicity as the view that ideas resemble and arise from their environments: intellectually fertile settings generate complex thought, while poorer settings produce simpler ideas. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli insisted that renewal begins by thoroughly understanding the old and changing our role from guarding and sanctifying heritage to studying it critically. RIFAI-KHULI (author): The author reads Khuli's 'killing' of the old as discernment, not destruction: identify inert inherited elements and understand how their concepts and questions restrict present life and future movement. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli allowed renewal to find new insight by drawing on existing old material, as well as by independent reasoning that produces something previously unknown. RIFAI-KHULI (author): The author says Khuli sought to breathe new life into old material after accreted misunderstanding had hardened it; he did not advocate discarding the entire past. RIFAI-KHULI (author): Khuli differed from reformers who repackaged old content in new forms and treated heritage as an exhaustive storehouse; he called for genuinely novel work. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli made evolution comprehensive across fundamentals, beliefs, worship, and transactions, extending reform beyond the commonly accepted scope of legal dealings; the author says including worship may be his distinctive position. RIFAI-KHULI (author): The author notes that worship is conventionally treated as fixed by revelation, unlike transactions, but Khuli still urged reconsidering legal and theological works in light of changing realities. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli argued that new events absent from old fiqh books cannot halt the world's course; rigidity risks alienating ordinary people from a religion unable to address their lives. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli fashioned a different path for understanding religion and interpreting its texts, beyond inherited foundations and principles. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): In a discussion with the Shaykh al-Azhar, Khuli rejected restricting change to a few worship rulings and said Islamic law selects what is easier to practice and best suited to endure. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli raised whether worshippers could follow congregational Friday and festival prayers through televised broadcasts, seeing and hearing the imam when local mosques are crowded. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): For Khuli, transactions turn on public benefit wherever it exists; evolving the presentation of beliefs, worship, and transactions should keep religious life connected to ordinary life. RIFAI-KHULI (author): The author says Khuli did not fully explain the basis or applications of evolving worship rulings and cautiously reads him as seeking easier performance of obligations through a broader use of hardship relief and secondary rulings. RIFAI-KHULI (author): The author judges general calls to adapt fiqh insufficient unless scholars rebuild the underlying principles and inference rules so they can yield alternative rulings responsive to changing times and places. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli defended Darwinian biological evolution, finding comparable hierarchical classifications of beings in the Ikhwan al-Safa, Miskawayh, Avicenna, and Ibn Tufayl. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli regarded renewal at the head of each century as a major revolutionary work the community needs, almost a periodic social revolution. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): He extended evolution across theology, law, language, and all moral, intellectual, social, and spiritual dimensions of human life, treating it as a universal law rather than biology's specialty. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli analogized the emergence of new ideas to biological evolution: social conditions and proponents' conviction help new ideas outcompete old ones until they take root. RIFAI-KHULI (author): The author sees Khuli's appeal to modern science as a contemporary reformist strategy, but criticizes some thinkers for forcing scientific theories onto the Qur'an until it seems to lack independent content.

RIFAI-KHULI (author): Al-Rifai treats a book as its own interpretive key: Qur'anic verses illuminate one another, but readers cannot attain complete neutrality because their formation and assumptions shape interpretation. RIFAI-KHULI (author): An exegete's field colors interpretation: a theologian produces kalam-oriented tafsir, a jurist legal tafsir, a Sufi mystical tafsir, and a literary scholar literary tafsir. RIFAI-KHULI (author): Al-Rifai stresses that even Qur'an-by-Qur'an exegesis is shaped by hidden assumptions when an interpreter chooses one verse or word to explain another. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli describes reciprocal effects between an exegete's worldview, specialized knowledge, and interpretation; connecting disciplines to tafsir can enrich those disciplines too. RIFAI-KHULI (author): Al-Rifai argues that applying disciplines in new fields helps them develop by exposing gaps, defects, and errors. RIFAI-KHULI (author): Al-Rifai says Khuli's position does not entail relativism; it frees Qur'anic meaning from exegetes' errors and treats their readings as historically conditioned rather than eternally authoritative. RIFAI-KHULI (author): Al-Rifai says Muhammad Ahmad Khalaf Allah embodied Khuli's reformist method, while Aisha Abd al-Rahman remained attached to inherited tafsir and did not adopt modern hermeneutics. RIFAI-KHULI (author): Al-Rifai suggests Bint al-Shati avoided departing from inherited methods out of fear after Khalaf Allah's dissertation drew fierce attacks; he adds that she may not have grasped Khuli's critique of inherited tafsir. RIFAI-KHULI (author): Al-Rifai argues that reform is emotionally and materially costly and requires courage to challenge convention. RIFAI-KHULI (author): Al-Rifai cites Muhammad Rashid Rida's Salafi turn after Muhammad Abduh's death as another example of students reverting to inherited tradition rather than following a reformist teacher. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli says interpreters color a text, especially a literary one: a reader's personality sets its intellectual level and the horizon within which its meaning is understood. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli describes readers as pulling a phrase in different directions and drawing from it only what their intellectual capacity permits; language's figurative range enables this coloring. RIFAI-KHULI (author): Al-Rifai suspects Khuli borrowed the image of coloring text from Junayd's saying that water takes its vessel's color, and sees Sufi and gnostic methods as valuable resources beyond inherited tafsir and legal theory. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli holds that interpreters' personalities mark every method and era of exegesis, whether transmitted or reasoned, despite claims of detachment and objectivity. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli rejects the claim that transmitted exegesis escapes the interpreter's personal imprint simply because it explains verses through reports without overt intervention. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): For Khuli, a narrator's choice to gather reports that seem relevant to a verse, and to accept or reject them, exposes the interpreter's horizon and prior assumptions. RIFAI-KHULI (author): Al-Rifai draws the consequence that transmitted tafsir is a form of opinion-based exegesis, and even Qur'an-by-Qur'an interpretation depends on the interpreter's selection of verses and words.

ITQAN (author): Al-Bukhari often cites Ibn Abi Talha’s Ibn Abbas tafsir through Abu Salih; al-Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmit it through intermediaries. ITQAN (author): The tafsir of Ata ibn Dinar may be recorded and used as evidence. ITQAN (author): The tafsir of Abu Ruwq, about one part, was judged sound. ITQAN (author): Al-Suddi’s tafsir has chains to Ibn Masud and Ibn Abbas; although leading imams narrated from al-Suddi, Asbat ibn Nasr’s compilation is disputed, yet al-Suyuti calls it the best tafsir. ITQAN (الخليلي): Ibn Jurayj did not aim to authenticate his tafsir and included both sound and weak reports for each verse. ITQAN (الخليلي): Maqatil ibn Sulayman was considered weak, though he met senior Successors and al-Shafi'i indicated his tafsir was usable. ITQAN (قوم): Some say Ibn Abi Talha did not hear Ibn Abbas’s tafsir and instead received it from Mujahid or Sa'id ibn Jubayr. ITQAN (الخليلي): Al-Khalili describes the Ibn Abbas tafsir as transmitted from Ali ibn Abi Talha through Mu'awiya ibn Salih and Abu Salih, the scribe of al-Layth. ITQAN (الحفاظ): Hadith critics agree Ibn Abi Talha did not hear directly from Ibn Abbas; long tafsirs attributed to Ibn Abbas with unknown transmitters are not acceptable, such as Juyaybir from al-Dahhak. ITQAN (author): The longest Ibn Jurayj tafsir route, through Bakr ibn Sahl, Abd al-Ghani ibn Sa'id, and Musa ibn Muhammad, is questionable. ITQAN (author): Shibl ibn Abbad’s tafsir, through Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid from Ibn Abbas, is close to sound.
SAMIN-DURR (ابن عباس ومجاهد وطاووس): The passive interpretation is also transmitted in tafsir from Ibn Abbas and the other named authorities.

IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Discussion of the Quran’s name, verses, suras, ordering, and titles directly serves tafsir, especially interpretation of sura openings and connections, and avoids repeated exposition.
