question: What other contextual material accompanies the verse?

positions.reasons: ITQAN (ابن سيرين): Ibn Sirin disliked extending the basmala’s initial baʾ through the mim before writing the sin. ITQAN (author): Writing the Qur’an with an impure substance is forbidden; writing it in gold is considered good by al-Ghazali. ITQAN (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas, Abu Dharr, and Abu al-Dardaʾ are reported to have disliked writing the Qur’an in gold. ITQAN (علي): A second report says Ali disliked writing the Qur’an on a small object. ITQAN (علي): Ali told Abu Hakim al-Abdi to sharpen his pen; after he trimmed it, Ali approved and said to illuminate the script as God had illuminated it. ITQAN (علي): A report attributed to Ali says a person who carefully embellishes the basmala is forgiven. ITQAN (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): A raised report from Anas promises forgiveness to anyone who writes the basmala beautifully. ITQAN (عمر بن عبد العزيز): ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz instructed his officials to extend the word الرحمن when writing the basmala.

IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The Quran associates knowledge with light and life, illustrating the point with verses describing the living, emergence from darkness to light, learned understanding, and the learned versus ignorant. | mentions 36:70, 2:257, 29:43, 39:9 IBNASHUR-FULL (author): For Arabs, the Quran’s sciences were inaccessible before its revelation; Ibn Ashur cites the statement that neither Muhammad nor his people knew them beforehand. | mentions 11:49 IBNASHUR-FULL (الشاطبي): Al-Shatibi says Quranic meanings and interpretation must stay within what is customary among Arabs. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Ibn Ashur suggests al-Shatibi may have been avoiding difficult objections economically, but asks how this view can deny the Quran’s continuing miracle to later peoples. IBNASHUR-FULL (محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم): The authentic report says every prophet received signs that people believed because of, while Muhammad’s gift was revelation and he hoped for the greatest following. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Unlike earlier action miracles such as the staff, water from stone, and healing, Muhammad’s miracle is the Quran’s wording and meanings, beyond human imitation and available for study in every age. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The fa of فأرجو marks a consequence: only a miracle lasting across ages explains the Prophet’s hope for the largest following, since generations with different capacities can recognize it; followers means adherents to true religion, not mere affiliation. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Ibn Ashur suggests the Prophet’s hope may mean more followers than all the other prophets combined, and says this has in fact occurred in true religious adherence.

MAWARDI-FULL (أهل الكوفة): An tadilla means “lest one of them err.” MAWARDI-FULL (أهل البصرة): An tadilla means “because one of them might err.” MAWARDI-FULL (عطاء وعطية العوفي): Answering the summons is recommended, not obligatory. MAWARDI-FULL (الشعبي): Answering the summons is a communal obligation. MAWARDI-FULL (قتادة والربيع): Answering the summons is an individual obligation. MAWARDI-FULL (author): The two men must be from your religious community. MAWARDI-FULL (مجاهد): The two men may be required to be free persons.

DURR-FULL (الحسن): God grants a servant occupation with Him and withdrawal to Him when He knows obedience is the servant's prevailing commitment. DURR-FULL (سفيان): Whoever acts on what he knows is granted success in what he does not know. DURR-FULL (النبي): The Prophet says that whoever acts on what he knows will inherit knowledge of what he did not know. DURR-FULL (النبي): When Yazid ibn Salama feared forgetting the many hadiths he had heard, the Prophet gave him a comprehensive instruction: fear God regarding what you know. DURR-FULL (عبد الله بن سلام): Ibn Salam tells ʿUmar that learned people are those who practice what they know, and that greed removes knowledge from people's hearts. DURR-FULL (جابر بن عبد الله): Jabir advises learning silence, patience, knowledge, acting on knowledge, and then spreading it. DURR-FULL (زياد بن جدير): Ziyad ibn Judayr says a people have not truly understood unless they attain piety.

JISHUMI (author): Safah means ignorance, with its root sense being lightness; the term describes a lightness of intellect. JISHUMI (author): Ibaʾ means refusing or refraining from something, as in Iblis's refusal. | mentions 2:34 JISHUMI (author): Irtiyāb is doubt arising from suspicion. JISHUMI (السلمي): Al-Sulami reads لا يسأموا with yāʾ, referring back to the preceding past context. JISHUMI (author): The phrase may instead be accusative, with an implied command to summon one man and two women as witnesses. JISHUMI (العامة): The common reading has the accusative and gemination; its form derives from لا تضارر with two r's assimilated.

IBNJAWZI-NUZHA (علي بن عبيد الله): Al-Dīn is what a person undertakes; religious commitment means undertaking what God requires. IBNJAWZI-NUZHA (غيره): Another definition makes religion divine speech that disciplines the self and restrains natural impulses. IBNJAWZI-NUZHA (ابن قتيبة): Ibn Qutayba derives God’s dīn from this sense of domination and submission. IBNJAWZI-NUZHA (القطامي): Al-Quṭāmī’s line uses tadīnuka for making someone submissive. IBNJAWZI-NUZHA (author): A second cited line also uses dīn for an authority or condition of subjugation. IBNJAWZI-NUZHA (author): Dīn can mean worship, as shown by a poem asking whether this is always his and the speaker’s religion.

IBNKATHIR-FULL (author): When an explanation is absent from the Qurʾan, Sunna, and Companions, many imams turn to the Successors; Ibn Kathīr names Mujāhid, Saʿīd b. Jubayr, ʿIkrima, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ḥasan, and others. IBNKATHIR-FULL (ابن أبي مليكة): Ibn Abī Mulayka says he saw Mujāhid ask Ibn ʿAbbās for the Qurʾan’s interpretation with writing tablets; Ibn ʿAbbās told him to write until he had asked about all of it. IBNKATHIR-FULL (سفيان الثوري): Sufyān al-Thawrī regarded an interpretation transmitted from Mujāhid as sufficient. IBNKATHIR-FULL (author): Apparent differences in Successor wording often are not real disagreements: one may state an implication or equivalent, while another states the point directly. IBNKATHIR-FULL (author): Ibn Kathīr agrees Successor opinions do not bind those who disagree, but consensus is evidence; where they differ, none overrides another, so consult Qurʾanic usage, Sunna, Arabic usage, and Companions’ views. IBNKATHIR-FULL (النبي): A report from Ibn ʿAbbās attributes to the Prophet a warning that whoever interprets the Qurʾan by opinion or without knowledge should take his seat in the Fire; Ibn Kathīr cites it to prohibit such tafsīr.

ITQAN (author): Zayd’s collection report lists palm midribs and small stones, with variant reports adding patches, leather, shoulder bones, ribs, and saddle wood. ITQAN (author): ʿAsab are palm midribs; scribes stripped off the leaflets and wrote on the broad end. ITQAN (الخطابي): Lihaf are small stones; al-Khattabi further describes them as slabs of stone. ITQAN (author): Riqāʿ are patches made of leather, parchment, or paper. ITQAN (author): Aktaf are camel or sheep shoulder bones, which were dried before writing on them. ITQAN (author): Aqtāb are wooden saddle frames placed on a camel’s back for riding.

SAMARRAI-ASRAR (author): A Qur’anic story has several lessons and evidentiary uses; it is not literally repeated, since each occurrence brings forward the aspect suited to its context and purpose. SAMARRAI-ASRAR (author): The story of Moses shows that God’s decree cannot be altered: Pharaoh killed Israelite boys to prevent his downfall, yet raised in his own house the person destined to end his rule. SAMARRAI-ASRAR (author): Moses’ story also displays the terrible end of Pharaoh as the consequence of injustice and unjust rulers. SAMARRAI-ASRAR (author): The Israelites’ formation in humiliation, cowardice, and worldliness explains their resistance to Moses’ reform; after forty years in the wilderness that generation died and a differently formed generation emerged. SAMARRAI-ASRAR (author): Once known and believed, truth has irresistible power against enticement and threat, shown by the sorcerers’ belief in Moses and the faith of Pharaoh’s wife. SAMARRAI-ASRAR (author): The Qur’an adapts each story to its context by omitting some details, expanding or summarizing others, changing sequence, and varying expression without changing the meaning.

BAGHAWI-FULL (author): God sent Muḥammad with guidance and the true religion as mercy to all, glad tidings for believers, and warning for opponents; through him prophethood was completed, the message sealed, and noble character perfected. BAGHAWI-FULL (author): God's Qur'an is a light that guides people away from error and saves them from ignorance. BAGHAWI-FULL (author): Those who follow the Qur'an attain success, while those who turn away after hearing it incur loss. BAGHAWI-FULL (author): The Qur'an commands and forbids, gives glad tidings and warnings, offers admonitions, recounts past peoples for reflection, presents parables, and points to signs of divine oneness for contemplation. BAGHAWI-FULL (author): Early scholars wrote books on Qur'anic sciences according to their understanding and knowledge; Baghawī thanks God for their efforts and asks mercy for them all.

KASHSHAF-FULL (author): ‘If you do so’ means if you harm one another; alternatively, it means doing anything forbidden in the passage. KASHSHAF-FULL (author): On a journey means while travelling. KASHSHAF-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās and Ubayy read kitāban; Ibn ʿAbbās asks what if a scribe is found but paper and ink are not. KASHSHAF-FULL (author): Abū al-ʿĀliya reads kutuban; al-Ḥasan’s kitāban is glossed as the plural of kātib. KASHSHAF-FULL (مجاهد والضحاك): Mujāhid and al-Ḍaḥḥāk restrict pledging to travel by the apparent wording and require possession; Mālik validates it by offer and acceptance without possession.

QURTUBI-FULL (أنس بن مالك): He reports that a mentally impaired trader's family asked the Prophet to interdict him; the Prophet stopped him from selling, then allowed him to trade only if he said there was no deception. Al-Tirmidhī calls the report sound. QURTUBI-FULL (البخاري): His historical record gives a related wording requiring the trader to say there is no deception and granting three nights' option on each purchase. QURTUBI-FULL (author): The trader was Habban ibn Munqidh, though another account calls Munqidh the grandfather of Yahya and Wasiʿ; he lived 130 years and a battle wound to his head impaired his mind and speech. QURTUBI-FULL (ابن عمر): Al-Dāraquṭnī transmits that Habban had poor sight and a head wound, so the Prophet gave him three days' option; his impaired speech rendered لا خلابة as لا خذابة. QURTUBI-FULL (author): He prefers interdiction under this verse and the family's request; the Prophet's concession was specific to Habban because he insisted on trading, while someone ordinarily cheated—especially through mental impairment—should be interdicted.

ITQAN (author): The response says Qasim’s objection does not weaken Ibn Qutayba: the listed variation types may have arisen incidentally and been recognized by induction. ITQAN (عياض): Qadi ʿIyad and followers take seven as a nonliteral number signifying ease, latitude, and abundance, as seven, seventy, and seven hundred can mean many. ITQAN (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): The Ibn Abbas report in both Sahihs supports an actual count: Gabriel began with one mode, and the Prophet kept asking for more until there were seven. ITQAN (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): A Nasaʾi wording has Gabriel and Michael ask the Prophet to keep requesting more until the allowance reaches seven. ITQAN (author): A fourth view says each word may have one or more readings up to seven, but this is challenged because some words have more than seven.

ALUSI-FULL (ابن الفرس): Ibn al-Faras infers that guardians may not be unbelievers or sinners but may be enslaved or women because the verse requires only justice; al-Alusi dismisses this inference. ALUSI-FULL (author): The person owing the debt must dictate because that person is the one against whom a claim is made and must acknowledge it; attaching the command to that description implies a restriction to the debtor. ALUSI-FULL (author): Pairing God's majestic name with 'his Lord' combines majesty and gracious care to intensify the debtor's admonition to fear God. ALUSI-FULL (سعيد بن جبير): The prohibition on reducing any part of the dictated debt, even a small amount, is the transmitted interpretation from Saʿīd b. Jubayr; variant readings omit or double the hamza in shayʾan. ALUSI-FULL (author): Minhu can attach directly to 'reduce,' with min marking origin, or be a fronted circumstantial phrase; shayʾan can be its object or a cognate accusative.

ELMALILI (author): Someone who recorded an event, later forgot it, and then recalls it clearly by consulting the record may testify. ELMALILI (author): Someone who only knows they made a record but still cannot recall the event must not testify. ELMALILI (author): Witnesses should not be prompted; one who has forgotten should be able to remember independently. ELMALILI (author): It is unjust to compel women to record events or, after a human lapse of memory, to make them recover recollection through outside prompts. ELMALILI (author): For matters men cannot witness, women’s reports alone may suffice, sometimes even one woman’s report, as with an incident in a women’s bath or a midwife’s report of birth.

IBNASHUR-FULL (author): A human trying to compose a medium-length sura would need prolonged revision and still leave awkward sentences; the Quran’s fluent composition entails no such labor. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Stylistic variety shows divine origin because literary geniuses usually excel in only one or two styles, and intensifies the challenge by denying opponents the excuse that they had not tried a given style. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Ibn Ashur cites the statement that only God and those firmly grounded in knowledge know its interpretation as an example of the Quran’s layered meanings and allusions to causes and purposes. | mentions 3:7 IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Ibn Ashur calls tafannun the artful movement between topics through parenthesis, analogy, conclusion, varied synonyms, and frequent grammatical shifts, before returning to the main subject and renewing attention. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The two parables of hypocrites, the fire and the rainstorm, exemplify this movement between styles and topics. | mentions 2:17, 2:18, 2:19, 2:20

IBNASHUR-FULL (ابن عبد البر): Ibn Abd al-Barr explains the seven as contextual latitude to substitute a fitting divine attribute, such as حكيم for عليم, while preserving contextual propriety after punishment or mercy passages. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Ibn Ashur rejects that categorical account as mismatched with the hadith’s transmitted context of concession and ease, and says its forced sevenfold classifications do not withstand objection. IBNASHUR-FULL (أبو بكر بن العربي): Ibn al-Arabi says the license lasted through the Prophet’s life, implying abrogation after his death either by the Companions’ consensus or prophetic instruction. IBNASHUR-FULL (عمر): Abrogation proponents cite Umar’s statement that the Quran was revealed in Quraysh speech and his ban on Ibn Masud’s Hudhayl form of حتى. | mentions 37:174 IBNASHUR-FULL (بعضهم): Another enumeration includes Quraysh, Banu Darim, and the upper Hawazin clans Sa'd, Jusham, and Nasr ibn Muawiya, plus Thaqif; some substitute Khuza'a for Tamim.

IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The Quran is God’s Arabic speech revealed to Muhammad through Gabriel, whose task is to convey to the community the wording revealed to him. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The community acts on the revealed wording and recites what it can in prayer; reciting the Quran is itself worship. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The Quran proves the Messenger’s claim for all people by challenging its first Arab hearers to produce something comparable, which they failed to do. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The challenge descends from ten suras, to one sura, to an explicit warning that they could never produce one; Ibn Ashur also cites the Quran’s answer to demands for a sign. | mentions 11:13, 11:14, 10:38, 10:39, 2:23, 2:24, 29:50, 29:51 IBNASHUR-FULL (محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم): The Prophet says each prophet received signs through which people believed, while his own gift was revelation; Ibn Ashur notes further meanings are discussed in his Bukhari commentary.

IBNASHUR-FULL (author): God ordered the Prophet to write all revelation as proof for converts who had not received it by memorizing it in their hearts. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The Prophet appointed companions to record revelation from its beginning; Ibn Ashur names Abdullah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh, Abdullah ibn Amr, Zayd ibn Thabit, and Muawiya ibn Abi Sufyan. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Dhikr means a reminder of what people must believe and do; in the cited verse, the Prophet is to explain that reminder to people. | mentions 16:44 IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Wahy is named for the angel’s delivery to the Prophet, which conveys God’s intent like translated human speech; its compositions were not made by humans. | mentions 21:45 IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The Quran is also called God’s speech, as in the command to shelter a polytheist until he hears the speech of God. | mentions 9:6

STUDYQURAN (author): This is the Quran’s longest single verse. STUDYQURAN (author): Some commentators infer women’s essential inability to judge objectively and intrinsic unreliability as witnesses. STUDYQURAN (Abū Bakr ibn ʿArabī): In Aḥkām al-Qur’ān he wondered why one man could not remind one woman if she erred, and found no answer. STUDYQURAN (Q): A seller must own production means and specify the product’s attributes, quantity, delivery time, and feasible place of delivery. STUDYQURAN (Q): The buyer should pay fungible or monetary material because agricultural sellers lack liquid wealth and hold assets not easily converted to money.

TAB-FULL (عامر): ʿĀmir says a witness may choose freely until he has testified. TAB-FULL (الحسن): Al-Ḥasan says a person who dislikes an initial invitation to testify may decline it. TAB-FULL (إبراهيم): Ibrāhīm says a person afraid of forgetting may decline an initial request to testify. TAB-FULL (سعيد بن جبير): Saʿīd ibn Jubayr understands the verse to concern witnesses who have already testified.

NAHHAS (author): The lām is present in وليكتب for the absent third person and omitted in فاكتبوه for the addressees; omitting it in second-person commands is common and preferable. NAHHAS (محمد بن يزيد): Ibn Yazid says a third-person command must retain its lām. NAHHAS (سيبويه والكوفيون): Sibawayh and the Kufans allow omission of the lām in a third-person command and cite a verse addressed to Muhammad. NAHHAS (author): The Hijazis and Banu Asad say يملي; Tamim says أمليت. The Qurʾan uses both language forms.

THALABI (بعضهم): Some read the summons command as requiring people to accept the burden of serving as witnesses. THALABI (عطاء وعطية): Ata and Atiyya take the summons as recommendation, leaving a person free whether or not to testify. THALABI (author): The construction places cause before effect, like the cited verse whose sense is that they would ask for a messenger if calamity struck them. | mentions 28:47 THALABI (author): Dhakkara and adhkara can both mean remind, like the paired forms nuzzila/anzala and karuma/akrama; a poem uses the sun as a reminder.

JISHUMI (العامة): The common reading has the imperative lām in وليكتب with sukūn. JISHUMI (زيد بن أسلم): Zayd ibn Aslam reads فتذاكر with an alif, as reciprocal discussion. JISHUMI (author): The light and doubled forms are both Arabic usage, like dhakkara/adhkara and nazzala/anzala. JISHUMI (عاصم والجحدري): ʿĀṣim and al-Jaḥdarī read تضل with passive morphology, ḍamma on the yāʾ and fatḥ on the ḍād.

JISHUMI (author): Writing is emphasized because scribes were few in the Prophet’s time. JISHUMI (مالك والأوزاعي والشافعي): Mālik, al-Awzāʿī, and al-Shāfiʿī restrict the male-and-two-women arrangement to financial matters. JISHUMI (الشعبي): Al-Shaʿbī describes a trustworthy witness as one not accused in matters of appetite or sexual conduct. JISHUMI (author): Mussammā means that the term is stated and known.

KASHSHAF-FULL (author): Some creditors trust a debtor because of their good opinion of him. KASHSHAF-FULL (أبي): Ubayy reads the passive ‘if the debtor is trusted,’ describing a person known for reliability, fulfillment, and independence from collateral. KASHSHAF-FULL (author): The debtor should honor the creditor’s trust by repaying the entrusted debt; it is called trust because the creditor relied on him without collateral. KASHSHAF-FULL (author): The phrase has alternative pronunciations; ʿĀṣim’s assimilation in ittaman is rejected because its yāʾ derives from hamza and remains hamza-like.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL (رؤبة): Ruʾba's verse about Arwā paying some debts and delaying others illustrates dāyantu as lending or dealing in debt. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الأعشى): Al-Aʿshā's verse uses rahīna for something pledged, and the author notes rahantu lisānī is said for pledging one's word, not arhantu. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Dāntuhu means I sold to him on credit; adantu means I borrowed on credit. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Ṣaghīr is the active participle of ṣaghura and means small in amount, also used for abstract things.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): The forms شهيد and كاتب shift from an active participle pattern to an intensive pattern. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): The verse uses fronting, delay, and ellipsis: writing precedes dictation, and the witness phrases imply the omitted relation. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): A long series of commands, safeguards, warnings, and reminders emphatically protects wealth in transactions from loss and breach of trust. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): The Prophet paired safeguarding wealth with safeguarding lives and bloodshed.

SAMIN-DURR (الفارسي): Al-Farisi analyzes إحدى as an irregular feminine of الواحد; the author prefers it as the regular feminine of أحد, paired in eleven and twenty-one. SAMIN-DURR (أبو العباس): إحدى pluralizes as إحد, like كسرة/كسر, because its final alif functions like feminine tāʾ; similar patterns include الكبرى/كبر and قصعاء/قواصع. SAMIN-DURR (author): إحدى is used only in annexation, unlike its masculine counterpart أحد. SAMIN-DURR (author): الأخرى is feminine of comparative آخر and can mean آخرة, as in 7:38; both forms pluralize أخر, but their declension and meanings differ. | mentions 7:38

SAMIN-DURR (author): One possible omitted subject of kāna is ‘transaction,’ understood from the preceding commands; Sibawayh gives a similar contextual ellipsis. SAMIN-DURR (author): A poem using ‘when there was stabbing and embracing’ supplies an omitted ‘matter’ as the subject of kāna. SAMIN-DURR (author): The author analyzes the fāʾ as conjunction to the whole exception clause, with clear causal force: the immediate transaction explains the dispensation. SAMIN-DURR (author): ‘That you do not write it’ means ‘in not writing it’; the preposition is omitted, leaving the two constructions discussed for an infinitive after its deletion.

IBNKATHIR-FULL (author): Ibn Kathīr says al-Bukhārī’s point is that the Qurʾan was revealed in Quraysh’s language, and Quraysh were the foremost branch of the Arabs. IBNKATHIR-FULL (عمر بن الخطاب): Another report says ʿUmar instructed his committee to use the language of Muḍar when linguistic differences arose, because the Qurʾan came in the language of a man from Muḍar, the Prophet. IBNKATHIR-FULL (author): Ibn Kathīr cites verses describing the Qurʾan as Arabic and revealed in clear Arabic as evidence for its language, also citing the challenge about a non-Arabic Qurʾan. | mentions 39:28, 26:192, 26:193, 26:194, 26:195, 16:103, 41:44 IBNKATHIR-FULL (يعلى بن أمية): Yaʿlā b. Umayya wished to witness revelation; when a man in iḥrām wearing perfume and a cloak asked about ʿumra, ʿUmar brought Yaʿlā close to observe the Prophet receive revelation, after which the Prophet ordered the cloak removed and perfume washed away.

BURHAN (شيخ المالكية): The Maliki shaykh forbids anomalous readings in prayer or elsewhere, even for readers ignorant of Arabic; the uninformed are taught, while knowing or persistent readers are disciplined. BURHAN (شيخ المالكية): He says replacing Qur’anic words such as آتينا and سولت with synonyms is not a variant reading but an even graver offense, deserving stronger discipline and prohibition. BURHAN (الشيخ شهاب الدين): Shihab al-Din dislikes repeatedly reciting a verse with different readings as some contemporaries do during a Qur’an completion, calling it an innovation without early precedent. BURHAN (ابن عبد البر): Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr transmits Muslim consensus that anomalous readings may not be recited and that one should not pray behind someone who uses them.

ITQAN (author): Al-Tabari often cites al-Suddi through several routes; Ibn Abi Hatim omits this compilation to restrict himself to the soundest reports, while al-Hakim authenticates some reports through Murra from Ibn Masud and others. ITQAN (ابن حجر): Ibn Hajar answers that the intermediary is known and trustworthy, so the missing direct hearing causes no problem. ITQAN (author): Muhammad ibn Thawr’s transmission from Ibn Jurayj comprises about three large parts and was judged sound. ITQAN (author): Hajjaj ibn Muhammad’s one-part transmission from Ibn Jurayj is sound and agreed upon.

ALUSI-FULL (قائل غير مسمى): The excerpt recalls a report that the Quran was being written on parchments in the Prophet's presence; the speaker is not identified in this continuation. ALUSI-FULL (زيد بن ثابت): While copying, Zayd noticed a missing verse of al-Ahzab that he had heard the Prophet recite; they found it with Khuzayma and inserted it in its surah. | mentions 33:23 ALUSI-FULL (author): The claim that the two witnesses meant one person who memorized the text and another who had it written has no basis. ALUSI-FULL (author): Reports that Ali stayed behind after the Prophet's death to compile the Quran include weak and fabricated routes; sound material may mean collecting it in memory or compiling it differently for another purpose.

TAB-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās says a writer or witness with an unavoidable need should be allowed to leave. TAB-FULL (عكرمة): ʿIkrima says a person who is ill or occupied must not be harassed. TAB-FULL (مجاهد): Mujāhid describes harassment as pressing an occupied scribe or witness to comply by invoking God's command when the person has asked that someone else be found.

IBNABIHATIM (ابن عباس): Do not pressure two people called to write or witness by demanding their help when they are occupied; many early authorities report similarly. IBNABIHATIM (عطاء): A scribe or witness should deliver what is entrusted to them. IBNABIHATIM (أبيه): The judge was to prevent people from abusing or insulting scribes and witnesses, in light of this command.

FARISI-HUJJA (author): The continuation glosses losing the sense of a matter; Abu Zayd then distinguishes a lost road or house from causing an animal or thing to go missing. FARISI-HUJJA (أبو زيد): Abu Zayd distinguishes ضللت الطريق or a house, becoming lost, from أضللت an animal or thing, causing it to go missing; a stationary animal is treated like a place. FARISI-HUJJA (أبو الحسن): Abu al-Hasan says ضللت دار فلان; al-Farazdaq's verse uses it for losing the way while searching for Darim.

THALABI (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): The Prophet describes the Quran appearing for its companion at resurrection, testifying to the reader’s devotion and leading to honor for the reader and the reader’s parents in Paradise. THALABI (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): In a report from Muadh ibn Jabal, the Prophet calls the Quran remembrance of the Merciful and protection from Satan, promising guidance, safety, shade, and salvation to its student. THALABI (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas compares one who reads the Quran without learning its interpretation to an Arab who recites without understanding what he says.

THALABI (أبو بحرية): Abu Bahriyya says al-Hasan told a reluctant person summoned to testify that he need not attend and may choose. THALABI (مغيرة): Mughira reports that Ibrahim advised him not to testify if he feared forgetting and did not wish to. THALABI (السلمي): Al-Sulami reads ولا يسأموا with a third-person yāʾ.

WAHIDI-BASIT (author): Here kāna means occur or come into being, as in the usage discussed at 2:280. | mentions 2:280 WAHIDI-BASIT (الفراء): Al-Farrāʾ allows tadīrūnahā to be accusative as the predicate of kāna; otherwise it is nominative describing a present transaction in circulation. WAHIDI-BASIT (أبو علي): Abū ʿAlī rejects treating tadāyun or the debt in a person’s liability as the name of kāna, since neither is the concrete trade meant here.

JISHUMI (author): Jishumi glosses the address as a call to affirm God and his messenger. JISHUMI (author): The word ‘debt’ is repeated because tadaayantum can mean either mutual repayment or dealings involving debt, so the repetition disambiguates the shared expression. JISHUMI (author): The repetition also reinforces the meaning in the mind, as in the emphatic Qur’anic phrases about the angels prostrating and birds flying with wings. | mentions 15:30, 38:73, 6:38

JISHUMI (author): There is no disagreement that a minor or an insane person's acknowledgment is invalid. JISHUMI (الشافعي): Al-Shafi‘i does not accept a profligate person's acknowledgment after interdiction. JISHUMI (author): The debt cannot be demanded before its due date; otherwise specifying a term would have no effect.

IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): The three categories are distinct, though one person may have one, two, or all three traits; the classification follows Malik and other discerning scholars. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): “With fairness” means truth and seeking what is correct. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): The verse then names three recurring categories that may need someone else to dictate for them.

IBNATIYYA-FULL (الشاعر): The cited line witnesses the form wa-anā in the phrase concerning the old man and poverty. IBNATIYYA-FULL (أبو الفتح): He calls the proposed explanation based on the hamza and alif sharing phonetic traits crude and unconvincing; he also cites Ibn Kathir’s ‘on their shins’ reading and ‘O you with a ring.’ IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): Because the verse speaks of witnesses whom people approve, it indicates that people are not presumed upright until their reliability is established.

IBNJAWZI-NUZHA (author): Ḥuḍūr is the opposite of absence; ḥaḍar contrasts with the open countryside, and ḥaḍāra means settled urban life. IBNJAWZI-NUZHA (author): With ḍamma, ḥuḍur means an enemy. IBNJAWZI-NUZHA (author): Ḥuḍūr can mean something immediately available or present, as with a spot transaction.

QURTUBI-FULL (author): Requiring liability excludes unknown goods and specified individual orchards whose fruit may fail; full description excludes unspecified kinds or qualities of dates, cloth, or fish. QURTUBI-FULL (author): Al-Qurṭubī distinguishes salam from currency exchange: exchange has many strict conditions, while salam more closely resembles ordinary transactions and tolerates more flexibility. QURTUBI-FULL (ابن العربي): He says the first requirement, liability, is self-evident because salam is a debt transaction sought for benefit and accommodation.

QURTUBI-FULL (author): إملال and إملاء are two forms: Hijaz and Banu Asad say أمل, Tamim says أملى; the Quran uses both, including 25:5, and the second lām becomes yāʾ for ease. | mentions 25:5 QURTUBI-FULL (قول): Some say سفيها means a minor, but al-Qurṭubī rejects this because an adult may also be financially foolish. QURTUBI-FULL (author): Arabic usage applies سفه to weakness of mind or body, as the cited lines demonstrate for judgment and weakened, swaying spear tops.

QURTUBI-FULL (author): بدين is emphatic; a debt is a transaction with one present countervalue and another deferred in liability, since Arabs call what is present عين and what is absent دين. | mentions 6:38, 15:30 QURTUBI-FULL (ابن عباس): He transmits the Prophet's rule for advance purchase of dates: specify measure, weight, and term; al-Qurṭubī says Bukhari, Muslim, and others recorded it. QURTUBI-FULL (ابن عمر): He says pre-Islamic buyers sold camel meat until the offspring of an offspring was born; the Prophet forbade this indeterminate term.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Because kātib is indefinite under a prohibition, the command is general. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Another gloss takes ʿallamahu as made known and understands the phrase as writing in the way God commanded, in truth. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): A further gloss makes the kaaf causal: write because God favored you with the skill, as in the command to do good because God did good to you. | mentions 28:77

ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): The author rejects claims that either or is redundant, since the coordinating particle is not added without meaning. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الزمخشري): The author's preferred distinctions largely follow al-Zamakhsharī's explanation. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Breaking the doubled lām in yumlil is a Ḥijāzī form when the final syllable is jussive or at pause, not in nominative or accusative; one reading doubles shayʾan's yāʾ.

SAMIN-DURR (author): The second object is omitted in this reading too; فعل and أفعل can be synonymous, while the more common doubled form is witnessed by the poet's يذكرنيك. SAMIN-DURR (عيسى بن عمر والجحدري): They read تضل in the passive; al-Jahdari also reads tuḍillu, from أضل, with the omitted object الشهادة. SAMIN-DURR (أبو البقاء): Abu al-Baqa says either woman can be parsed as subject because the semantic roles are recoverable, despite the usual ordering rule.

SAMIN-DURR (author): The phrase may instead be purely temporal, without conditional force. SAMIN-DURR (author): Alternatively, it is conditional, with an omitted answer: when called, they should not refuse. SAMIN-DURR (author): Another analysis supplies the preposition min before the infinitive; a second poem shows ‘tire’ used with min.

SAMIN-DURR (author): These etymologies assume the triliteral means injustice and the quadriliteral means justice. SAMIN-DURR (سعيد بن جبير): When al-Hajjaj asked his judgment, Saʿid b. Jubayr called him ‘qāsiṭ, ʿādil,’ making a pointed double-edged description. | mentions 72:15, 6:1 SAMIN-DURR (author): If q-s-ṭ can mean both justice and injustice, the ambiguity is straightforward; Ibn al-Qattaʿ records both opposite senses.

SAMIN-DURR (author): ‘When you trade’ may be conditional, answered by a preceding clause or an omitted ‘then bear witness’; alternatively it is purely temporal. SAMIN-DURR (author): The readings and explanations alternate because the verse permits both interpretations. SAMIN-DURR (author): On the temporal reading, the instruction is to witness at the time of trading.

SAMIN-DURR (ابن محيصن): Ibn Muhaysin reads the rāʾ nominative as a negation whose report-like form conveys a prohibition, as in 2:197. | mentions 2:197 SAMIN-DURR (author): The related grammatical and reading issues were discussed under the prohibition against a mother being harmed in 2:233. | mentions 2:233 SAMIN-DURR (author): ‘If you do’ means any act forbidden by God; its object is omitted because context supplies it.

SAMIN-DURR (author): The intensive form شهيدين suggests choosing witnesses who testify repeatedly. SAMIN-DURR (author): If كان is incomplete, its dual subject refers to the two witnesses: if the creditor fails or chooses not to secure two men, the alternative applies. SAMIN-DURR (author): If كان is complete, رجلين is an emphatic circumstantial: the alternative is used only when two male witnesses cannot be found.

SAMIN-DURR (author): Other analyses make the phrase a subject of complete or incomplete كان, or passive فليستشهد رجل; complete كان is preferable because it requires fewer deletions. SAMIN-DURR (author): A reading gives وامرأتان with a silent hamza; one account treats the hamza as replaced by alif and then rehamzat, though that is not its regular softening. SAMIN-DURR (أبو البقاء): Abu al-Baqa explains the silent hamza as first softened between hamza and alif, then treated as alif and rehamzat, as in عألم and خأتم.

IBNKATHIR-FULL (author): The messenger between God and Muḥammad was Gabriel, a noble and honored angel; Ibn Kathīr says God praised both Gabriel and Muḥammad and cites descriptions of them in the Qurʾan. | mentions 26:193, 26:194, 81:19, 81:20, 81:21, 81:22 IBNKATHIR-FULL (author): Ibn Kathīr notes a virtue for Umm Salama, who saw Gabriel, and for the handsome Dihya b. Khalīfa al-Kalbī, whose appearance Gabriel often assumed when visiting the Prophet. IBNKATHIR-FULL (أبو هريرة): Abū Hurayra reports the Prophet saying every prophet received a sign by which people believed, while Muḥammad’s gift was revelation from God; he hopes to have the greatest following on Resurrection Day, and Ibn Kathīr notes its transmission by al-Bukhārī, Muslim, and al-Nasāʾī.

NASHR (أبو عمرو والكسائي وأبو جعفر وقالون): These readers silence the medial hāʾ of هو when it follows waw, fāʾ, or lām, as in وهو, فهو, لهو, وهي, فهي, and لهي; al-Kisai also does so in ثم هو. NASHR (أبو جعفر): Abu Jaʿfar has both sukūn and ḍamma routes for the hāʾ in ثم هو and يمل هو; Ibn al-Jazari accepts both as sound. NASHR (قالون): Qalun likewise has both hāʾ forms in these two phrases, though the sukūn route is rare through Abu Nashit; Ibn al-Jazari read both through the cited routes.

DURR-FULL (مجاهد): Mujahid says it is obligatory for a scribe to write. DURR-FULL (مقاتل): The command addressed a time when there were few scribes. DURR-FULL (قتادة): Qatada likewise notes that scribes were few at that time.

ITQAN (author): The wāw of oath governs genitive, as in “By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists.” | mentions 6:23 ITQAN (author): Conjunction wāw merely joins items and can connect accompanying, preceding, or following elements without itself specifying sequence. | mentions 10:73, 57:26, 42:3 ITQAN (author): Unlike other conjunctions, wāw occurs with إما, with لا after negation, and with لكن; it can also join a general and its specific, the reverse, synonyms, or coordinated genitives by proximity. | mentions 8:41, 33:40, 2:98, 71:28, 2:196, 5:6

ITQAN (author): The phrase about a bird flying with its wings reinforces literal bird and flight, since bird can be metaphorical and flying can mean running quickly. ITQAN (author): “They say with their mouths” reinforces literal speech, since saying can also describe inward thought. | mentions 58:8 ITQAN (author): “Hearts that are in the chests” specifies literal hearts because heart can metaphorically mean eye; likewise eyes may metaphorically refer to hearts. | mentions 18:101

BURSEVI (author): The second lesson concerns servants’ relation to God: carefulness over fleeting worldly transactions should teach even greater care over enduring afterlife matters, for every atom of good and evil is rewarded or punished. BURSEVI (author): The third lesson concerns people’s dealings with one another: imitate God’s gentleness, keep His limits in agreement and disagreement, love, accompany, guide, and advise one another for His sake. BURSEVI (author): In all three conditions, remain mindful of God, who teaches through explicit statements and indications.

ALUSI-FULL (author): A variant reads both occurrences of yasʾamu in the plural masculine form. ALUSI-FULL (الربيع): Al-Rabiʿ says the verse came when a man went around asking many people to witness and nobody responded. ALUSI-FULL (author): The particle ma after idha is an extra particle, a regular construction.

ELMALILI (Fuzûlî): Fuzuli curses scribes who ruin fine writing; his Arabic stanza opens with a deliberate echo of the 'tabbat yada' wording. ELMALILI (author): A prose rendering conveys the Arabic stanza's sense—bad scribes ruin a work founded on learning and adab and spoil copies—but cannot equal the poem's effect. ELMALILI (author): Fuzuli's Turkish version is not identical in content but expresses an equivalent idea and preserves literary value by supplying features absent from the Arabic wording.

IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Ibn ʿAṭiyya’s inference is unsound: securing evidence is a different situation from voluntarily giving away a right. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): If either party cannot write, a third party writes their agreement, two witnesses attest it, and the document goes to the creditor; this was the common Arab situation because literacy was scarce and localized. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): At revelation, illiteracy was widespread among Arabs; writing was found in a few places and among only a small number in Mecca and Medina.

ABDURRAZZAQ (مجاهد): Mujahid interprets the summons as applying to witnesses who have already testified. ABDURRAZZAQ (مجاهد): Mujahid, as reported by Jabir al-Ju‘fi, says a witness may choose whether to testify until he has testified.

ZAJJAJ (author): The command to disperse after Friday prayer likewise permits people to resume business once prayer ends. | mentions 62:10 ZAJJAJ (author): The analogy fails: those commands permit actions after a prohibition on hunting in ihram or trading during prayer, whereas the debt verse has no preceding prohibition to lift. | mentions 5:95, 62:9
IBNABIHATIM (سعيد بن جبير): Among you means the buyer and seller. IBNABIHATIM (السدى): Fairness means writing the truth.
IBNABIHATIM (سعيد بن حبير): The phrase about God teaching the scribe refers to writing that He taught him. IBNABIHATIM (الربيع): The instruction to write was obligatory.
IBNABIHATIM (الربيع بن أنس): The provision allowing one man and two women as witnesses applies to debts. IBNABIHATIM (مقاتل بن حيان): God commands the use of just men and women as witnesses.
IBNABIHATIM (سعيد بن جبير): Do not grow tired of writing the debt. IBNABIHATIM (الضحاك): The prescribed procedure is obedience to God.

IBNABIHATIM (السدى): An immediate transaction means one carried out locally, in the same town. IBNABIHATIM (سعيد بن جبير): A transaction circulated between the parties has no deferred term; Muqatil ibn Hayyan reports similarly.

NAHHAS (author): فسوق بكم refers either to this act itself or specifically to causing harm. NAHHAS (author): Al-Nahhas calls that analogy wrong: hunting after ihram and dispersing after prayer are permissions after restriction, unlike debt documentation. | mentions 5:2, 62:10

THALABI (عمر بن الخطاب): Umar says judges infer a person's character from visible conduct, and should not doubt someone whose neighbors, relatives, and companions praise him. THALABI (ابن عباس والربيع ومقاتل): Ibn Abbas, al-Rabiʿ, and Muqatil instead identify the person who dictates as the creditor, who knows the debt best.

THALABI (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): A prophetic report disqualifies a treacherous witness, someone punished for a ḥadd, a hostile witness, a known perjurer, a household dependent, and a suspect relative or client. THALABI (أبو حنيفة): The sole disagreement about those four matters concerns nursing: Abu Hanifa requires either two men or one man and two women for it.

WAHIDI-BASIT (الفراء): Al-Farrāʾ allows both interpretations of who the wali is. WAHIDI-BASIT (الضحاك وابن زيد): Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn Zayd say the wali is the guardian of a child, incapable person, or fool: a trustee, heir, or other person acting for him.

JISHUMI (الفراء): Al-Farrāʾ takes the phrase conditionally: one woman reminds the other if she strays; fronting أن makes it attach to the preceding governor. JISHUMI (author): The clause after أن is accusative either as an infinitive meaning its writing, or after deletion of the preposition من.

JISHUMI (author): God’s knowledge is glossed as universal, knowledge of people’s deeds and recompense, or knowledge of their interests that informs his commands and prohibitions. JISHUMI (author): The term is explained as the due date of the debt or, alternatively, the witness’s term.

JISHUMI (author): The instruction to avoid doubt means one must not testify while uncertain and should testify only with certainty. JISHUMI (رسول الله): The Prophet says: testify only if you know something as clearly as the sun; otherwise do not testify.

KASHSHAF-FULL (author): A passive feminine reading of ‘if one errs’ is reported; the gloss that two women together become one man is a bizarre interpretation. | mentions 5:95 KASHSHAF-FULL (author): The explanation that the two women together count as a male is a bizarre gloss.

KASHSHAF-FULL (author): ‘His heart is sinful’ can make the heart the subject of āthim or the topic with a fronted predicate; both mean the heart itself sins. KASHSHAF-FULL (author): Naming the heart emphasizes that concealment begins inwardly; the heart is the body’s chief organ and root of its deeds, so the sin is grave, not merely a failure of speech.

IBNATIYYA-FULL (الجمهور): The majority reads ‘if there are not two men’ as addressing a claimant who omitted two male witnesses, deliberately or through some excuse. IBNATIYYA-FULL (حميد بن عبد الرحمن): He reports that some Meccans read imra’atān with a hamza followed by a quiescent alif.

IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): Ibn ʿAṭiyya explains that if you differ concerns differences in transmitted readings; every one of the seven language forms in the Qurʾān must derive from the Prophet and have been recited to him. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): No Qurʾānic meaning was lost when noncanonical wording was left out, because the meanings remain in the established text.

IBNJAWZI-NUZHA (ابن فارس): Ibn Fāris distinguishes hamzated danīʾ, meaning low or inferior, from unhamzated danī, meaning near. IBNJAWZI-NUZHA (ابن فارس): Ibn Fāris says the world is called al-dunyā because it is near, and gives dunyāwī as its relative form.

IBNJAWZI-NUZHA (author): Shahīd means witness, related to shāhid as ʿalīm is related to ʿālim, and derives from witnessing. IBNJAWZI-NUZHA (author): Shahīd can mean a witness testifying truth against the person testified against, including debt witnesses. | mentions 2:143
IBNJAWZI-ZAD (مجاهد): Mujahid and al-Suddi say “weak” means a fool. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (القاضي أبو يعلى): Qadi Abu Yaʿla gives “minor” as a third meaning of weak.

RAZI-FULL (author): The command to write does not require every person to write; it requires that the record be made by someone, as the command to cut a thief’s hand is fulfilled by an authorized agent. | mentions 5:38 RAZI-FULL (author): Meeting those standards requires a writer skilled in jurisprudence and in distinguishing similar expressions.

QURTUBI-FULL (author): By analogy, an oath has stronger evidentiary standing than two women because women have no role in mutual imprecation, whereas an oath does. QURTUBI-FULL (author): Once sound Sunnah is established, it must be followed and needs no supporting precedent; those who oppose it are answered by it.

QURTUBI-FULL (أبو حنيفة): Abū Ḥanīfa regards any apparently Muslim person free of manifest wrongdoing as upright, even when character is unknown. QURTUBI-FULL (author): A Bedouin may testify for a town-dweller if upright: Qurʾānic general wording does not distinguish them, and al-Qurṭubī rejects a restrictive report. | mentions 65:2

QURTUBI-FULL (مجاهد والضحاك وطاوس والسدي): Mujāhid, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ṭāwūs, and al-Suddī understand the verse to forbid harassing a busy scribe or witness who gives a reasonable excuse; Ibn Masʿūd has a similar reading. QURTUBI-FULL (author): God promises that reverent people receive understanding and discernment to distinguish truth from falsehood, sometimes placed directly in the heart. | mentions 8:29

QURTUBI-FULL (مالك): He alone allows salam in a designated item under two conditions: it comes from a secure village, and collection has begun, as with milk from a sheep or ripe fruit from a palm. QURTUBI-FULL (author): He accepts Malik's exceptions: a secure location makes non-delivery unlikely enough to tolerate slight uncertainty, and daily collection of milk or dates meets a recurring need when buyers lack cash or prices fluctuate and sellers need money.

QURTUBI-FULL (مالك): If a salam seller cannot deliver at maturity and the buyer releases him, the buyer may take only the original currency or exact capital; exchanging it for another good before receipt would sell food before possession, which the Prophet forbade. QURTUBI-FULL (ابن جريج): He says a lender should write while a seller should obtain witnesses.

QURTUBI-FULL (محمد بن إسحاق عن محمد بن يحيى بن حبان): The Prophet told Habban to say لا خلابة when selling and gave him three nights to keep or return each purchase; Habban invoked this right even when mocked by sellers, and Companions confirmed his claim. Al-Dāraquṭnī records it; Abu ʿUmar cites al-Bukhari's historical transmission. QURTUBI-FULL (الطبري): He takes وليه to refer to the debt itself, with reports from al-Rabiʿ and Ibn ʿAbbās; al-Qurṭubī rejects this as unsound and says Ibn ʿAbbās's report is not reliable.
NASAFI-FULL (مكي): Makki reads تذكرة with accusative from dhikr rather than the other derivation. NASAFI-FULL (بصري): Baṣri shares the accusative reading تذكرة from dhikr.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Repetition stresses following the right: “right” recurs, while ʿalā signals the creditor's position and claim. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): The passage pairs opposites in forgetting/reminding and small/large; it also uses comparison, specification, and repetition.

SAMIN-DURR (الفراء): Al-Farraʾ estimates كي تذكر إحدى الأخرى إن ضلت, with the result fronted and أن opened; his analogy is delighting in giving a petitioner when asked. SAMIN-DURR (الزجاج): Al-Zajjaj says he cannot see why a conditional should change أن to فتح when moved before its clause.

SAMIN-DURR (author): ‘So that you do not doubt’ has a deleted preposition; proposed choices are lām, ilā, or min, but min does not fit the sense. SAMIN-DURR (author): Omission is smoother when the comparative is a predicate than when it is an adjective or circumstantial phrase.

SAMIN-DURR (ابن عطية): Ibn Atiyya attaches the bā to وليكتب, not كاتب, since a child or slave may write a document even if not personally just. SAMIN-DURR (author): A third analysis makes باء extra, yielding كاتب العدل, the just writer.

SAMIN-DURR (الواحدي): Al-Wahidi had already proposed the conditional clause as an adjective of the two women, citing a relative clause followed by a condition and response. | mentions 22:41 SAMIN-DURR (author): The apparent reading treats the conditional as an independent statement answering why two women are assigned in place of one man.

IBNKATHIR-FULL (زيد بن ثابت): Zayd says the copyists noticed a verse missing from al-Aḥzāb that he had heard the Prophet recite; they found it with Khuzayma ibn Thābit and inserted it in its sūra. | mentions 33:23 IBNKATHIR-FULL (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): Ibn Kathir cites the Prophet’s instruction to follow his Sunnah and the Sunnah of the rightly guided caliphs in support of their united decision.

IBNKATHIR-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAṭiyya cites Ibn ʿAbbās, who says he learned فاطر from an Arab describing a well he had begun digging as one he had fathomed or started. | mentions 35:1 IBNKATHIR-FULL (الطحاوي): Al-Ṭaḥāwī and others explain the seven-language allowance as a concession because many people struggled with Quraysh speech, lacking writing, precise notation, and secure memorization.

IBNKATHIR-FULL (author): Someone who knows how to write should not refuse a request; writing for those unable to do so is charity, as supported by reports about helping a worker and concealing knowledge. IBNKATHIR-FULL (مجاهد وعطاء): They hold that it is obligatory for a capable writer to write.

BURHAN (أبو الفتح عن المتنبي): Al-Fath recounts asking al-Mutanabbi whether he wrote قرحى or قرحا; al-Mutanabbi chose the latter because the following بهارا is a plural, an example of deliberate balance in wording. BURHAN (author): The verse has parallel clauses for error and reminder; repeating the subject before the second action preserves its form and lets the clause close with balanced structure, while الأخرى clarifies the intended contrast.

NASHR (author): Some authorities treat alternative stops as mutually exclusive: choosing one stop bars the other, including the paired stops inside this verse. NASHR (أبو الفضل الرازي): Abu al-Fadl al-Razi was the first to point out this mutual monitoring between pause locations, borrowing the idea from prosody.

BIQAI-FULL (أبو الحسن الحرالي): Al-Harali says the conditional wording indicates that people will inevitably enter debt transactions. BIQAI-FULL (author): Mention of an appointed term points toward resurrection, when the promise of fulfillment is realized.

BIQAI-FULL (author): Since most people cannot write, the directive to appoint a just scribe does not select one specific person. BIQAI-FULL (author): Just writing follows the model of Gods trustworthy recording angels. | mentions 82:10, 80:15
DURR-FULL (الربيع): The witnesses whom believers approve are upright people. DURR-FULL (الربيع): When a man called many people around to testify and no one followed, the verse was revealed.

ITQAN (author): Restriction divides into restricting a described subject to a quality or a quality to a subject; either can be literal or figurative. ITQAN (author): Literal restriction of a subject to one quality, such as Zayd is only a writer, is exceptionally rare and absent from the Qur’an because exhaustive knowledge of every quality is difficult.

ITQAN (بهاء الدين): He objects that coordination with بل is even less suitable because negation and affirmation do not consistently continue through it. ITQAN (author): A fifth construction is fronting the object, as in إياك نعبد and لإلى الله تحشرون; some scholars disagree that this conveys restriction. | mentions 1:5, 3:158

ITQAN (author): On the alternate vocalization, the verse forbids the claimant from injuring the scribe or witness by burdening them improperly or compelling them to act. ITQAN (author): A word shared between two literal senses, or literal and figurative senses, may carry both; if polysemous use is denied, the wording can be understood as addressed twice with each sense intended.

ALUSI-FULL (author): The verse names people whose outward reliability you approve, rather than implying access to their inward state; God judges the hidden reality. 'Among the witnesses' is a circumstantial phrase, with women included in the masculine plural by convention. ALUSI-FULL (أبو حنيفة): The verse does not address unbelievers testifying among themselves, but Abū Ḥanīfa allows this by analogy even when their religious communities differ.

ALUSI-FULL (author): Al-Alusi says making two women into one figurative male witness requires layered metaphors and still fails to explain the need for a male witness if both women are present. ALUSI-FULL (author): A passive feminine reading of an tadilla is reported, along with the variant فتذاكر.

IBNASHUR-FULL (الربيع): Al-Rabīʿ, Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, and al-Ṭabarī hold that the ban is prohibitive, making acceptance an individual duty; the author endorses this as the sound view. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The author considers it plausible that literate people in the debtor’s locality owe a communal duty, made individual for whichever person the creditor selects to secure the debt.

IBNASHUR-FULL (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): In the Khaybar killing report, the Prophet asked the Ansar for proof, then proposed that the Jews swear fifty oaths; the Ansar feared they would kill them and swear, so he paid the blood-money from charity funds. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The author takes the report as confirming the Ansar’s claim that the Jews would not hesitate to kill them all and swear falsely.

IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Two witnesses are the stipulated number for financial transactions. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The incomplete kāna avoids implying that women count only when two men are impossible, contrary to the majority; it also brings women into public affairs after their exclusion in pre-Islamic practice.

IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Ḥāḍirah means immediate, without delay; ḥāḍir, ʿājil, and nājiz are synonyms, as are debt, term, and deferred payment. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Al-Zamakhsharī treats tudīrūnahā as an explanation of trade, like the poet’s explanation of two needs by asking how they can meet; it may also be a second descriptive phrase.

QIRAAT-ER (author): Reading in as a conditional yields if one of them errs; an instead makes the phrase purposive, so that or lest one errs. Both are canonical. QIRAAT-ER (author): Form IV tudhkira is a simpler causative than Form II tudhakkira; both are canonical readings with related causative senses.
FARRA (author): In وإن كان ذو عسرة, nominative ذو is possible; ʿAbd Allāh and Ubayy instead read accusative ذا, implying an omitted subject of كان.
MAJAZ (author): فسوق means sin in this context.
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB (الآخر): An unnamed interpreter says each woman is made equivalent to a male, so the two together stand for one man and one reminds the other.

TAB-FULL (ابن عباس): A report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās assigns five modes to the ʿajuz of Hawāzin and two to Quraysh and Khuzāʿa, but al-Ṭabarī rejects its chains as proof: al-Kalbī/Abū Ṣāliḥ and Qatāda, who never met Ibn ʿAbbās.
TAB-FULL (الحسن): Al-Ḥasan says witnessing protects one's claim, but omitting it is not blameworthy.
TAB-FULL (عطاء): ʿAṭāʾ says the writer and witness should deliver the knowledge they hold.
TAB-FULL (الضحاك): He describes these rules as instruction from God that people should follow.
TAB-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas again identifies the setting as forward purchase of wheat, with its measure and date specified.
TAB-FULL (مجاهد): Mujāhid says it is obligatory for a scribe to write when asked.

TAB-FULL (author): Al-Ṭabarī also rejects treating the commands to write and not refuse as mere guidance without evidence, challenging that standard's inconsistent application to other divine commands.
TAB-FULL (الربيع): Al-Rabīʿ identifies the person who dictates for the debtor as the creditor entitled to the right.

TAB-FULL (author): Al-Ṭabarī says that even if Ibn ʿUyaynah meant strengthening the forgetful woman's recall, that approaches his own interpretation, but no one reports that reading-based explanation and the light reading remains unsupported.
ZAJJAJ (author): The author says he does not understand why advancing the conditional should require فتح on أن.
IBNABIHATIM (سعيد بن جبير): To dictate means to state what is owed.
IBNABIHATIM (مجاهد): Mujahid says responding to a summons to testify is obligatory, while al-Shaʿbi says it is optional until one has testified.
IBNABIHATIM (سعيد بن جبير): They are warned to fear God and not disobey Him in these matters.
NAHHAS (author): An anonymous verse says that a fool rushes toward what he is forbidden, apparently continuing the preceding discussion of harm and wrongdoing.

FARISI-HUJJA (author): A predicate-taking كان may be omitted because its mention is recoverable from earlier wording; an existential كان is also possible and is simpler because it requires only one omitted element.
FARISI-HUJJA (أحمد بن يحيى): Ahmad ibn Yahya records الواحد، الوحد، and الأحد as synonymous forms.
FARISI-HUJJA (author): كان can mean an event occurred, can be a temporal auxiliary with an accusative predicate, can mean became, or can be redundant without adding meaning. | mentions 19:29
THALABI (author): Alternatively, the repeated word emphasizes the point, like saying a bird flies with its wings or all the angels prostrated. | mentions 6:38, 15:30
THALABI (الفراء): Al-Farra chooses the discretionary reading, comparing the writing command to commands to hunt after ihram and disperse after Friday prayer. | mentions 5:2, 62:10
THALABI (آخرون): On the passive reading, the parties must not harass a busy writer or witness; if they are occupied, the requester should find someone else.
MAWARDI-FULL (مجاهد): The command for a scribe to write is a recommendation.
QUSHAYRI (author): Religious legislation shows gentleness toward people in need by allowing borrowing to meet an immediate need while awaiting God's future provision; lending also earns great reward.
WAHIDI-BASIT (المفسرون): The exegetes say every right whose due date is deferred is covered by this verse.

WAHIDI-BASIT (ابن الأنباري): Ibn al-Anbārī agrees that the command is nonbinding because most scholars hold this and obligatory documentation would impose severe hardship; the Prophet described his mission as easy and tolerant.
WAHIDI-BASIT (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās glosses the phrase as what God enabled the person to understand and says one known to write should not refuse the good deed.
WAHIDI-BASIT (أبو علي): Abū ʿAlī says iḥdā is a feminine form of wāḥid that is used only in an annexed phrase, not by itself.

WAHIDI-BASIT (سيبويه): By analogy with 5:95, Sibawayh posits a deleted subject after the apodosis fāʾ, meaning in the matter that one woman reminds the other; the condition and answer modify the indefinite two women. | mentions 5:95
WAHIDI-BASIT (author): The command to witness transactions was discussed at the beginning of the verse.
DAMGHANI (author): Ḥāḍirah means a current, immediate transaction conducted between the parties.
DAMGHANI (author): Ḥaqq can mean money or a financial debt owed by one party to another.
DAMGHANI (الأعرابي): A Bedouin used the phrase دعاك الله to mean that God punished you; this is a detached lexical fragment in the segment.
DAMGHANI (author): Kabīr can mean much or numerous, paired with ṣaghīr for little; examples concern recording debts and spending. | mentions 9:121

JISHUMI (أبو يوسف): In an anecdote before al-Muʿtadid's vizier, judge Abu Hazim cites Abu Yusuf's definition of integrity: avoid major sins and persistence in minor ones, show more concealment than scandal and more correctness than error, display muruʾa, and restrain from lying through piety or honor.
BAGHAWI-FULL (سفيان الثوري وأصحاب الرأي): One group permits women with men in nonfinancial matters except criminal penalties.
BAGHAWI-FULL (الشعبي): A witness may choose whether to testify until he has formally borne witness.

BAGHAWI-FULL (ابن كثير وأهل البصرة): They read fa-tadhakkara lightly; the other readers read it with gemination. Dhakara and adhkara are synonymous, transitive forms connected with memory opposite to forgetting.
KASHSHAF-FULL (author): The debt may be owed by or to the person, as bāyaʿtuhu can mean selling to or buying from him.
KASHSHAF-FULL (ابن أبي عبلة): Ibn Abī ʿAbla reads athima qalbuhu, meaning he made his heart sinful.
IBNATIYYA-FULL (سعيد بن المسيب): Saʿid says he heard that the debt verse was the latest Quranic text at the Throne.
IBNATIYYA-FULL (مالك): Mālik says only someone knowledgeable about documents, personally upright and trusted, should write them, citing the command to write justly.
IBNATIYYA-FULL (ابن كثير وأبو عمرو): Their light pronunciation of the kaf has the same sense as the doubled form, from the root meaning remembrance.

IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): An is accusative as a disconnected exception. “You turn it over between yourselves” implies possession transfers; land, houses, and much livestock cannot be handed over cleanly in the same way, so debt-like documentation suits them.
IBNATIYYA-FULL (أبو عبد الرحمن السلمي): He reads yasʾamū, yaktubū, and yartābū with yāʾ throughout, reporting the absent parties’ speech.
TABRISI (سيبويه): A third analysis supplies an omitted predicate for the subject فرجل وامرأتان, understood as فرجل وامرأتان يشهدون. | mentions 5:95
TABRISI (author): The opening continues the previous direction to defer an insolvent debtor by explaining rules for deferred claims and debt transactions.
TABRISI (author): The command is emphasized because scribes were scarce in the Prophet's time; combining a command with a prohibition against neglect makes compliance more likely.
TABRISI (سفيان بن عيينة): Sufyān b. ʿUyayna reads the doubled form as making one woman equivalent to a man; al-Ṭabrisī says the memory-based reading is stronger.
TABRISI (ابن مسعود ومجاهد): With fatḥ on the first rāʾ, the prohibition tells people not to impose writing on a busy scribe or summon a witness when excused, or to mistreat either.
IBNJAWZI-NUZHA (author): In Arabic, bayʿ may also mean buying; the cited line says to buy a cloak for a shepherd.
IBNJAWZI-NUZHA (author): Al-marʾa means an adult female descendant of Adam; al-marʾ means a man.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD (author): Al-ʿadl means what is right; Qatada says to omit no rightful due and add nothing false.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD (author): Al-ʿadl means fairness or equity.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD (قتادة): Qatada says the verse followed an incident where a man called around a large tented gathering for witnesses and no one came.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD (author): “If you do so” refers to committing this harm.
RAZI-FULL (author): The verse repeats the writing instruction after commanding it earlier as reinforcement of the documentation rule.
RAZI-FULL (author): A variant reading has ياء in both instances of ولا.
RAZI-FULL (author): The exception is justified by the frequency of everyday cash exchanges and the absence of denial risk when both parties exchange their due in the same sitting.
RAZI-FULL (author): فسوق بكم may refer specifically to committing the prohibited harm, or generally to doing anything forbidden or omitting any commanded duty.
RAZI-FULL (author): A further interpretation makes the duty conditional: whoever writes must follow God’s taught rules and preserve every safeguard for the parties.
QURTUBI-FULL (ابن عباس): He transmits the Prophet's instruction that a witness should testify only to what is as clear as seeing the sun, establishing direct certainty rather than inference.

QURTUBI-FULL (الجمهور): The one-man-and-two-women arrangement applies to financial matters and requires a man, since financial transactions are common and have multiple safeguards: writing, witnesses, collateral, and guarantees.
QURTUBI-FULL (أبو عمرو): Abū ʿAmr calls the report's chain the soundest and its transmitters trustworthy, citing Muslim and other critics.
QURTUBI-FULL (author): Reports of the Prophet's judgments and earlier prophets support accepting reliable signs and indications as evidence.

QURTUBI-FULL (author): Immediate reciprocal possession reduces disputes, while real estate and animals are less readily transferred or hidden; deferred transactions need written safeguards against changed circumstances and distrust.
QURTUBI-FULL (author): Al-Qurṭubī notes that the obligation was attributed to several authorities besides al-Ḍaḥḥāk, correcting Ibn al-ʿArabī's account.

QURTUBI-FULL (author): Later rules for different situations do not abrogate earlier rules; some note both clauses may have been revealed together, since abrogation cannot occur simultaneously. | mentions 5:6, 4:92, 58:4

QURTUBI-FULL (عمارة بن خزيمة): ʿUmāra ibn Khuzayma reports that his Companion uncle witnessed the Prophet's purchase of a horse from a Bedouin, and Khuzayma ibn Thābit testified from trust in the Prophet.
QURTUBI-FULL (author): The promise that piety gives believers discernment is linked to the verse promising a criterion by which to distinguish right from wrong. | mentions 8:29
QURTUBI-FULL (الكوفيون والثوري): They require the delivery location for goods involving transport and invalidate salam if it is omitted; al-Awzāʿī calls omission disliked.
QURTUBI-FULL (author): Writing with justice means accurately recording the claim without adding or subtracting anything.
BAYDAWI-FULL (ابن كثير وأبو عمرو ويعقوب): Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, and Yaqub read fa-tudhakkira from the form ifkār, to remind.
BAYDAWI-FULL (author): The second command to write may emphasize the ban on refusal, or the prohibition may be general while the command specifies the form.
NASAFI-FULL (author): Tadāyantum means dealing with one another by debt, whether one lends or borrows.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Writing acts as a substitute for the tongue, just as the tongue conveys what is in the heart.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Writing justly means truthfully and impartially, without favoring either side in the scribe's mind or pen.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): “If the two are not men” may mean the creditor failed or chose not to obtain two men; another view requires that two men be unavailable before two women may be called.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL (أبو يوسف): Abū Yūsuf accepts a person whose good conduct outweighs minor sins and who avoids major offenses; he excludes gamblers, habitual prayer neglecters, notorious liars, and those who insult the Companions or neighbors, among other conduct.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الليث، الأوزاعي، الحسن بن حيي، الثوري، مالك): Their positions differ on wills, emancipation, marriage, divorce, penalties, retaliation, agency, and lineage: al-Layth allows wills and emancipation; al-Awzāʿī bars marriage; al-Ḥasan b. Ḥayy bars penalties; al-Thawrī bars only penalties; Mālik excludes penalties and personal-status matters.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Muruwwa means restraint, dignified bearing, respect for social obligations, and avoiding vulgarity and frivolity, not fine clothing, mounts, tools, or appearance.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): On the conditional reading, the clause may describe the two women as an adjective, though its placement after the earlier descriptor raises a syntactic concern.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Either woman may forget and either may remind, so “one of them” is generic; the ordinary parse makes the other woman the one reminded, though object-first order is possible.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL (لبيد): Labīd's line about tiring of life witnesses the construction saʾima min.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL (السلمي): Al-Sulamī reads “they should not tire” and “they should write”; the plural likely refers to witnesses, but may shift to parties or scribes.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الحسن وجماعة، ابن العربي): They treat the command as recommendation and guidance, not compulsion; Ibn al-ʿArabī identifies this as the majority position.
SAMIN-DURR (الشيخ): The Shaykh says Sibawayh did not explicitly state that comparatives derive from quadrilaterals; this is inferred from his rules for the exclamative form.
SAMIN-DURR (الفارسي): Al-Farisi also rules out ‘the right’ as kāna’s subject because it is a debt, so an omitted subject must be supplied.
SAMIN-DURR (ابن عطية): كما may attach to لا يأب causally: since God favored him with literacy, he should not refuse but write generously; the Sheikh calls this unlikely.
SAMIN-DURR (author): It may be apposition to من رجالكم with the preposition repeated; the Sheikh objects that apposition would still restrict the phrase to the men.
IBNKATHIR-FULL (محمد بن سيرين): Ibn Sīrīn conjectures that the group delayed disputed material so they could identify who had most recently heard the final presentation and write accordingly.

IBNKATHIR-FULL (أبو هريرة): Abū Hurayra reports the Prophet’s parallel saying: one taught the Qurʾan recites it night and day, and one given wealth spends it for the right; neighbors wish they could do likewise.

IBNKATHIR-FULL (أبو هريرة): A Prophetic story tells of an Israelite borrower who could find no ship to repay a thousand dinars, placed the money and a note in a sealed log, and entrusted it to the sea after invoking God as witness and guarantor; the lender found it, and the borrower later came with repayment too.
IBNKATHIR-FULL (author): Ibn Kathir says witnessing remains the prudent safeguard.
IBNKATHIR-FULL (author): Disobeying these directions and doing what was forbidden is an abiding sin from which people cannot escape.
BURHAN (ابن الأنباري): Ibn al-Anbari rebuts Ibn Qutayba's claim that no word has multiple readings by listing forms such as ʿabada al-taghut, yartaʿ wa-yalʿab, baʿid, and bāʾis.
BURHAN (الطرطوشي): Al-Tartushi offers a poem that incorporates Qur'anic expressions, as another example of literary quotation.
BURHAN (بعضهم): An objection says يكونا already refers to the two male witnesses, since شهيدين was restricted to men, making the wording appear to say “if the two men are not men.”
BURHAN (author): Intensive forms such as faʿʿāl, faʿīl, and faʿlān express more than the ordinary active participle and can count as a form of concision.
BURHAN (author): The third kind negates the object or related term while leaving the subject and predicate intact, as in I struck Amr, not Zayd.
BURHAN (author): The author explains that whenever God gives beneficial knowledge, piety accompanies it accordingly.
BURHAN (author): When context supplies the comparison, an elative used predicatively often omits the less-preferred object of comparison.
BURHAN (الكوفيون): The Kufans analyze أن in the witness verse as conditional; the following ف is their evidence for that reading.
BURHAN (الزمخشري): Al-Zamakhshari assigns fa with adjectives three functions: ordering events in time, ranking by degree, or ordering the qualities of the things described.

NASHR (author): Two Bazzī-related readings, known through Ibn Badahan alone from al-Zaynabi, were absent from the other authorities’ routes; al-Dani included them by textual analogy, and al-Shatibi followed, while this author includes them because they appear in the Taysir and Shatibiyya and fit the Bazzī rule.
BIQAI-FULL (أبو الحسن الحرالي): Al-Harali analogizes the two debt witnesses to reflection on visible signs and consideration of heard signs.
BIQAI-FULL (أبو الحسن الحرالي): Al-Harali divides the surah into three parts, each with a foundation and warning at its close, while the final part receives added emphasis as the completion.
DURR-FULL (سعيد بن المسيب): Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib says it reached him that the debt verse was the last Qur'anic verse with the Throne.
DURR-FULL (إبراهيم): Ibrahim says to have witnesses when selling or buying, even for a small bundle of greens.

ITQAN (محققي أهل السنة): Quranic content, location, and order must all be transmitted mutawatir; the central miracle and ordinary conditions make detailed mass transmission inevitable, so isolated reports cannot establish Quran.
ITQAN (ابن الجزري): Ibn al-Jazari credits Abu al-Fadl al-Razi as the first to identify pause-muraqaba, borrowing the notion from prosodic meter.

ITQAN (ابن عبد البر): Ibn Abd al-Barr says the claim that the Quran descended in Quraysh speech means it was predominantly so, since non-Quraysh features occur in readings, including hamza pronunciation that Quraysh lacks.

ITQAN (author): An unqualified expression denotes a thing without restriction; restrict it when evidence does so, but otherwise leave both absolute and qualified wording as stated, following ordinary Arabic usage.
ITQAN (author): The debt verse is hopeful because God guides people in worldly interests down to writing out debts, large or small, showing His great care and grounds for hoping in His forgiveness.

BURSEVI (author): The first of three lessons concerns God’s relation to servants: His care in worldly dealings prevents loss and dispute and indicates that religious duties likewise express mercy and bring His blessings. | mentions 5:6
BURSEVI (author): A Persian poem compares the unseen to a decorated palace and desire to a cloud of dust: abandoning desire removes the screen and enables sight of the desired reality.
ALUSI-FULL (قيل): A further view says the indefinite debt denotes debt generally and allows its division into current and deferred kinds; without the word, one might think debt is always deferred.

ALUSI-FULL (author): On another parsing, the command requires writing in the taught, just manner after forbidding refusal of writing generally; this is not a repetition. Al-Alusi rejects the claim that repetition must follow, calling the distinction arbitrary when unrestricted and restricted commands concern one event.

ALUSI-FULL (author): The construction with an means reminder is so strongly desired that the normally unwanted lapse appears to be sought as its means; this is better than calling lapse a metonym for reminder.

ALUSI-FULL (author): The clauses differ as exhortation, promise, and declaration, which explains their connective pattern; treating the middle clause as a circumstantial clause is possible but less preferred.
ELMALILI (author): Some read the command to keep writing as an explanation and emphasis of the earlier command, directed to scribes; the author finds the broader contextual reading more fitting.
IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The verse supports the majority’s acceptance of written handwriting as evidence, since commissioning a scribe only helps if his handwriting can later be read.
IBNASHUR-FULL (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): The author connects the duty of truthful writing with the Prophet’s instruction to consult one’s own conscience even when people give contrary advice.
IBNASHUR-FULL (ابن الحاجب): Ibn al-Ḥājib proposes that Arabic places the cause of a cause first and joins the actual cause with fa, a rule he presents as characteristic of the language.
IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The ban on refusing witnesses follows the command to the parties to seek them and ensures that the person asked will agree to attend.
IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Ṣaghīran aw kabīran is parsed either as a circumstantial accusative describing the debt or as a phrase with kāna and its subject omitted.

IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The verse grounds procedural protections: avoid distant travel and destabilizing questioning after long delays; public funds should cover witnesses’ travel, lodging, and resulting family losses to support justice.
IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Repeating the divine name across three clauses gives each independent force, so hearing one without another still conveys its point; it also creates awe.
QIRAAT-ER (author): The indicative ending presents her reminding as an independent fact; the subjunctive makes it a purpose or result. Both are canonical.

positions.position: The sale imagery can symbolize God's covenant with believers.
positions.reasons: BURSEVI (author): God’s covenant with believers is a purchase of their lives and property for Paradise, witnessed by the angels; the written contract records a jewel from Paradise deposited as the Black Stone.

turns_on: The notes offer different readings, referents, grounds, or applications.
